sections.title: _intro
lines: This page is for adult patients. For pediatric patients, see: undifferentiated shock

sections.title: Overview
lines: - Goal to increase the flow of oxygenated blood to the tissues
- MAP<50 in dog studies brain will become ischemic and patients might presents as an altered mental status

sections.title: Undifferentiated Hypotension Algorithm
lines: - Too slow or too fast (to the point where CO is affected)?
- If so, HR is likely primary etiology of hypotension
- What is the LV end-diastolic volume?
- Approximated by the IVC diameter or CVP
- Assess for blood loss versus fluid loss
- Treat with IVF and/or pRBCs depending on cause
- Is the myocardium severely depressed in its contractile function (cardiogenic shock)?
- Treated based on likely etiology of distributive shock (see below)

sections.title: Shock
lines: - Drug toxicity (e.g. beta blocker, CCB, or bupropion OD)

sections.title: Shock index (SI)
lines: - Used when HR and SBP do not predict severity of hypovolemia in early stages
- May be used as secondary triage tool in mass casualty incidents
- >0.70-0.75 for occult shock or requirement of life-saving intervention
Simple Shock Index (sSI) was recently proposed. Subtracting SBP from HR is a good SI substitute. Working with integers is easier than dividing them, improving value availability.

sections.title: Vasopressors
lines: Vasopressors may be initiated peripherally while central access is being obtained — do not delay for central line placement (SSC 2021).

Norepinephrine 2-5 mcg/min (0.01-0.03 mcg/kg/min), max 0.5-1 mcg/kg/min IV drip — 1st line for septic shock (SSC 2021) Epinephrine 1-10 mcg/min (0.01-0.1 mcg/kg/min), max 0.5 mcg/kg/min IV drip — 1st line for anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest Vasopressin 0.03 U/min (fixed dose), max 0.04 U/min IV drip — Add to NE rather than escalating NE (SSC 2021) Dopamine 2-5 mcg/kg/min, max 20 mcg/kg/min IV drip — SSC 2021 suggests against as 1st line; more arrhythmogenic than NE Dobutamine 2-5 mcg/kg/min, max 20 mcg/kg/min IV drip — Inotrope, not a vasopressor; use with vasopressor if hypotensive Phenylephrine 100-180 mcg/min, then 40-60 mcg/min IV drip — Pure alpha-1 agonist; short duration 5-20 min Milrinone 0.375-0.75 mcg/kg/min (loading often omitted) IV drip — Inodilator; causes hypotension; useful in RV failure/pulmonary HTN Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV bolus over 15 min IV — Salvage for refractory vasodilatory shock; contraindicated in G6PD deficiency Angiotensin II (Giapreza) 20 ng/kg/min, max 40-80 ng/kg/min IV drip — Salvage for refractory vasodilatory shock (ATHOS-3 trial)

sections.title: Causes of non-response to vasopressors
lines: - Tx: treat underlying cause, consider bicarbonate gtt
- Dx: Clinical, cortisol level, hyperkalemia + hyponatremia
- Tx: Calcium chloride or calcium gluconate
- Dx: Clinical (consider GI bleed and retroperitoneal hematoma)
- Tx: Transfusion, treat coagulopathy, surgery/IR interventions
- Dx: Clinical (consider beta blocker toxicity, calcium channel blocker toxicity, TCA overdose, etc)
- Tx: Depends on etiology (glucagon, hyperinsulin euglycemia therapy, sodium bicarbonate, ECMO, etc)

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - All patients with shock require ICU admission
- Early identification and treatment of reversible causes is critical
- Reassess frequently for response to interventions
- Consider transfer to higher level of care if cause cannot be identified or adequately treated

sections.title: _intro
lines: This page is for adult patients. For pediatric patients, see: congestive heart failure (peds)

sections.title: Background
lines: - Assume valvular problem in new-onset CHF
- Assume valve thrombosis in CHF with a prosthetic valve
- Do not give vasodilators in aortic stenosis, HOCM; yes in mitral regurgitation

sections.title: Classification
lines: - Systolic: poor contraction (↓EF) and decreased forward flow
- Diastolic: good contraction (normal EF) but stiff ventricles and poor filling
- Left-sided: LV failure, poor organ perfusion, dyspnea from backup in lung
- Most common cause is left-sided failure

sections.title: NYHA Classes
lines: - Severely limits activity or symptoms with minimal activity

sections.title: History & Physical Examination
lines: - shortness of breath, pulmonary edema, narrow pulse pressure, signs of poor end-organ perfusion, altered mental status, cool peripheries, decreased urine output, increased HR, sBP < 90 mmHg
- Weight gain, peripheral edema, less shortness of breath, +/- rales
- sBP > 140 mmHg, preserved LV function, marked shortness of breath, minimal weight gain, rales, increased HR, pulmonary edema on CXR
- Severe respiratory distress, relative hypertension, cool dipahoretic skin, +/- rales, JVD (94% specific, 39% sensitive), +/- peripheral edema, S3 (99% specific)

sections.title: Causes of CHF Decompensation
lines: - Acute hypoxia or other respiratory problems

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: - Bedside to assess global function, B lines, assessment of IVC

sections.title: Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP)
lines: - <100 pg/mL: Negative for acute CHF (Sn 90%, NPV 89%)
- 100-500 pg/mL: Indeterminate (Consider differential diagnosis and pre-test probability)
- >500 pg/mL: Positive for acute CHF (Sp 87%, PPV 90%)
- Combination of BNP with clinician judgment 94% sensitive 70% specific (compared to 49% sn and 96% spec clinical judgement alone)

sections.title: Lung ultrasound of pulmonary edema
lines: - Predominance of A lines has 90% sensitivity, 67% specificity for pulmonary artery wedge pressure <= 13mm Hg
- A line predominance suggests that intravenous fluids may be safely given without concern for pulmonary edema
- White lines from the pleura to the bottom of the screen
- Highly sensitive for pulmonary edema, but can be present at low wedge pressures

sections.title: Acute Pulmonary Edema and Hypertensive Heart Failure
lines: See Pulmonary Edema or Sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary edema (SCAPE)

sections.title: Hypotensive Heart Failure
lines: - Consider in severe LV dysfunction and low output syndrome
- Diminished peripheral perfusion and end organ damage
- Vasodilatory treatment inadequate response or limited by symptomatic hypotension
- Must have obvious evidence of elevated filling pressures
- Inotropes are not indicated in setting of preserved systolic function

sections.title: Heart Failure Without Pulmonary Edema
lines: - Do not use with sildenafil, severe AS, or if right-sided MI
- Start sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4mg delivered over 4 min = 0.10mg/min
- If no improvement IV nitroglycerin drip, start 0.3-0.5mcg/kg/min, but may increase to 3-5mcg/kg/min
- Consider nitroprusside 0.3 mcg/kg/min if hypertension or nitroglycerin ineffective
- Hold if no symptoms of fluid overload
- Give double home dose, or up to 2.5x dose.
- If lasix 40mg po QD, then lasix 40-100mg IV
- Increases intrathoracic pressure and thus reduces preload
- Enalaprilat at 0.004mg/kg as IVB or 1mg drip over 2hr
- Digoxin and Amiodarone are the only medications indicated for use in decompensated HF for rate control if needed
- Evidence suggests that treating rate in acutely ill patients including CHF leads to worse outcomes
- Compensated HF (not acutely symptomatic from failure)
- May benefit from a fib rate control, but calcium-channel blockers and beta-blockers first line, goal of < 85 bpm per RACE II trial
- AVOID in severe heart failure, preexcitation syndrome
- Metoprolol 2.5 - 5.0mg over 2 min, then q5 as needed to max of 15mg
- Esmolol 0.5mg/kg bolus over 1 min, then 50 mcg/kg/min, may increase q30 min by 50 mcg/kg/min

sections.title: Medications to Avoid
lines: - Anti-dysrhythmics other than digoxin and amiodarone
- NSAIDs - sodium retention, worsen toxicity of diuretics and ACE-I
- Morphine - chart reviews show increased morbidity in ADHF patients

sections.title: Admission Criteria
lines: CCORT - Emergent Heart Failure Mortality Risk Grade Calculator
- 7 day mortality risk score calculator for patients presenting to the ED with decompensated HF

sections.title: CHF Drug Target Doses
lines: - Carvedilol 3.125mg BID start; 25mg BID goal (50mg BID goal if weight > 85 kg)
- Metoprolol ER 12.5mg QD start; 190mg QD goal
- Hydralazine/isosorbid dinitrate 10-20mg (1 tab) tid start; 100-80mg (5 tabs) goal for black patients with NYHA III-IV already on BB and ACEi
- Spironolactone 25mg QD start; 50mg QD goal for indications:
- LVEF < 40% post-MI, goal ACE-I, symptomatic CHF, or DM

Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL q5min x3; or IV drip start 10-20 mcg/min, titrate to BP (keep >95) SL/IV drip — Avoid with sildenafil, severe AS, or right-sided MI Nitroprusside 0.3 mcg/kg/min IV drip IV drip Furosemide (Lasix) Double home dose IV or up to 2.5x dose (e.g., if 40 mg PO daily → 40-100 mg IV) IV Enalaprilat 0.004 mg/kg IV bolus or 1 mg IV drip over 2 hours IV — Avoid in pregnancy, hyperkalemia, angioedema Dobutamine 2-20 mcg/kg/min IV drip IV drip — For severe LV dysfunction with low output and elevated filling pressures Milrinone 0.375-0.75 mcg/kg/min IV drip IV drip — Use if patient on beta-blockers

items: Acute hypoxia or other respiratory problems

sections.title: Background
lines: - Also known as "sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary edema" (SCAPE)
- Different from acute CHF exacerbation or hypotensive cardiogenic shock, which do not have sympathetic overdrive
- Patients can decompensate rapidly, so rapid intervention required
- Patients are generally more fluid depleted despite "wet" lungs, so do not give diuretics
- Usually history of poorly controlled hypertension
- Acute afterload increase causes pulmonary edema and poor peripheral perfusion
- Sympathetic surge occurs as a result of decreased systemic perfusion
- Afterload further increases and patient rapidly decompensates

sections.title: Pulmonary Edema Types
lines: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure <18 mmHg differentiates noncardiogenic from cardiogenic pulmonary edema

sections.title: Workup
lines: - CXR - signs of pulmonary congestion may not show for hours after acute flash pulmonary edema, so normal CXR is frequently seen
- Bedside to assess global function, B lines, assessment of IVC
- Consider arterial line monitoring for titration of NTG

sections.title: Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP)
lines: - <100 pg/mL: Negative for acute CHF (Sn 90%, NPV 89%)
- 100-500 pg/mL: Indeterminate (Consider differential diagnosis and pre-test probability)
- >500 pg/mL: Positive for acute CHF (Sp 87%, PPV 90%)
- Combination of BNP with clinician judgment 94% sensitive 70% specific (compared to 49% sn and 96% spec clinical judgement alone)

sections.title: Lung ultrasound of pulmonary edema
lines: - Predominance of A lines has 90% sensitivity, 67% specificity for pulmonary artery wedge pressure <= 13mm Hg
- A line predominance suggests that intravenous fluids may be safely given without concern for pulmonary edema
- White lines from the pleura to the bottom of the screen
- Highly sensitive for pulmonary edema, but can be present at low wedge pressures

sections.title: Management
lines: Vasodilate arterial side, while maintaining oxygenation
- High dose nitroglycerin over 2 min (at these doses, nitroglycerin has vasodilation > venodilation)
- Goal BP at the patient's norm
- Load 800 mcg over 2 min (may start at 100 mcg/min, then titrate rapidly to 400 mcg/min for 2 min)
- Then start maintenance at 100 mcg/min, titrate up as needed
- NOTE: it takes time to set up nitroglycerin drip, so consider SL nitroglycerin in interim
- 0.4mg tab during 5 min = ~80 mcg/min (2 tabs = ~160 mcg/min, etc.)
- Difficult to titrate if giving more than 1-2 tabs
- Patients are likely more dehydrated that overloaded but should be recurrently volume assessed
- Consider captopril 12.5 - 25mg SL for continuation of afterload reduction
- Wean CPAP after sustained BP at patient's baseline
- Wean PEEP down 2 cm H2O q10 min

sections.title: Other Interventions
lines: - Targets kidneys which are poorly perfused in BOTH hypotension and catecholamine surge
- Consider waiting until BiPAP and nitroglycerin control hypertension first
- Nitroprusside, alternative when insufficient response to NTG
- Start 0.5 mcg/kg/min, titrate to blood pressure
- Cyanide toxicity risk increases proportionately with infusion rate as well as length of time
- If intubation required, consider delayed sequence intubation

sections.title: Medication Dosing
lines: Nitroglycerin 800mcg IV load over 2 min, then 100mcg/min maintenance (titrate up PRN) IV — Goal BP at patient's norm; at high doses, vasodilation > venodilation Nitroglycerin 0.4mg SL q5min while setting up IV drip SL

sections.title: _intro
lines: See Acute coronary syndrome (main) for ACS-specific workup and risk stratification; see Chest pain (peds) for pediatric patients.

sections.title: Background
lines: - Chest pain accounts for approximately 6-8% of all ED visits
- The primary ED goal is to rapidly identify and treat immediately life-threatening causes ("the big 5"):
- Most chest pain in the ED is ultimately non-cardiac, but the evaluation is driven by the need to exclude dangerous etiologies

sections.title: Risk of Acute Coronary Syndrome
lines: Clinical factors that increase likelihood of ACS/AMI:
- Chest pain radiating to both arms > R arm > L arm
- Chest pain associated with nausea OR vomiting
- Chest pain with exertion that is improved with rest
Clinical factors that decrease likelihood of ACS/AMI:
- Less likely to be treated with guideline-directed medical therapies
- Less likely to undergo cardiac catheterization
- Less likely to receive timely reperfusion therapy
- More likely to report fatigue, dyspnea, indigestion, nausea or vomiting, palpitations, or weakness, although some studies have found fewer differences in presentation
- More likely to report central chest pain
- Quality: crushing/pressure (ACS), tearing/ripping (dissection), pleuritic/sharp (PE, pericarditis, pneumothorax)
- Onset: sudden (PE, dissection, pneumothorax) vs gradual (ACS, musculoskeletal)
- Associated symptoms: diaphoresis, dyspnea, nausea/vomiting, syncope
- Risk factors: cardiac history, DVT/PE risk factors, cocaine use, connective tissue disease, recent procedure
- New ECG changes (ST elevation/depression, new LBBB)
- Unequal blood pressures or pulses (aortic dissection)
- Tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds (tension pneumothorax)

sections.title: Workup
lines: - ECG - within 10 minutes of arrival; repeat if symptoms change or initially nondiagnostic
- Vital signs including bilateral blood pressures if dissection suspected
- Troponin - serial troponins (0h and 1-3h with high-sensitivity assay; 0h and 3-6h with conventional assay)
- D-dimer or CT-PA - if PE suspected (use validated pretest probability tools: Wells score, PERC rule, YEARS algorithm)
- CT angiography of chest/abdomen/pelvis - if aortic dissection suspected
- Point-of-care echo - for pericardial effusion, RV strain, wall motion abnormalities, aortic root dilation

sections.title: Risk Stratification
lines: - HEART Score: Validated tool for risk stratification in undifferentiated chest pain
- Score 0-3: Low risk; consider early discharge
- Score 4-6: Moderate risk; admission/observation with serial troponins
- Score 7-10: High risk; admission with cardiology consultation
- Wells score: For pretest probability of PE
- PERC rule: If low pretest probability, PERC can exclude PE without D-dimer

sections.title: Management
lines: - ACS: ASA, anticoagulation, cardiology consultation; PCI for STEMI (see ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction)
- PE: Anticoagulation; thrombolytics for massive PE (see Pulmonary embolism)
- Aortic dissection: HR and BP control; emergent surgical consultation for Type A (see Nontraumatic thoracic aortic dissection)
- Tension pneumothorax: Needle decompression followed by chest tube
- Pain control: Avoid NSAIDs if ACS suspected; nitroglycerin for ischemic pain (avoid in RV infarct, recent PDE5 inhibitor use, hypotension)

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - STEMI, unstable ACS, hemodynamically significant PE, aortic dissection, pericardial tamponade
- Moderate HEART score with pending serial troponins
- Low HEART score (0-3) with negative serial troponins
- Clear non-cardiac cause identified (e.g., musculoskeletal, GERD)
- PE ruled out with validated approach
- Arrange appropriate follow-up (PCP within 72 hours for intermediate-risk patients)

sections.title: HEART Score
lines: HTN, hypercholesterolemia, DM, obesity (BMI >30), smoking, family hx CVD, or hx atherosclerotic disease

lines: For risk stratification see ACS - Risk Stratification

sections.title: Background
lines: - Refers to a spectrum of conditions compatible with acute myocardial ischemia and/or infarction that are usually due to an abrupt reduction in coronary blood flow.

sections.title: Clinical ACS Categories
lines: - The new title, “Non-ST-Elevation Acute Coronary Syndromes,” emphasizes the continuum between UA and NSTEMI
- NSTEMI myocardium is damaged enough to increase biomarkers, UA is not.

sections.title: MI Types by Causation
lines: - Atherosclerotic plaque rupture or intraluminal thrombus in one or more of the coronary arteries
- Type 2: Myocardial Infarction Secondary to an Ischemic Imbalance
- Condition other than CAD contributes to an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and/or demand (e.g. coronary spasm, embolism, low or high blood pressures, anemia, or arrhythmias)
- Type 3: Cardiac Death Due to Myocardial Infarction
- Sudden cardiac death with symptoms suggestive of myocardial ischaemia without elevated biomarkers
- Type 4: Myocardial Infarction Associated With Revascularization Procedure
- Type 5: Myocardial Infarction Related to CABG Procedure

sections.title: Risk of Acute Coronary Syndrome
lines: Clinical factors that increase likelihood of ACS/AMI:
- Chest pain radiating to both arms > R arm > L arm
- Chest pain associated with nausea OR vomiting
- Chest pain with exertion that is improved with rest
Clinical factors that decrease likelihood of ACS/AMI:
- Less likely to be treated with guideline-directed medical therapies
- Less likely to undergo cardiac catheterization
- Less likely to receive timely reperfusion therapy
- More likely to report fatigue, dyspnea, indigestion, nausea or vomiting, palpitations, or weakness, although some studies have found fewer differences in presentation
- More likely to report central chest pain

sections.title: False (Non-CAD) Positives
lines: - Assume true positive until proven otherwise
- no difference in post-MI troponin-I clearance rate in ESRD vs. normal GFR

sections.title: Workup
lines: - ECG is normal in 8% of all confirmed MI's

sections.title: ACS Anatomical Correlation Chart
lines: Q waves in V1-V3 over time
STD in aVL (most common lead to see reciprocal change)
STE V1 (only lead looking at RV) STE III > II (III more R facing) STE V1 > V2, STE V1 + STD V2
STD in V1, V2, V3; R>S in V1 Tall R waves in V1-V3 (Q waves on back of heart) w/ upright TWs

sections.title: Management
lines: Intensity of treatment should be based on ACS likelihood

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - ACC/AHA rec need for provocative testing withing 72 hrs, consider admitting
- For low risk (HEART) pts, may be better off discharge home with follow up
- Risk of MACE after neg ED work up 1/2422 vs Risk of preventable adverse event in hospital is 1/164

lines: Not to be confused with traumatic aortic transection

sections.title: Background
lines: - Most commonly seen in men 60-80 yrs old
- Intimal tear with blood leaking into media
- Mortality in first 48 hours of acute presentation is high
- Commonly quoted as 1-2% per hour, but this is based on a series from the 1950s
- More recent data suggests mortality for type A dissection is 0.5% per hour when treated medically, and 0.1% per hour when managed surgically
- Connective tissue disease (e.g. Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos, collagen vascular disease)
- Atherosclerotic risk factors (smoking, hypertension, HLD, DM)

sections.title: General
lines: - 64% described the pain as sharp vs 50.6% who described it as tearing or ripping
- Hypertension at time of presentation (49% of all cases)

sections.title: Specific
lines: - Acute aortic regurgitation, leading to a diastolic decrescendo murmur, hypotension, or heart failure, in 50%-66%
- MI/Ischemia on ECG, usually inferior (dissection affects the right coronary artery more often than the left coronary artery)
- Voice hoarseness - recurrent laryngeal nerve compression
- Hypertension at time of presentation (35.7% of all cases)
- Chest pain, back pain, abdominal pain
- Pain abrupt, severe (90% of patients) radiating to back
- Hypertension at time of presentation (70.1% of all cases)

sections.title: Hypertension
lines: - Drug use or overdose (e.g stimulants, especially alcohol, cocaine, or Synthroid)

sections.title: Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score (ADD-RS)
lines: A score 1 should be awarded for each of the 3 categories that contain at least one of the listed features
Chest, back, or abdominal pain described as:
- Focal neurological deficit (in conjunction with pain)
- Murmur of aortic insufficiency (new or not known to be old and in conjunction with pain)

sections.title: No Risk Factor Screening
lines: - Widening of aortic contour (seen in 48%), displaced calcification (6mm), Calcium sign (look for white line of calcium within aortic knob and measure to outer edge of the aortic knob - distance greater than 0.5 cm is positive and > 1 cm is highly suspicious for dissection), aortic kinking, double density sign

sections.title: Low-Intermediate
lines: - D-dimer for ADD-RS ≤ 1 (low or intermediate risk)

sections.title: High Risk/Definitive
lines: - Similar sensitivity/specificity to TEE and MRA
- If CT delayed due to contrast allergy or availability, or patient instability.
- TEE has a sensitivity of 98% and 95% specific

sections.title: Other Findings
lines: - Can help in ruling in patients when AOFT is >4cm
- Rule out pericardial effusion and tamponade, especially in hypotension, syncope, dyspnea

sections.title: Aortic Dissection Classification
lines: - Type A: Involves any portion of ascending aorta
- Type B: Isolated to descending aorta
- Type I: Involves the ascending and descending aorta
- Type II: Involves only the ascending aorta
- Type III: Involves only the descending aorta

sections.title: General Principles
lines: - Control pain to reduce sympathetic stimulation.
- Fentanyl is easily titratable with minimal cardiovascular effects
- Right radial arterial line or right arm blood pressure will generally be the most accurate
- Reducing heart rate while maintaining low-normal blood pressure reduces aortic flow acceleration, thereby reducing shear force on the intimal wall
- Control heart rate before blood pressure
- Beta blockers are good first-line option, since they reduce heart rate and aortic wall tension
- Use β-blockers with caution in severe, acute aortic regurgitation - may worsen shock if dependent on compensatory tachycardia

sections.title: Heart Rate control
lines: - Advantage of short half life, easily titratable
- Bolus 0.5mg/kg over 1min; infuse 0.05mg/kg/min (titrate upward in 0.05mg/kg/min increments to a maximum of 0.3 mg/kg/min)
- Labetalol - has both α and beta effects
- Push dose - 10-20mg with repeat doses of 20-40mg q10min up to 300mg
- Diltiazem - Use if contraindications to beta-blockers
- Loading 0.25mg/kg over 2–5 min, followed by a drip of 5mg/h

sections.title: Blood pressure control (vasodilators)
lines: - 5mg/hr start, then titrate up by 2.5mg/hr every 10 min until goal
- Once at goal, drop to 3mg/hr and re-titrate from there
- Double dose every 90 seconds until approaching goal BP, then increase in smaller amounts every 5-10 minutes until goal achieved.
- Nitroprusside 0.3-0.5mcg/kg/min - Risk of cerebral blood vessel vasodilation and CN/Thiocynate toxicity

sections.title: Surgery
lines: - Type A (any portion of ascending aorta)
- Primarily medical management with surgery consultation

sections.title: Medication Dosing
lines: Esmolol 0.5mg/kg bolus, then 50-200mcg/kg/min infusion IV — Bolus over 1 minute Labetalol 20mg bolus, then 40-80mg q10min (max 300mg) or 1-2mg/min drip IV Diltiazem 0.25mg/kg load over 2-5min, then 5mg/hr infusion IV Nicardipine 5mg/hr, titrate by 2.5mg/hr q10min IV — Once at goal, drop to 3mg/hr and re-titrate Clevidipine 1-2mg/hr, double q90sec until approaching goal IV Nitroprusside 0.3-0.5mcg/kg/min IV — Risk of cerebral vasodilation and cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity

sections.title: Etiology
lines: - Primary cancers of the pericardium are rare but potential causes
- Connective tissue disease or other autoimmune conditions
- Cardiac injury (can see up to weeks later)

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Radiates to chest, back, trapezius ridge (inferior portion of the scapula)
- trapezius ridge muscles innervated by phrenic n. which also traverses pericardium.
- Fever, chills, myalgias (systemic signs with viral infection)

sections.title: ST Elevation
lines: - Previous MI with recurrent ischemia in same area
- RV pacing (appears as Left bundle branch block)
- Drugs of abuse (eg, cocaine, crack, meth)

sections.title: Diagnostic Criteria for Acute Pericarditis
lines: - Chest pain (typically sharp and pleuritic, improved by sitting up and leaning forward)
- Pericardial friction rub (best heard at the LSB, with pt leaning forward at end-expiration)

sections.title: Work-Up
lines: - Consider TSH, ANA based on clinical suspicion
- Troponin elevation may indicate a concurrent myocarditis which predispose to risk of CHF or arrhythmia.
- Typically normal if no pericardial effusion.
- Will not see increase in cardiac silhouette size until > 300mL of pericardial fluid has accumulated
- Bedside Ultrasound to rule out effusion
- ~2/3 of cases will have pericardial effusion
- Can consider CT or cardiac MRI if workup non-diagnostic and clinical suspicion persists

sections.title: Classical Teachings with Caveats Below
lines: - Must differentiate from STEMI (classical teachings are not specific enough to do that)
- However, pericarditis may generate localized ST-elevations
- Pericarditis should never produce ST-depressions (suggestive of reciprocal changes), except in V1 and aVR
- Classically pericardidits has concave upwards STE
- However, STEMI may have concave upwards ST-segment morphology as well
- Rather, it is STE convex upwards or horizontal that favors STEMI
- Classically pericardititis has PR-depression in viral pericarditis (or PR-elevation in AVR)
- Less reliable in post-MI patients and those with baseline ECG abnormalities
- PR-depression is often early and transient in pericarditis
- In STEMI, PR-depression is associated with atrial injury, though usually not as marked as in viral pericarditis
- PR-elevation in aVR may also be present in STEMI and is infrequently seen in constrictive pericarditis

sections.title: Other Findings
lines: - STE II > STE III favors pericarditis
- STE III > STE II very strongly favors STEMI
- STD not in aVR or V1 (reciprocol changes) suggestive of STEMI
- May see low voltage/alternans if effusion present
- If early repolarization confounding interpretation check ST:T ratio
- If (STE)/(T height) in V6 or I > 0.25, then it is likely pericarditis
- If predominantly inferior STE, ST-depression in aVL is sensitive for STEMI
- Spodick's sign- Downsloping of the TP segment; often best seen in lead II and lateral precordial leads
- Suggestive but not diagnostic for acute pericarditis
- TWI don't invert in pericarditis until STE resolved; if TWI and STE simultaneously present, more likely ACS/MI

sections.title: Stages of Progression
lines: - Global concave up ST elevation in all leads (especially V4-6, I, II) except aVR, V1 and III
- PTa depression (depression between the end of the P-wave and the beginning of the QRS- complex)
- T wave flattening progressing to inversion

sections.title: Initial Treatment
lines: - NSAIDS or Aspirin: first line treatment (in absence of contraindications) for viral or idiopathic pericarditis.
- Aspirin 650mg every 6 hours for 7 to 10 days, followed by tapering during a period of 3 to 4 weeks OR
- Ibuprofen 600mg every 8 hours for 7 to 10 days, followed by tapering during a period of 3 to 4 weeks
- Colchicine add to NSAIDs as first line treatment for viral/idiopathic acute and recurrent pericarditis to improve remission rates and prevent recurrence.

- Glucocorticoid therapy second line agent for viral/idiopathic pericarditis, can consider low-moderate doses for patients with contraindications to NSAIDs or persistent symptoms despite appropriate therapy with NSAIDs + colchicine for at least 1 week. Also used for etiologies that are steroid responsive diseases.
- Prednisone 0.2 to 0.5mg/kg of body weight per day for 2 weeks with gradual tapering

sections.title: Recurrent or Refractory
lines: For recurrent or refractory cases consider colchicine and or steroids although literature suggests it can be used as first line
- If patients develop serious diarrhea decrease their dosing to the next weight class or stop treatment.

sections.title: Contraindications to Colchicine
lines: - Liver disease or aminotransferase levels ≥1.5x upper limits of normal
- Myopathy or CK > upper limits of normal

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Hospitalization is not necessary in most cases
- Patients likely to have a specific cause (i.e. uremia, malignancy)

sections.title: Complications
lines: - Usually weeks to months after initial episode
- Related to etiology; increased risk with bacterial pericarditis, rare with viral/idiopathic etiology
- Also can be caused by radiation exposure
- Restrictive picture with pericardial calcifications on CXR, thickened on TTE

- Ibuprofen 600 mg q8hr x7-10 days, then taper over 3-4 weeks PO

sections.title: Background
lines: - Pericardial effusion: abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space
- Cardiac tamponade: hemodynamic compromise from pericardial fluid compressing the heart
- Rate of accumulation matters more than volume
- Acute: as little as 100-150 mL can cause tamponade (e.g., trauma)
- Chronic: up to 1-2 L may accumulate before tamponade (e.g., malignancy, uremia)
- Pathophysiology: increased pericardial pressure → decreased RV filling → decreased cardiac output
- Always consider in penetrating thoracic trauma within the cardiac box (80% result in tamponade)
- Gunshot wounds less likely to cause tamponade (larger pericardial defect allows decompression)
- RV is most commonly injured chamber due to anterior position

sections.title: Etiology
lines: - Trauma (penetrating or blunt), iatrogenic (central line, pacemaker, post-cardiac surgery)
- Ventricular free wall rupture (post-MI, typically day 3-5)
- Aortic dissection (type A with rupture into pericardium)
- Malignancy (most common cause of large effusions): lung, breast, lymphoma, melanoma
- Melanoma has particular predilection for cardiac metastasis

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Tachycardia (most reliable sign; bradycardia is ominous/preterminal)
- Friction rub (may be absent with large effusion)
- Pulsus paradoxus: >10 mmHg drop in systolic BP during inspiration
- Beck's triad (present in only ~33% of cases):
- Kussmaul sign: paradoxical rise in JVP with inspiration
- May present as PEA arrest or cardiogenic shock

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis
lines: - Tension pneumothorax (absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation)

sections.title: ECG
lines: - Electrical alternans (pathognomonic but insensitive — alternating QRS amplitude)
- Limb leads: all QRS <5 mm or I+II+III <15 mm
- Precordial leads: all QRS <10 mm or V1+V2+V3 <30 mm

sections.title: CXR
lines: - May be normal with small or acute effusions

sections.title: Pulsus Paradoxus
lines: - >10 mmHg decrease in systolic BP during inspiration
- Measure with manual sphygmomanometer (inflate above systolic, slowly deflate noting first Korotkoff sounds in expiration vs inspiration)
- False negatives: aortic regurgitation, ASD, severe hypotension, positive-pressure ventilation

sections.title: Bedside Ultrasound (Test of Choice in ED)
lines: - POCUS is the fastest and most reliable bedside diagnostic tool
- Key views: subxiphoid (most sensitive), parasternal long axis (PLAX), apical 4-chamber
- Distinguish from pleural effusion on PLAX: pericardial effusion tracks anterior to descending aorta; pleural effusion tracks posterior

sections.title: Classic Findings of Tamponade
lines: - Diastolic collapse of RA (earliest sign; >1/3 of cardiac cycle = significant)
- Plethoric (non-collapsing) IVC (>2 cm, <50% collapse — sensitive but nonspecific)

sections.title: Advanced Echo Assessment
lines: - M-mode: position through RV free wall on PLAX to identify diastolic collapse timing
- Helpful when RV is thickened (chronic pulmonary hypertension)

sections.title: Immediate Stabilization
lines: - IV fluid bolus 500-1000 mL NS (patient is preload-dependent)
- Avoid preload-reducing medications: nitroglycerin, diuretics, morphine
- Avoid positive-pressure ventilation if possible (reduces preload further)
- Position patient upright or leaning forward if tolerated

sections.title: Pericardiocentesis (Definitive for Non-hemorrhagic Tamponade)
lines: - Indications: hemodynamic compromise, suspected purulent pericarditis
- Insert needle 1-2 cm inferior to left xiphosternal junction, aimed toward left shoulder
- Advance at 30-45° angle under US guidance
- As little as 30-50 mL removal can dramatically improve hemodynamics
- Send fluid for: cell count, protein, LDH, glucose, cytology, gram stain/culture, AFB
- Complication rate <2% with US guidance (vs ~20% blind)

sections.title: Traumatic Tamponade
lines: - Pericardiocentesis is a temporizing measure only — definitive treatment is thoracotomy
- IV fluid resuscitation and emergent surgical consultation
- Can occur if ECG read as STEMI and heparin started inadvertently

sections.title: Specific Etiologies
lines: - Malignant effusion: pericardiocentesis + consider pericardial window for recurrent effusions
- Post-MI free wall rupture: emergent cardiac surgery

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Unstable traumatic tamponade: emergent OR for thoracotomy
- All patients with tamponade physiology: ICU admission
- Large effusion without tamponade: admit with cardiology consultation
- Small effusion, stable, known etiology: may be managed as outpatient with close follow-up

sections.title: Background
lines: - Inflammatory cardiomyopathy caused by damage and necrosis of myocytes
- Viral-induced is the most common etiology
- Clinical presentation ranges from smoldering heart failure to fulminant cardiogenic shock or sudden death
- Maintain high index of suspicion in younger patients without traditional CAD risk factors
- Incidence: estimated 1.5 million cases worldwide annually
- Giant cell myocarditis is a rapidly fatal variant requiring early recognition

sections.title: Causes
lines: - Enterovirus (Coxsackie B) and adenovirus (historically most common)
- Parvovirus B19 and HHV-6 (currently most detected on biopsy)
- Influenza A and B, HIV, hepatitis B/C, COVID-19
- Bacterial: Lyme disease, beta-hemolytic strep, Mycoplasma, diphtheria
- Parasitic: Chagas disease (most common cause worldwide), toxoplasma, trichinosis
- Autoimmune: sarcoidosis, SLE, giant cell myocarditis
- Drugs/toxins: cocaine, doxorubicin, immune checkpoint inhibitors, amphetamines

sections.title: Phases
lines: - Acute: direct cytotoxicity and focal necrosis from viral, autoimmune, or toxins
- Subacute: host immune response (viral molecular mimicry, anti-myocyte antibody production)
- Chronic: diffuse myocardial fibrosis and cardiac dysfunction

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Typically young patients (20-50 years) with few risk factors for CAD
- Preceding viral illness in 50-80% of cases (1-2 weeks prior)
- Chest pain or chest pressure/tightness (mimics ACS)
- Flu-like symptoms: fever, fatigue, myalgias, nausea/vomiting
- Tachycardia out of proportion to fever
- New-onset heart failure: fatigue, orthopnea, dyspnea on exertion
- Consider this diagnosis in the septic-appearing patient who worsens after IV fluids
- May present with sudden cardiac arrest (especially in young athletes)

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis
lines: - Acute coronary syndrome (most important to rule out)

sections.title: ECG
lines: - Must be obtained to rule out STEMI
- Diffuse ST changes, nonspecific ST-T wave abnormalities
- AV block (especially with Lyme disease or sarcoidosis)
- Normal ECG does NOT rule out myocarditis

sections.title: Labs
lines: - Troponin: elevated in ~50% of cases; sensitivity limited
- BNP/NT-proBNP: reflects degree of heart failure
- Consider viral serologies, Lyme titer, ANA (if autoimmune suspected)

sections.title: Imaging
lines: - CXR: cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema, or pleural effusion
- Decreased LVEF, global hypokinesis or regional wall motion abnormalities
- Fulminant myocarditis may show normal LV dimensions with increased wall thickness
- Cardiac MRI (noninvasive gold standard): myocardial edema and late gadolinium enhancement
- Endomyocardial biopsy: invasive gold standard, reserved for unexplained cardiomyopathy or suspected giant cell myocarditis

sections.title: ED Management
lines: - Rule out ACS: may require coronary angiography if ST elevation or high clinical suspicion
- Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin in acute phase (animal studies suggest increased inflammation)
- Volume status: use caution with IV fluids — may worsen heart failure
- If cardiogenic shock: consider vasopressors/inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone)
- Temporary pacing for complete heart block
- Anticoagulation consideration if severely reduced LVEF with LV thrombus risk

sections.title: Definitive Treatment
lines: - Supportive care is mainstay; most viral myocarditis self-resolves
- GDMT for heart failure: ACE-I/ARB, beta-blockers, diuretics (as tolerated by hemodynamics)
- Mechanical circulatory support (ECMO, VAD) for refractory cardiogenic shock
- Giant cell myocarditis: requires immunosuppression (cyclosporine + corticosteroids)
- Activity restriction: no competitive sports for 3-6 months per AHA guidelines

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Admit all patients with suspected myocarditis to a monitored bed
- ICU admission for hemodynamic instability, arrhythmias, or reduced LVEF
- Consider transfer to center with mechanical circulatory support capability

sections.title: Prognosis
lines: - Fulminant myocarditis paradoxically has the best long-term prognosis if patient survives the acute phase
- Overall mortality: ~20% at 1 year, ~50% at 5 years for non-fulminant forms
- Most patients with mild disease recover completely

sections.title: Background
lines: - Defined as an infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, affecting native (or prosthetic) heart valves as well as in-dwelling cardiac devices
- Consider in patients with known risk factors and unexplained fever
- Mitral valve most commonly affected overall; tricuspid valve most common in IVDA
- Noninfectious vegetations can arise in patients with malignancy/SLE/Hypercoagulable state ("Marantic" endocarditis)
- S. aureus is single most common cause (accounts for 1/3 of all cases)
- Strep viridans is the most common cause of native valve endocarditis, excluding risk factors below
- Blood cultures are falsely negative ~5% (think HACEK organisms)
- Only 20% have an increase in a known murmur and only 48% have a new murmur

sections.title: Prophylaxis
lines: - No longer recommended at all in the United Kingdom
- In United States, only recommended for invasive dental procedures (not routine cleanings) and invasive respiratory procedures in setting of:
- Repaired congenital heart disease/valvulopathy with prosthetic material

sections.title: Risk Factors
lines: - Coagulase negative staphylcocci are substantial etiologies in this patient population
- Rheumatic heart disease (biggest risk factor in low-income countries)
- Fungal endocarditis risk factors, with Candida most common

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Preexisting murmur found in 85% of cases; new murmur found in 48%
- Tender red/purple nodules on distal finger and toes
- Nail bed hemorrhages not extending the length of the nail
- Non-tender, small erythematous or hemorrhagic macular, papular or nodular lesions on the palms or soles only a few millimeters in diameter
- Associated with multiple systemic illnesses, most commonly bacterial endocarditis

sections.title: Non-infectious
lines: - Drug fever (except as in NMS and Serotonin Syndrome)

sections.title: Work-Up
lines: - Subacute endocarditis: WBC may be normal or elevated
- Difficulty obtaining clear TTE images (obesity, COPD)

sections.title: Diagnosis
lines: - Inpatient diagnosis is based on the Duke's Criteria although many of the criteria are not filled in the ED
- Heightened clinical suspicion is necessary even if diagnosis does not meet the official criteria.

sections.title: Major Criteria
lines: - Positive blood culture with typical IE microorganism, defined as one of the following:
- Typical microorganism consistent with IE from 2 separate blood cultures, as noted below:
- Streptococcus bovis including nutritional variant strains, or
- Community-acquired Enterococci, in the absence of a primary focus
- Microorganisms consistent with IE from persistently positive blood cultures defined as:
- Two positive cultures of blood samples drawn >12 hours apart, or
- All of 3 or a majority of 4 separate cultures of blood (with first and last sample drawn 1 hour apart)
- Coxiella burnetii detected by one positive blood culture or IgG
- Staphylococus lugdunensis should raise concerns for endocarditis with a single positive blood culture
- Evidence of endocardial involvement with positive echocardiogram defined as:
- Valvular mass or supporting structures or
- New disruption of a prosthetic valve or new valvular regurgitation

sections.title: Minor Criteria
lines: - Predisposing factor: known cardiac lesion, recreational drug injection
- Evidence of emboli: arterial emboli,pulmonary infarcts, Janeway lesions, conjunctival hemorrhage
- Positive blood culture (that does not meet a major criterion) or serologic evidence of infection

sections.title: CHF/Cardiogenic Shock
lines: - Often due to valve failure, rupture, or a new defect.

sections.title: Pulmonary edema
lines: - Often due to mitral or aortic valve rupture causing severe regurgitation

sections.title: Respiratory failure (emboli)
lines: - Often requires intubation with failure either due to CHF or Pneumonia
- Multi-lobar pneumonia suggests a tricuspid or pulmonary valve lesion with emboli to lungs

sections.title: Antibiotics
lines: Start after 3 sets of blood cultures are obtained (if possible)
- Whether the patient has received prior antibiotic therapy
- Local antibiotic resistance patterns or knowledge of prior endocarditis cultures
- Prior hospitalizations and risk of MRSA

sections.title: Native Valves
lines: - Ampicillin/Sulbactam 12g/day IV in 4 doses + Gentamicin 3mg/kg/day IV in 2 or 3 doses
- Amoxicillin/Clavulanate 12g/day in 4 doses + Gentamicin 3mg/kg/day IV in 2 or 3 doses
- Oxacillin 2g IV six times daily or Nafcillin 2g IV six times daily + Gentamicin 1mg/kg IV three times daily AND Ampicillin 2g IV six times daily
- Gentamicin 3mg/kg/day IV in 2 or 3 doses PLUS
- Ciprofloxacin 1000mg/day PO in 2 doses or 800 mg/day IV in 2 doses

sections.title: Prosthetic Valves (Early)
lines: - Gentamicin 3mg/kg/day IV in 2 or 3 doses PLUS

sections.title: IV Drug User without Prosthetic Valve
Prosthetic Valve (Late)
lines: - Same as native valve endocarditis empiric therapy

sections.title: Dental Procedure Prophylaxis
lines: All antibiotics options are given as a single dose 1 hour prior to the dental procedure
- Cefazolin 1g (50mg/kg) IM or IV or Ceftriaxone 1g (50mg/kg) IM or IV
- Ampicillin 50mg/kg IV/IM (max 2g) 30min before procedure if unable to take PO
- PCN allergy: Clindamycin 20mg/kg PO or IV (max 600mg) OR

sections.title: Pediatric Empiric
lines: - Vancomycin 15mg/kg IV q6hrs (max 2g/dose) + Gentamicin 1mg/kg IV q8hrs
- Nafcillin 50mg/kg IV q6hrs (max 2g/dose) if MSSA confirmed
- Ceftriaxone 100mg/kg/day IV divided q12h (max 4g/day) as alternative

sections.title: Disposition
lines: Admit all suspected cases and consult Cardiothoracic surgery for endocarditis complicated by:
- New Heart failure suspected due to severe regurgitation
- Fungal endocarditis (penetration of antifungals into vegetation walls poor)

sections.title: Miscellaneous
lines: - Anticoagulation carries higher risk of bleeding without delivering mortality benefit or reducing embolic complication
- Most common culture growths are MSSA, MRSA, and candida
- Furthermore, therapeutic anticoagulation not indicated for septic pulmonary embolism

sections.title: Cardiac
lines: - Most common cause of death due to IE

sections.title: Embolic
lines: - Unusual pain syndromes (due to splenic or renal infarction)

sections.title: Background
lines: - High blood pressure without symptoms is NOT hypertensive emergency (see asymptomatic hypertension)
- Definition: acute target-organ damage due to severely elevated blood pressure
- Blood pressure is generally ≥180/110-120, but presence of end-organ damage defines disease (not absolute blood pressure number)
- 1%-6% of all ED patients will present with severe hypertension, but less than half of those will have target organ damage
- From 2006-2013, hypertensive emergencies occurred in approximately 2 per 1000 adult ED visits

sections.title: Updated Terminology (AHA 2024)
lines: The 2024 AHA Scientific Statement recommends retiring the terms "hypertensive urgency" and "hypertensive crisis"
- Hypertensive emergency: SBP ≥180 or DBP ≥110-120 mmHg with new or worsening target-organ damage
- Asymptomatic markedly elevated BP: SBP ≥180 or DBP ≥110-120 mmHg without target-organ damage (replaces "hypertensive urgency")
- Asymptomatic elevated BP: SBP >130 or DBP >80 mmHg without target-organ damage

sections.title: Prehospital
lines: - Prehospital BP measurements should be considered reliable
- Acute lowering of BP is not typically recommended in the prehospital setting
- Focus on ABCs (assess need for intubation or respiratory support)

sections.title: End-Organ Dysfunction (BARKH Mnemonic)
lines: Use the BARKH mnemonic to systematically evaluate for target-organ damage:
- Acute kidney injury (often with microscopic hematuria)
- Acute LV failure with pulmonary edema

sections.title: Hypertension
lines: - Drug use or overdose (e.g stimulants, especially alcohol, cocaine, or Synthroid)

sections.title: BP Measurement
lines: - Ensure proper cuff size and technique before initiating treatment
- Confirm with repeat measurement in both arms; patient should be seated, back supported, feet on floor
- For patients receiving IV antihypertensives, arterial line monitoring is preferred for accuracy

sections.title: Workup
lines: Consider any of the following based on the patient's clinical presentation
- CBC with peripheral smear — assess for microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes)
- Chem 8 — assess renal failure and possible secondary causes
- Urinalysis — assess renal failure, glomerulonephritis, preeclampsia
- Ultrasound — evaluate for aortic dissection, bladder outlet obstruction, or depressed myocardial function
- Fundoscopic Exam — evaluate for hypertensive retinopathy or papilledema
- CXR — evaluate for pulmonary edema or widened mediastinum (dissection)
- CT head — in hypertensive encephalopathy, may not show acute hemorrhage or other acute pathology

- Hypertensive encephalopathy is thought to be secondary to alteration in cerebral auto-regulation leading to posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. Most patients will show changes on MRI, although this is not necessarily indicated in the emergency department.

sections.title: Diagnosis
lines: - Must have evidence of end-organ dysfunction
- High blood pressure without symptoms is NOT hypertensive emergency (see asymptomatic hypertension)
- Symptoms such as headache, epistaxis and dizziness are not evidence of acute end-organ damage and they are not indication for acute BP reduction

sections.title: Management
lines: High blood pressure without end organ damage is NOT hypertensive emergency (see asymptomatic hypertension)
- Goal: Lower MAP by 20-25% in the first hour
- Then lower gradually to 160/100 mmHg over the next 2-6 hours
- Then cautiously to normal over the next 24-48 hours
- Exception is aortic dissection which requires rapid reduction of systolic BP to 100-120 mmHg
- Be careful of lowering BP in patients with CVA
- Do NOT use IV antihypertensives for asymptomatic elevated BP, even if markedly elevated

sections.title: First-Line Agents
lines: 4. Achieves target BP in >90% within 30 min (CLUE trial)
1. Avoid in decompensated CHF, severe aortic stenosis
2. Often considered first-line for most hypertensive emergencies
3. In CLUE subgroup with EOD, 3.65× odds of reaching target vs labetalol

Then titrate by smaller increments q5-10 min

3. Risk of rebound HTN after discontinuation

3. Similar initial BP control to nicardipine; nicardipine may have more sustained control

2. Less effective at reaching target BP than nicardipine in CLUE trial (82.5% vs 91.7%)
3. First-line in aortic dissection (provides rate and BP control)

sections.title: Second-Line / Specific-Use Agents
lines: If ineffective, repeat load and increase infusion by 50 mcg/kg/min up to 300 mcg/kg/min
1. Avoid in COPD, decompensated CHF, severe bradycardia
2. Does not significantly lower BP alone in severe HTN

Drug of choice in patients with cardiac ischemia, LV dysfunction, or pulmonary edema

Used for catecholamine-induced hypertension (pheochromocytoma, sympathomimetic toxicity)

Note: Oral clonidine loading ("clonidine slam") is an outdated practice and is not recommended for hypertensive emergency in the ED. IV titratable agents are preferred.

sections.title: Aortic Dissection
lines: - Target SBP 100-120 and HR <60 within 20 min
- Beta-blockade BEFORE vasodilation to prevent reflex tachycardia
- Esmolol (preferred for titratability) OR labetalol alone
- Add nicardipine or clevidipine if BP remains elevated after adequate beta-blockade
- Adequate analgesia will decrease sympathetic drive

sections.title: Pulmonary Edema
lines: - Nitroglycerin is drug of choice (reduces preload)
- Avoid beta-blockers in acute decompensated heart failure

sections.title: ACS
lines: - No more than 20-30% reduction for SBP >160
- Consider beta-blocker (esmolol or labetalol) if no contraindication
- Avoid nicardipine/clevidipine as sole agents (lack antianginal properties)

sections.title: Cocaine/Amphetamine Toxicity
lines: - If refractory: nicardipine or clevidipine (pure vasodilators)
- Avoid pure beta-blockers (risk of unopposed alpha-stimulation)
- Labetalol (mixed alpha/beta) remains debated; some guidelines permit, others advise against

sections.title: Renal Failure
lines: - Reduce BP by no more than 20%
- Avoid nitroprusside (cyanide metabolite accumulates in renal failure)
- Clevidipine (organ-independent metabolism), nicardipine, or fenoldopam (increases renal blood flow)

sections.title: Eclampsia/Pre-eclampsia
lines: - Avoid ACE inhibitors/ARBs, nitroprusside (teratogenic/fetal cyanide risk)

sections.title: Intracerebral Hemorrhage
lines: - Target SBP <140 mmHg, initiated within 1 hour (INTERACT3 care bundle)
- INTERACT3 demonstrated improved functional outcomes (OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.76-0.97) and reduced mortality with bundled care approach
- Care bundle also includes concurrent management of hyperglycemia, pyrexia, and anticoagulation reversal
- See current ICH guidelines for full recommendations

sections.title: Ischemic Stroke
lines: - If thrombolytic treatment is planned: goal SBP <185 and DBP <110 before administration
- If no thrombolytics: consider BP reduction only if SBP >220 or DBP >120
- Nicardipine, clevidipine, or labetalol are all effective and safe
- Clevidipine may facilitate faster door-to-thrombolytic times due to rapid onset

sections.title: Pheochromocytoma
lines: - Then add beta-blocker only after adequate alpha-blockade

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Hypertensive emergency: Admit to ICU or monitored setting for IV antihypertensive titration and close hemodynamic monitoring
- Do NOT treat with IV antihypertensives in the ED
- Assess for and address contributing factors (pain, anxiety, medication nonadherence, urinary retention)
- Evidence suggests potential harm from acute IV treatment of asymptomatic elevated BP

Nicardipine 5-15 mg/hr IV drip (onset 5-15 min, duration 4-6 hr) — Preferred 1st line; titratable Labetalol 20 mg IV bolus, double q10 min (max 300 mg) or 0.5-2 mg/min drip IV (onset 5-10 min, duration 3-6 hr) Clevidipine 1-2 mg/hr, titrate by doubling q90 sec IV drip (onset 2-4 min) (max 32 mg/hr) — Ultra-short acting Nitroglycerin 5-200 mcg/min IV drip (onset 1-5 min) — Preferred for ACS or pulmonary edema Nitroprusside 0.25-10 mcg/kg/min IV drip (onset immediate) — Cyanide toxicity risk; use only when others fail Esmolol 500 mcg/kg bolus then 50-300 mcg/kg/min IV drip (onset 1-2 min, duration 10-30 min) — Ultra-short acting beta-blocker Hydralazine 5-20 mg IV q4-6 hr IV (onset 10-30 min, duration 2-6 hr) — Unpredictable; generally avoid Enalaprilat 0.625-1.25 mg IV q6 hr IV (onset 15-60 min) — Avoid in renal artery stenosis Fenoldopam 0.1-1.6 mcg/kg/min IV drip (onset 5-15 min) — DA-1 agonist; renal protective Phentolamine 5-15 mg IV IV (onset 1-2 min, duration 10-30 min) — For catecholamine excess states

sections.title: Background
lines: - Sudden decrease in perfusion that may result in irreversible limb loss
- Amputation occurs in 10%-15% of patients during hospitalization
- Etiology may be thrombotic (80%) or embolic (20%)
- Thrombosis occurs in vessels with existing atherosclerosis
- Embolism occurs in vessels usually free of atherosclerosis
- Generally do not have existing collateral circulation
- Results in higher level of limb ischemia than thrombosis

sections.title: 6 Ps
lines: - Pain - Claudication or pain with leg elevation; typically earliest sign
- Paraesthesia - May be associated with weakness; preservation of light touch is good guide to viability
- Pulselessness - May be accompanied by skin changes; late finding
- Poikilothermia - Limb is cool to touch when compared to other side; late finding

sections.title: Ankle-brachial index (ABI)
lines: - Measure SBP from both brachial arteries using cuff and handheld Doppler over the AC fossa
- Measure SBP from both DP and PT arteries using cuff placed just proximal to the malleoli with Doppler over artery (5-8% of normal patients have absent DP pulse)
- Calculate ABI on each leg by taking the highest ankle SBP (between DP and PT) on that leg divided by the highest brachial SBP and record to 2 decimal places

sections.title: Imaging
lines: - CTA as a diagnostic is near the level of formal angiography (96% sensitive, 95% specific)
- US is sensitive for proximal extremity occlusions, but sensitivity markedly falls off distally and is operator dependent

sections.title: Laboratory Evaluation
lines: - Not useful for diagnosis, but essential for monitoring co-existing conditions and response to anticoagulant therapy. Should include:

sections.title: Management
lines: - Vascular surgery consultation (clot retrieval, balloon angioplasty, intraarterial tPA, stenting, bypass)
- Management of embolism = embolectomy (limb salvage decreases after 4-6 hours)
- Management of thrombus = intra-arterial thrombolysis (if non-limb threatening), thrombectomy (if limb-threatening ischmia)
- Interventional radiology if delay in vascular surgery intervention or if unavailable

sections.title: Medication Dosing
lines: Unfractionated heparin 80 units/kg bolus, then 18 units/kg/hr infusion IV

sections.title: Admission
lines: - Patients with an ABI of <0.5 warrant admission after immediate consultation with vascular surgery

sections.title: Discharge
lines: - Patients with stable ABI measurements, resolved pain, and chronic occlusive disease can be discharged with vascular surgical follow-up.

sections.title: Clinical Spectrum of Venous thromboembolism (VTE)
lines: Only 40% of ambulatory ED patients with PE have concomitant DVT

sections.title: Leg Vein Anatomy
lines: - (Superficial) femoral vein is part of the deep system, not the superficial system as the name suggests!

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Leg swelling with circumference >3cm more than unaffected side
- Homan's sign - pain during dorsiflexion of foot (SN 60-96% and SP 20-72%)

sections.title: Unilateral leg swelling
lines: - Hypertrophy of soft tissue or bone (Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome)

sections.title: Lower Extremity
lines: - Risk stratification for further testing indicated using (e.g., see Modified Wells Score below)

sections.title: Modified Wells Score
lines: Can be applied for patients whose clinical presentation is concerning for a DVT in order to risk stratify.
- Paralysis, paresis, or immobility of extremity (1pt)
- Bedridden >3 days because of symptoms within 4 weeks (1pt)
- Unilateral calf swelling >3cm below tibial tuberosity (1pt)
- Alternative diagnosis as likely or more likely than DVT (-2pts)

- A score of 0 or lower → minimal risk - DVT prevalence of 5%. D-dimer testing is safe in this group - negative d-dimer decreases the probability of disease to <1% allowing an ultrasound to be deferred.
- A score of 1-2 → moderate risk - DVT prevalence of 17%. D-dimer testing still effective and a negative test decreases post-test probability disease to <1%
- A score of 3 or higher → high risk - DVT prevalence of 17-53% → patients should receive an ultrasound

sections.title: Upper Extremity
lines: Requires ultrasound for diagnosis. Cannot be ruled out with d-dimer.
- Generally involves axillary or subclavian veins
- Primary upper extremity DVT typically presents in young healthy individuals
- Secondary upper extremity DVT often due to indwelling catheters
- Obtain a chest x-ray to rule out bony abnormalities that may be causing venous obstruction

sections.title: Management
lines: The distinction between distal and proximal relates to veins below and above the knee respectively. Patients with superficial venous thromboses such as the long saphenous and short saphenous are at risk of developing a DVT, especially in patients who have a history of prior DVT although management with anticoagulation is controversial.

sections.title: Proximal DVT
lines: Proximal veins are the external iliac, common femoral, greater saphenous, profound (deep) femoral, (superficial) femoral vein, popliteal vein
- Anticoagulate with apixaban, rivaroxaban, or heparin/coumadin x 3 months
- Anticoagulate with apixaban, rivaroxaban, or heparin/coumadin x 3 months

sections.title: Mechanical Thrombectomy
lines: Consider pharmaco-mechanical (IR) management of proximal DVTs with the following charateristics:
- New edema of calf or thigh (CEAP ≥3)
- Limited mobility or bed bound due to pain / swelling

sections.title: Distal DVT
lines: Distal veins are the anterior tibial, posterior tibial, peroneal, gastrocnemius, soleus.
- Anticoagulate with apixaban, rivaroxaban, or heparin/coumadin x 3 months
- Asymptomatic with extension of thrombus toward proximal veins
- Anticoagulate with apixaban, rivaroxaban, or heparin/coumadin x 3 months
- Discharge with compressive U/S q2 weeks
- 2020 review from JAMA recommend treat calf DVT if "severe symptoms or risk factors for pulmonary embolism or extension to proximal veins (such as hospitalization, history of VTE, and cancer)."

sections.title: VTE in Pregnancy
lines: - Therapeutic LMWH or unfractionated heparin anticoagulation dose in:
- Antepartum outpatient with multiple prior VTEs or any VTE with high-risk thrombophilia until 6 weeks postpartum
- Postpartum inpatient with prior unprovoked, estrogen-provoked VTE, or low-risk thrombophilia for duration of admission
- Antepartum outpatient with prior unprovoked, estrogen-provoked VTE, or low-risk thrombophilia until6 weeks postpartum
- Patients admitted > 72 hrs, not at high risk for bleeding or imminent delivery
- Resume 12 hours after C-section and removal of epidural / spinal needle in indicated patients
- Halt anticoagulation if imminent delivery, C-section, epidural / spinal needle

sections.title: Recurrent DVT on Therapeutic Anticoagulation
lines: - Admit patients for vascular surgery and hematologist consult
- Typically start heparin for additional anticoagulation

sections.title: Upper extremity DVT
lines: - If secondary to catheter, do not necessarily have to remove
- Anticoagulation as per lower extremity DVTs.
- Consider admission for catheter directed thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy, especially with any of the following characteristics
- Thrombus extending from subclavian to axillary vein
- Other features that suggest success for thrombolysis and decrease risk:

sections.title: Anticoagulation Options
lines: - Give 7d supply with first dose in ED
- Then 20mg PO daily (duration depending on risk factors)
- Then 5mg PO BID daily (duration depending on risk factors)
- Check PTT after 6hr; adjust infusion to maintain PTT at 1.5-2.5x control
- Check creatinine on all patients prior to initiation
- No dosage adjustments necessary for renal impairment
- However, CrCl <25 mL/minute were excluded from clinical trials

sections.title: Discharge
lines: Consider if all of the following are present:
- Low risk of bleeding in patient
- Able to administer anticoagulation with appropriate monitoring
- Able to arrange for 2-3 day follow-up

sections.title: Admit
lines: - Ileofemoral DVT that is a candidate for thrombectomy (should have the following):
- Good functional status and reasonable life expectancy
- High risk of bleeding on anticoagulation
- Recent (within 2 weeks) stroke or transient ischemic attack
- History of heparin sensitivity or Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia
- Upper extremity DVT, if indicated for thrombolysis vs outpatient for anticoagulation alone if low risk

sections.title: _intro
lines: This page is for adult patients. For pediatric patients, see: acute dyspnea (peds)

sections.title: Background
lines: - Dyspnea (shortness of breath) is one of the most common ED chief complaints
- Can be life-threatening — rapid assessment for immediately dangerous causes is essential
- The approach should focus on pattern recognition using vital signs, lung exam, CXR, and ECG to quickly narrow the differential
- Key question: Is this cardiac, pulmonary, or other?

sections.title: Emergent
lines: - Other Associated with Normal/↑ Respiratory Effort

sections.title: Immediate
lines: - CXR — pneumothorax, effusion, pulmonary edema, consolidation, widened mediastinum
- Bedside ultrasound — pneumothorax, pleural effusion, B-lines (pulmonary edema), pericardial effusion, RV dilation, cardiac contractility

sections.title: Labs (guided by clinical suspicion)
lines: - BNP/NT-proBNP — helps differentiate cardiac from pulmonary dyspnea
- D-dimer — if PE suspected and low-to-moderate pretest probability
- BMP — metabolic acidosis (consider DKA, sepsis, toxic ingestion)
- VBG/ABG — acid-base status, pCO2, carboxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin
- Lactate — if sepsis or shock suspected

sections.title: Advanced Imaging
lines: - CT chest — if parenchymal disease, mass, or empyema suspected
- CT angiography — if aortic dissection suspected

sections.title: Bedside Lung Ultrasound in Emergency (BLUE) Protocol
lines: - Landmark study by a French intensivist that described various profiles of specific pulmonary disease found on US
- Ultrasound approaches include anterior zones and PLAPS (posterior or lateral alveolar and/or pleural syndrome) point, which is located at the posterior axillary line similar to FAST view
- Predominant A lines anteriorly + lung sliding = Asthma/COPD
- Multiple predominant B lines anteriorly + lung sliding = Pulmonary Edema
- Predominant A lines anteriorly + lung sliding + positive DVT = PE
- Absent anterior lung sliding + anterior A lines + positive lung point = Pneumothorax (PTX)
- PLAPS findings +/- A or B lines +/- abolished lung sliding = Pneumonia
- PLAPS describes changes at the PLAPS point, usually related to consolidations and pleural effusions
- Consolidations may include lung hepatization, shred sign, air bronchograms
- Note that mirroring (normal) may appear similar to hepatization, but mirroring only shows in specific spots due to specific echogenic windows
- Pleural effusions are visualized as anechoic/hypoechoic areas with possible spine sign or floating lung sign (sinusoid sign on M-mode)
- A suggested BLUE protocol guides diagnosis of dyspnea; this should be modified as needed based on clinical presentation
- Check lung sliding in anterior lung fields ---> check for A and B lines ---> check for PLAPS findings

sections.title: Management
lines: - Oxygen: Titrate to SpO2 >94% (88-92% if COPD/CO2 retainer); use high-flow nasal cannula, BiPAP, or intubation as needed
- Tension pneumothorax: Needle decompression then chest tube
- Asthma/COPD exacerbation: Albuterol, ipratropium, systemic steroids
- BiPAP for CHF or COPD exacerbation (avoids intubation in many cases)
- Intubation if impending respiratory failure, GCS decline, or refractory hypoxia

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Intubated or on BiPAP with impending respiratory failure
- Severe asthma/COPD unresponsive to initial treatment
- Pneumonia with hypoxia or significant comorbidities
- Asthma/COPD exacerbation with adequate response to ED treatment and baseline PEF restored
- Mild CHF exacerbation with adequate response to diuresis and stable vitals
- Low-risk PE (if outpatient anticoagulation pathway available)
- Anxiety-related dyspnea after exclusion of organic causes

lines: - Normal A-a gradient ≈ (Age/4) + 4 on room air
- Elevated A-a gradient suggests: V/Q mismatch, shunt, or diffusion impairment
- Normal A-a gradient + hypoxia suggests: hypoventilation or low FiO₂
- Kanber GJ, et al. The alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient in young and elderly men during air and oxygen breathing. Am Rev Respir Dis. 1968;97(3):376-381. PMID 5637791.

sections.title: Background
lines: - Coughing of blood that originates from respiratory tract below level of larynx
- Death usually occurs from asphyxiation, not exanguination
- Easy to confuse with epistaxis or oropharynx bleeding

sections.title: Hemoptysis
lines: - Blood-laced mucus from the sinus or nose area

sections.title: Workup
lines: - Nml in 30% (most of whom end up having bronchitis)
- Indicated for gross hemoptysis or suspicious CXR

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: - Massive = A single expectoration of ≥ 50cc OR >600cc/24h
- May differentiate from hematemesis with pH litmus paper
- Hematemesis tends to be acidic, and stomach acid tends to turn bright red blood in stomach to brown/black fragments unless massive

sections.title: Management
lines: - Placing patient with affected lung down may actually worsen V-Q mismatch
- Use 8-0 tube to allow for subsequent bronchoscopy
- If possible can selectively intubate the unaffected bronchus to prevent aspiration
- After tube passes through cords rotate 90degrees left or right and advance
- Can also use coude tip of bougie
- Emergent bronchoscopy or embolization for life-threatening hemorrhage
- IV TXA may reduce in-hospital mortality, length of stay, and total healthcare costs
- Absolute in-hospital mortality reduction was 2.5% in the retrospective study of nearly 20,000 patients
- No particular dosing regimen, but in this study, no association was found between TXA and seizures, in part per the authors, due to most patients receiving no more than 2 g of TXA total
