lines: See pulmonary embolism in pregnancy for pregnancy specific information.

sections.title: Background
lines: Pulmonary embolism is an obstruction of one of the branches of the pulmonary arteries by material; typically a thrombus
- Fat, Air, and tumor embolisms can similarly and obstruct a branch of the pulmonary artery, but are not covered in this section
- A pulmonary embolism is on the spectrum of Venous thromboembolism (VTE)
- Most emboli are thought to arise from lower extremity proximal veins (iliac, femoral, and popliteal), whereas a thrombus of the distal veins (calf) resolves spontaneously ⅔ of the time

sections.title: Epidemiology
lines: - In the US, approximately 370,000-390,000 PE’s are diagnosed annually
- Hemodynamically stable (AHA/ACC Class A & B or ESC Low Risk) patients with a PE have a direct mortality of about 1%, however hemodynamically unstable patients mortality ranges from 25-50%
- For almost one quarter of PE patients, the initial clinical presentation is sudden death

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Diagnosis of PE is challenging, with less than 10% of patients evaluated for a PE ultimately diagnosed with a PE

sections.title: Symptoms
lines: - Dyspnea at rest or with exertion (75-80%)
- Pleuritic pain, pain that halts respiration, is only seen in 20% of patients
- Syncope is caused by PE <5% of the time

sections.title: Signs
lines: - Tachycardia (HR>100), Tachypnea (RR>20), Hypoxemia (SpO2<95%) are seen ~50% of the time
- Hypotension (SBP<90) only seen 10% of the time, but largest predictor of mortality
- Unilateral calf tenderness or edema, suggestive of a DVT
- Other signs may include accentuated pulmonic component of second heart sound, JVD, or decreased breath sounds

sections.title: Emergent
lines: - Other Associated with Normal/↑ Respiratory Effort

sections.title: Assessing Pretest Probability
lines: - A thorough H&P is paramount to assess probability of PE
- Objective scoring systems (Wells, revised Geneva) performs similarly to experienced clinician gestalt in assessing pretest probability

sections.title: If pretest probability of PE is low (<15%)
lines: - If all criteria are "No", very low probability of PE, and no further testing is required
- However, if even 1 criteria is met, proceed as if patient is of intermediate risk

sections.title: If pretest probability of PE is intermediate (15-50%), or unable to rule out with PERC:
lines: - Perform d-dimer testing and assess YEARS criteria
- ≥1 YEARS criteria and d-dimer <500ng/mL, or age adjusted threshold
- PE not excluded, perform diagnostic imaging
- ≥1 YEARS criteria and d-dimer ≥500ng/mL, or age adjusted threshold
- PE not excluded, perform diagnostic imaging

sections.title: If pretest probability of PE is high (>50%)
Diagnostic Imaging
lines: - Computed Tomography Pulmonary Artery (CTPA) is the standard and preferred imaging modality
- If a CTPA is unable to be obtained, a high probability ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan is sufficient
- V/Q Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is preferred over a planar V/Q scan
- SPECT combines a non-contrast CT with a planar V/Q and has equivalent sensitivity to CTPA

sections.title: Labs
lines: - Typically obtained to rule out other conditions and to help with risk stratification
- Important to include troponin, BNP, lactate
- Elevated troponin has a pooled OR of 4.33 for mortality
- Elevated BNP has a 6.57 odds of short term all cause mortality
- An elevated lactate leads to 9.05 odds of PE related mortality

sections.title: Echocardiogram
lines: - Beneficial for short term risk stratification
- POCUS is an alternative to formal transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) if TTE is unavailable
- Goal is to evaluate for RV dysfunction as these signs are predictive of mortality
- D sign (Left ventricular septal wall flattening)
- McConnell's Sign (Mid-RV wall akinesis with hyperdynamic apex)
- Tricuspid Annular Plane Systolic Excursion (TAPSE), <1.6cm is abnormal

sections.title: CXR
lines: - Often obtained to rule out other etiologies of chest pain and dyspnea
- Can be confused for a peripheral pneumonia as a wedge shaped peripheral opacity that indicates the presence of a pulmonary infarct
- A focal area of oligemia or reduced blood flow and increased lucency distal to the pulmonary embolism

sections.title: ECG
lines: - PE's can be associated with ECG changes that indicate acute pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain
- Abnormal in 70% of patients with a PE, however nonspecific
- Most common arrhythmia associated with PE
- Symmetric T wave inversions in the anterior leads (V1-V4)
- Incomplete or complete right bundle branch block

sections.title: Classification
lines: - Both the ESC and the AHA/ACC proposed classification of patients with acute PE into categories based on their potential risk for adverse outcomes

- ESC 2019 Guidelines: Updated the 2011 AHA/ACC tool by splitting the intermediate or previously referred to as "submassive" patient group into those that present with low-risk features and those that present with high-risk features while maintaining stable hemodynamics.

- AHA/ACC 2026 Guidelines: A new, 5 tier, non-validated tool using an A-E category system with multiple subcategories is presented in a way to capture higher risk patients who may not have underlying RV dysfunction or cardiac biomarker abnormalities but appear to have a higher risk for adverse outcomes as noted in their proposed D group
- Categorization of PE patients allows for guidance in management decisions

sections.title: Anticoagulation
lines: - Anticoagulation is the cornerstone of PE management and should be started in the ED

- If bleeding risk is very high, based on tools such as VTE Bleed or RIETE, consider discussing anticoagulation strategies with hematology, pulmonology, or PERT (if available at your institution) prior to initiating anticoagulation
- 10mg twice daily for 1 week, then 5mg twice daily
- 15mg twice daily for 3 weeks, then 20mg once daily
- Initiate heparin treatment for 5-10 days; then 150mg twice daily
- 80 units/kg bolus; then 18 units/kg/hr continuous infusion
- Can be used in patients undergoing advanced therapies
- Can be used in patients undergoing advanced therapies
- Patients with mechanical prosthetic heart valve
- Patients with mechanical prosthetic heart valve
- If BMI >40kg/m2, reduce dose (0.8mg/kg BID of enoxaparin)
- If Stage IV or greater CKD (GFR<30 mL/min), adjust to 1mg/kg QD
- Consider starting at 2.5mg PO if frail, elderly, malnourished, or with a history of liver disease
- 3-6 mo, if time limited risk factor (post-op, trauma, estrogen use)
- 6 mo to life, if idiopathic etiology or recurrent

sections.title: Advanced Therapies
lines: - Systemic thrombolytics, catheter directed therapy, and less often surgical embolectomy may be considered for specific patients with acute PE, typically in categories C-E in the AHA/ACC guidelines or the intermediate-high risk/high risk in ESC guidelines
- However, decisions to pursue these therapies should be made with multidisciplinary specialty input
- Thrombolytic therapies are a group of IV medications that activate fibrinolysis and break up clots
- In general, should only be reserved for patients in categories D/E or High risk, however some evidence suggests it may be beneficial for specific patients within category C3
- Thrombolytics should NOT be used over anticoagulation due to increased risk of major bleeding and ICH in patients within categories A-C2
- Thrombolytic dosing is debated, however current standard dosing of rt-PA (alteplase) is 100mg IV over 2hrs
- Some evidence supports 25-50mg IV tPA, highlighting similar efficacy and a lower bleeding risk, but no high quality trials have definitively proven this
- PEITHO-3 trial currently ongoing and hopes to elucidate this question
- Tenecteplase, while studied in certain trials, has not been FDA approved for PE thrombolysis, and has no head to head data comparing it with tPA
- For patients in cardiac arrest with a presumed PE, thrombolytics may be considered, but there is no clear benefit and a paucity of evidence
- Duration of CPR after lytic administration is not quantified, however best estimates are to continue high quality CPR for 30-60min after administration of thrombolytic medication
- Catheter directed therapies continue to be studied for varying PE classifications with wide heterogeneity in methodology, leading to difficulty comparing treatment strategies
- Generally considered for patients in categories C-E and often on a case by case basis
- Combination of mechanical thrombectomy and catheter based thrombolytic administration
- Efficacy of surgical embolectomy vs anticoagulation alone has not been studied
- Majority of evidence is retrospective and often for patients who have had CPR and as a salvage therapy after systemic thrombolytics
- IVC filters can be used when standard anticoagulation therapy is contraindicated or when patients develop recurrent PE despite being on anticoagulation

sections.title: Supportive care
lines: - Hypoxemia (SpO2<90%) causes hypoxemic vasoconstriction, worsening acute pulmonary hypertension
- Be cautious about intubation as the increase in intrathoracic pressure from positive pressure can worsen RV preload and precipitate cardiovascular collapse
- Small (250-500mL) fluid boluses may be used as part of resuscitation in patients who are hemodynamically unstable
- Excessive IV fluids can worsen RV dilation and further compress LV, worsening hemodynamics
- May be used once fluids are no longer helpful
- Has a favorable SVR/PVR ratio with doses < 15 μg/min
- Vasopressin is a second line agent
- Consider adding once norepinephrine doses exceed 15 μg/min, as norepi at higher doses can lead to an increase in PVR

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - 20-30% of patients with a PE can be discharged from the ED, presuming they are able to start anticoagulation and have a stable social situation in which they are able to return for appropriate follow-up with an outpatient provider
- Hestia Criteria can be used to guide decision making for patients who are safe to discharge from the ED

sections.title: Prognosis
lines: Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h SC — Preferred in cancer, liver disease, coagulopathy, pregnancy Heparin (UFH) 80 units/kg IV bolus, then 18 units/kg/hr continuous infusion IV drip — Short half-life; preferred if considering thrombolytics or bleeding risk Rivaroxaban 15 mg PO BID x3 weeks, then 20 mg PO daily PO — Preferred if parenteral therapy to be avoided Apixaban 10 mg PO BID x1 week, then 5 mg PO BID PO

sections.title: Additional Topics
lines: - Pulmonary embolism response team (PERT) is a multidisciplinary group that provide real time expertise in management of patients at higher risk for adverse events in the setting of an acute PE
- Often composed of emergency medicine, pulmonology, critical care, interventional radiology, vascular surgery, cardiology, as well as nursing and pharmacy
- 60% of all PERT activations originate in the ED and have been shown to improve overall care and reduce disposition times, as well as facilitate advanced therapies
- A ‘clot in transit’, a free floating blood clot discovered within the cardiac chambers either on echocardiogram or CT, is found in 2-4% of patients with PE
- Leads to 2.26 OR of increased mortality
- Some evidence to support that these patients fare better with systemic thrombolysis compared to anticoagulation alone
- Patients with renal failure are at increased risk of both VTE as well as bleeding
- DOACs are preferred to VKA in Stage II-III CKD (GFR 30-89 ml/min)

- Patients with Stage IV, V, or on renal replacement therapy were excluded from randomized trials, but data from US Renal Data System shows apixaban is as safe and effective as warfarin in Stage IV and higher CKD
- When LMWH is used, transition to once daily dosing due to extended half-life
- Patients who are obese have less lean body mass, often leading to supratherapeutic anticoagulation when using standard LMWH dosing
- Evidence supports reduced dosing of LMWH to 0.8 mg/kg BID in BMI ≥40 kg/m2 with no clear increased thrombotic events, but less rate of major bleeding and lower rates of supratherapeutic events
- Patients with cancer are at increased VTE risk
- Treatment for most stable patients is preferred with a DOAC, however LMWH may be indicated if;
- oral ingestion or gastrointestinal absorption is limited

items: Other Associated with Normal/↑ Respiratory Effort

sections.title: _intro
lines: This page is for adult patients. For pediatric patients, see: asthma (peds)

sections.title: Background
lines: - Establish severity of current presentation based of vital signs, clinical presentation, and history of prior severe exacerbations (e.g. need for hospitalization, ICU admission, intubation, etc.)
- Identify any treatable precipitant (e.g. pneumonia, URI, GERD, exposure to irritants, aspirin/NSAIDs)
- Status asthmaticus is a life-threatening form of asthma in which progressively worsening reactive airways are unresponsive to usual appropriate therapy leading to pulmonary insufficiency.

sections.title: History
lines: Wheeze, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and/or cough that:
- Occur variably over time and vary in intensity
- Are often worse at night or on waking
- Are often triggered by exercise, laughter, allergens, or cold air
- Often appear or worsen with viral infections

sections.title: Physical
lines: - Dyspnea, wheezing, and cough (+/- sputum production)
- Cyanosis is uncommon (respiratory alkalosis -> left shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve)

sections.title: Signs of impending ventilatory failure
lines: - Paradoxical respiration (chest deflation and abdominal protrusion during inspiration)

sections.title: Airway — Intrathoracic Lower
lines: - Parasitic infection (eosinophilic pneumonia; in endemic areas)

sections.title: Airway — Extrathoracic (typically stridor ± wheeze)
lines: - Vocal cord dysfunction / paradoxical vocal fold motion

sections.title: Other
lines: - Pulmonary embolism (may present with wheeze in up to 25%)
- Vocal cord dysfunction (often misdiagnosed as refractory asthma)

sections.title: Emergent
lines: - Other Associated with Normal/↑ Respiratory Effort

sections.title: Workup
lines: - For uncomplicated exacerbations in patients with known asthma, CXR is not routinely indicated.
- Asymmetric lung auscultation findings, after treatment with albuterol
- Poor response to medications/treatment, if history and exam are not consistent with asthma
- ABG in general unlikely to add to clinical decision making
- May consider if concerned that the patient is getting tired (fatigue vs elevated CO2?)
- A CO2 >45 is abnormal and may suggest impending respiratory failure (asthmatics typically hypocapneic during exacerbation)

sections.title: Diagnosis
lines: - Asthma and asthma exacerbation determination in the ED is a clinical diagnosis, which can be used to guide initial treatment
- Subsequent outpatient testing/consideration for new onset asthma is recommended to confirm the diagnosis.

sections.title: Classification
lines: - The current concept of asthma severity is based on how difficult the patient's asthma is to treat.
- Use of older classification systems describing asthma severity based on exacerbation frequency and lung function tests (e.g., "intermittent" and "mild persistent") are no longer recommended.

sections.title: Oxygen PRN
lines: - Titrate to an arterial oxygen saturation >90% (>95% in pregnant women and with coexistent heart disease)

sections.title: Albuterol
lines: Favor continuous nebulization to decrease the chance of admission when compared to intermittent dosing
- Intermittent: 2.5-5mg q20min x3, then 2.5-10mg q1-4hr as needed OR
- If using intermitent nebs at home PTA, start on continuous
- 6-12 puffs q20min up to 4h, then q1-4hr as needed
- Levalbuterol is pure R-enantiomer, whereas racemic albuterol as above is 50:50 mix of R and S albuterol
- Most clinical studies fail to show benefit over racemic albuterol
- Levalbuterol at 5x the cost, may not warrant the small benefits seen in some studies
- In severe asthma exacerbation, be aware of lactic acidosis that develops due to pathology and the added lactic acidosis from albuterol,
- Manifests as worsening respiratory distress, tachypnea, compensatory increase in ventilation
- Ensure adequate intravascular volume, but carefully volume expand as acute asthma may increase ADH secretion
- Rarely, clinically important hypokalemia, alongside hyperglycemia and leukocytosis, may result from repeated beta agonists and sympathomimetics

sections.title: Ipratropium
lines: - Only shown to be effective in the acute setting to reduce hospitalization rates and improve lung function
- No benefit of adding to inpatient, hospitalized regimens

sections.title: Steroids
lines: Should be given in the first hour with effects to reduce admission and rate of relapses
- As effective as prednisone especially in children
- Single dose dexamethasone may be equally effective to 5 days of prednisone in adults
- 0.6mg/kg IV or PO (max 16mg); 2nd dose 24hr later may be an equally good option as single dose therapy
- Only use IV if cannot tolerate PO since equal effectiveness between dosing routes
- Oral and IV steroids are safe during pregnancy (though technically Category C)
- Inhaled corticosteroids may be considered as a rescue effort for severe asthma, given over a 90 min period

sections.title: Magnesium
lines: - 25-75 mg/kg over 30 min (2-3 g IV in most adults)
- Duration of action approximately 20 min, beware of hypotension in rapid administration due to smooth muscle relaxation mechanism
- In patients with moderate to severe asthma there is a decreased rate of admission with an NNT of 2
- High-dose, prolonged magnesium may expedite discharge from the ED in non-infectious asthma in pediatric study
- MAX 8,000 mg for 4 hours, monitor for cardiopulmonary complications
- No interventions or discontinuations of magnesium sulfate due to adverse events in the study
- NNT of 2-3, for hospital discharge before 24 hours

sections.title: Non-invasive ventilation
lines: - Consider as alternative to intubation or pre-oxygenation prior to intubation
- Alleviates muscle fatigue which leads to larger tidal volumes
- May drive nebulized treatments deeper into airways
- PEEP 0-3, only enough to match patient's auto-PEEP

sections.title: Other Beta-Agonists
lines: - Inhalation is preferred route of administration, but adequate drug delivery to small airways may be hampered in severe attacks
- Terbutaline and epinephrine can be administered IM/IV/SubQ
- Need to monitor for arrhythmias, tachycardia, hypertension, cardiac ischemia

sections.title: Epinephrine
lines: - 1:1000 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5mg) subQ or IM Q20min x3
- Nebulized racemic epinephrine 0.03 mL/kg (2.25% solution) diluted in 3-5 mL NS via jet nebulizer q3-4hr PRN shown to be as safe as nebulized albuterol
- In severe, life-threatening asthma, IV epinephrine may be safe to consider, substantiated only by a case series of adults in 2003, however
- Epinephrine infusion for adults at 5mcg/min (0.05mcg/kg/min for pediatrics) after requiring multiple epinephrine doses.

sections.title: Terbutaline
lines: - Caution in elderly/CHF with greater potential for cardiotoxicity
- Then followed by infusion at 1 µg/kg/min, titrated up by increments of 1 to max of 10 1 µg/kg/min
- Elevated troponins q4hrs during infusion, more common in cTnI vs. cTnT, with EKG changes of ischemia should prompt re-evaluation for stopping infusion
- Some experts have nebulized IV form

sections.title: Intubation and Invasive Ventilation
lines: - Relative indications include worsening hypercapnea, exhaustion, altered mental status, CO2 narcosis without any specific number endpoint on blood gases, refractory hypoxemia, status asthmaticus
- Provides bronchodilation and sedation however it does promote secretions
- Ketamine is the preferred induction agent for intubation in an asthmatic.
- Ventilation of asthmatic patients requires deep sedation
- Avoid long-term administration of neuromuscular blocking agents such as succinylcholine for prolonged periods in ICU (>12 hours), if possible, given higher rates of complication
- A large ET tube is preferred (>8.0 mm)
- Goal: obtaining a pH above 7.2 and plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O
- If Pplat >30 must lower respiratory rate
- If Pplat under 30 cannot be maintained, other causes of decreased respiratory system compliance must be considered (i.e. pneumothorax, misplaced endotracheal tube, pulmonary edema, etc.)
- Low peak pressure/avoidance of breath stacking more important than correcting CO2
- Keep FiO2 minimum to achieve SpO2 > 90%
- Monitor for breath stacking (inspiratory holds, plateau pressures)
- Most common cause of post-intubation hypotension

sections.title: Asthma Arrest
lines: - Consider empiric bilateral chest tubes or rapid ultrasound to identify pneumothorax

sections.title: Antibiotics
lines: - Administration of antibiotics only when physical exam or ancillary testing supportive of bacterial infection
- Antibiotics may be considered for select patients and may improve symptoms and peak expiratory flow, further understanding needed to identify which patients may be most likely to benefit

sections.title: Heliox
lines: - 60 to 80% helium is blended with 20 to 40% oxygen
- Heliox improves laminar flow and may increase the diffusion of carbon dioxide by improving ventilation

sections.title: Leukotriene Modifiers
lines: - Zafirlukast (20 mg bid) and montelukast (10 mg/day)

sections.title: Outpatient Treatment
lines: Every patient with asthma should be on an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) or a combination medication with an inhaled corticosteroid; treatment with a short-acting beta2-agonist (SABA) alone is no longer recommended.

sections.title: Preferred Approach
lines: - Use as both rescue and maintenance inhaler (simplifies and increases compliance)

- GINA recommends budesonide or beclomethasone as the inhaled corticosteroid, and formoterol as the long acting beta2 agonist. The only U.S. formulation meeting this recommendation is Symbicort (budesonide-formoterol).

sections.title: Alternative Approach
lines: Use only if preferred approach above (i.e., LABA) is not available
- Treatment plan: if reliever is SABA, take ICS whenever SABA is used

sections.title: Non-Pharmacological Treatment
lines: In addition to, not as a replacement for, medical management.

sections.title: Disposition
lines: Disposition is based on response to treatment (and remaining symptoms after treatment)

sections.title: Discharge
lines: - Often, patients will still have mild wheezing, but should have complete resolution of tachypnea, hypoxia, and work of breathing if being discharged
- A short course of glucocorticoids decreases chance of relapse
- Prednisone in adults (40-60 mg/day for 5-10 days without tapering), OR

sections.title: Admit
lines: - If symptoms persist or are severe
- Peak flow measurements are typically not performed in the ED; however, if performed:
- PEF >70% predicted → high likelihood of successful discharge

sections.title: External Links
lines: - Internet Book of Critical Care - Asthma

Other Associated with Normal/↑ Respiratory Effort

sections.title: Background
lines: - Persistent airflow limitation (FEV1:FVC < 0.70) that is progressive and not fully reversible
- The new definition from the GOLD initiative avoids either chronic bronchitis (85%) and emphysema (15%); most patients have mixture of both
- Although smoking is a major risk factor for developing COPD, only 15% of smokers actually develop COPD
- Characterized by a combination of parenchymal destruction and small airway disease with failure of gas exchange
- Acute exacerbations due to increased V/Q mismatch, not expiratory airflow limitation
- Relative chronic hypoxia present in many
- Chronic hypoxia can induce pulmonary hypertension, polycythemia and cor pulmonale

sections.title: Pseudomonas Risk Factors
lines: - Recent hospitalization (>2 days within previous 3 months)
- Frequent antibiotic treatment (>4 courses within past year)

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Increase in cough, sputum, or dyspnea beyond the normal day-to-day variation

sections.title: Airway — Intrathoracic Lower
lines: - Parasitic infection (eosinophilic pneumonia; in endemic areas)

sections.title: Airway — Extrathoracic (typically stridor ± wheeze)
lines: - Vocal cord dysfunction / paradoxical vocal fold motion

sections.title: Other
lines: - Pulmonary embolism (may present with wheeze in up to 25%)
- Vocal cord dysfunction (often misdiagnosed as refractory asthma)

sections.title: Emergent
lines: - Other Associated with Normal/↑ Respiratory Effort

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: - Perform if SpO2 <90% or concerned about symptomatic hypercapnia, however its routine use is not recommended
- Monitoring the patient's clinical status and pulse oximetry is often sufficient
- The decision to start noninvasive ventilation or to intubate should be guided to by the clinical state of the patient, presence of fatigue and response to therapy
- For every increase in PaC02 of 10 mmHg, the pH should change by 0.08
- Consider if concerned for alternative/additional diagnoses (e.g. pneumonia, CHF, pneumothorax, effusions)
- Usually not indicated except for patient with recent antibiotic failure
- The most common dysrhythmias are atrial fibrillation and multifocal atrial tachycardia
- Blood tests add little to the treatment of a COPD exacerbation
- GOLD Grading (based on post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC less than 70%):
- IV (very severe COPD) -> FEV1 < 30% of predicted

sections.title: Oxygen
lines: - Some COPD patients accustomed to relative hypoxia, thus higher oxygen levels may--> loss of hypoxic vasoconstriction-->increased shunt + increased alveolar dead space + haldane effect --> suppression of respiratory drive cause high levels of oxygen may cause loss of hypoxic vasoconstriction causing areas of increased shunt and increased alveolar dead space along with the Haldane effect and suppression of the respiratory drive.
- Do not withhold O2 if SpO2 <88%
- Maintain PaO2 above 60 mmHg or SpO2 88-92%
- SpO2 >93% associated with higher inpatient mortality
- If unable to correct hypoxemia with a low FiO2 consider alternative diagnosis
- Adequate oxygenation is essential, even if it leads to hypercapnia
- If hypercapnia leads to altered mental status, dysrhythmias, or acidemia consider Intubation

sections.title: Albuterol/ipratropium
lines: - Improves airflow obstruction and treatment should involve rapid administration upon recognition of COPD exacerbation.

sections.title: Steroids
lines: Similar efficacy between oral and intravenous. Treatment options include:
- Prednisone 60mg x 1, then 40mg PO daily x 5 days
- For outpatients a 5 day dose appears equally effective as longer doses and a taper is not required.

sections.title: Magnesium
lines: - Studies have found that while helpful in asthma, results fail to demonstrate positive benefit for COPD

sections.title: Antibiotics
lines: Indicated for patients with purulent sputum, increased sputum production, or requiring Non Invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (NNT = 3 to prevent treatment failure and 8 to prevent death)
- Antibiotics for COPD exacerbations have an NNT of:

sections.title: Outpatient Healthy
lines: - Antibiotics should be a 3-5 day course and options include:

sections.title: Inpatient
lines: - If Pseudomonas risk factors then use:
- Levofloxacin PO or IV OR Cefepime IV OR Ceftazidime IV OR Piperacillin/Tazobactam IV
- Levofloxacin or Moxifloxacin PO or IV OR Ceftriaxone IV OR Cefotaxime IV

sections.title: Noninvasive ventilation (CPAP or BiPaP)
lines: - CPAP: start at low level and titrate up to max 15

sections.title: Outcomes
lines: - Improves acidosis and ease respiratory distress
- Inability to clear secretions, high aspiration risk
- Upper airway obstruction, craniofacial trauma, recent craniofacial surgery

sections.title: Mechanical ventilation
lines: - Severe dyspnea with use of accessory muscles and paradoxical breathing
- RR>35 bpm with anticipated clinical course for respiratory failure
Consider ketamine for sedation for intubation (in combination with paralytic) as ketamine has bronchodilatory effect
- Consider pressure control to prevent markedly elevated peak pressures
- Maximize expiratory time by modifying I:E ratio
- If patient with worsening hypercarbia, may benefit from paradoxically decreasing respiratory rate to improve expiratory time and improve gas exchange

sections.title: Antibiotic Dosing
lines: - Azithromycin 500mg PO x1 on day 1, then 250mg PO q24h x4 days; Alt: 500mg PO q24h x3 days
- Clarithromycin 1000mg ER PO q24 x 7d (with food, do not cut/crush/chew); Alt: 250-500mg PO q12h x 7-14d

sections.title: Antibiotic Dosing
lines: - Azithromycin 500mg PO x1 on day 1, then 250mg PO q24h x4 days; Alt: 500mg PO q24h x3 days
- Clarithromycin 1000mg ER PO q24 x 7d (with food, do not cut/crush/chew); Alt: 250-500mg PO q12h x 7-14d

sections.title: Antibiotic Dosing
lines: - Azithromycin 500mg PO x1 on day 1, then 250mg PO q24h x4 days; Alt: 500mg PO q24h x3 days
- Clarithromycin 1000mg ER PO q24 x 7d (with food, do not cut/crush/chew); Alt: 250-500mg PO q12h x 7-14d

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Marked increase in intensity of symptoms (e.g. sudden development of resting dyspnea)

sections.title: Pneumonia Empiric Categories
lines: The term "health care-associated pneumonia" (HCAP) is no longer used. - Nosocomial pneumonia: Acquired in a hospital setting
- Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP): Acquired ≥48 hours after hospital admission
- Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP): Acquired ≥48 hours after endotracheal intubation

sections.title: Resistant Pathogen Risk Factors
lines: IDSA recommends covering empirically for resistant pathogens (e.g., MRSA, pseudomonas) in adults with CAP only if there is a treatment regimen based on "locally validated" risk factors. In that case, may give empiric coverage while awaiting culture results.
- Commonly accepted risk factors historically include:
- Prior respiratory isolation of MRSA or P. aeruginosa
- Recent hospitalization AND receipt of parenteral antibiotics (in the last 90 days)

sections.title: Commonly Encountered Pathogens by Risk Factor
Viral
lines: - Cause other diseases, but sometimes cause pneumonia

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Fever, chills, pleuritic chest pain, productive cough
- Abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, diarrhea may be seen with Legionella infection

sections.title: ED Pearls
lines: - Elderly/immunocompromised patients may present atypically: altered mental status, falls, functional decline, or hypothermia rather than classic fever and cough
- Tachypnea (RR >24) is the most sensitive vital sign finding in elderly patients and should prompt evaluation even in the absence of typical symptoms
- Sepsis screening should be performed in all patients with suspected pneumonia; pneumonia is the most common cause of sepsis
- Patients with lower lobe pneumonia may present with predominantly upper abdominal pain, mimicking an acute abdomen

sections.title: Emergent
lines: - Other Associated with Normal/↑ Respiratory Effort

sections.title: Workup
lines: - May have negative CXR early in disease or in cases of dehydration; infiltrate may "blossom" after providing rehydration and repeat imaging
- Absence of CXR findings does not preclude diagnosis; high clinical suspicion with adventitious breath sounds can be consistent with pneumonia despite negative imaging
- Immunocompromised patients may not manifest radiographic evidence of pneumonia despite suggestive clinical findings
- Clinical and radiographic findings do not necessarily correspond: the patient may be improving clinically despite having a worsening appearance on the CXR
- Can be considered as an alternative to CXR
- Key findings: hepatization of lung tissue, dynamic air bronchograms, B-lines, and subpleural consolidation
- Particularly useful for identifying parapneumonic pleural effusion
- Chemistry (including BUN, glucose for PSI scoring)
- IDSA does not support using initial serum procalcitonin levels to determine whether empiric antibiotics should be initiated
- Clinical judgement plus radiographic evidence alone should guide therapy (strong recommendation, moderate quality of evidence)
- Procalcitonin sensitivity for detecting bacterial infection ranges from 38% to 91%; not accurate enough to justify withholding antibiotics
- Blood Cultures are ONLY indicated for CAP patients with:
- Empiric treatment for MRSA or P. aeruginosa (required)
- Prior MRSA or P. aeruginosa respiratory infection
- Recent hospitalization AND parenteral antibiotics in the last 90 days
- The yield of blood cultures is low (2% to 9%) in adults without severe CAP, and empiric therapy is rarely changed based on these results
- Sputum Gram stain and culture: recommended for the same indications as blood cultures above
- Lower respiratory tract samples from intubated patients should be sent for Gram stain and culture shortly after intubation (higher yield than sputum)
- MRSA nasal PCR (if available): High negative predictive value (~95%) for ruling out MRSA pneumonia; useful for de-escalation of empiric MRSA coverage
- Legionella and Pneumococcal urinary antigen testing: Not routinely recommended; consider for:
- Legionella antigen in alcoholics, outbreaks, or recent (within 2 weeks) travel history
- Influenza testing: Recommended when influenza is circulating in the community; molecular testing (PCR) preferred over rapid antigen

sections.title: IDSA Severe Pneumonia Criteria
lines: Severe pneumonia can be diagnosed with either one major criterion or three or more minor criteria. These criteria have a pooled sensitivity of 84% and specificity of 78% for predicting ICU admission.

sections.title: Major criteria
lines: - Septic shock with need for vasopressors

sections.title: Outpatient
lines: Coverage targeted at S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae, and Legionella

sections.title: Healthy
lines: No comorbidities (chronic heart, lung, liver, or renal disease; diabetes mellitus; alcoholism; malignancy; or asplenia) and no risk factors for MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa (include prior respiratory isolation of MRSA or P. aeruginosa or recent hospitalization AND receipt of parenteral antibiotics (in the last 90 d))
- Amoxicillin 1 g three times daily (strong recommendation, moderate quality of evidence), OR
- Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily (conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence), OR
- Macrolide in areas with pneumococcal resistance to macrolides <25% (conditional recommendation, moderate quality of evidence).
- Azithromycin 500 mg on first day then 250 mg daily OR
- Clarithromycin 500 mg BID or clarithromycin ER 1,000 mg daily

sections.title: Unhealthy
lines: If patient has comorbidities or risk factors for MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa

- 500 mg/125 mg TID OR amox/clav 875 mg/125 mg BID OR 2,000 mg/125 mg BID. Duration is for a minimum of 5 days and varies based on disease severity and response to therapy; patients should be afebrile for ≥48 hours and clinically stable before therapy is discontinued
- Cefpodoxime 200 mg BID OR cefuroxime 500 mg BID
- Azithromycin 500 mg on first day then 250 mg daily
- OR clarithromycin 500 mg BID OR clarithromycin ER 1,000 mg daily (strong recommendation, moderate quality of evidence for combination therapy)
- OR doxycycline 100 mg BID (conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence for combination therapy)
- Monotherapy: respiratory fluoroquinolone (strong recommendation, moderate quality of evidence):

sections.title: Inpatient
lines: - Monotherapy or combination therapy is acceptable
- Combination therapy includes a cephalosporin and macrolide targeting atypicals and Strep Pneumonia

- Adjunctive corticosteroids in severe CAP: The SCCM 2024 Focused Update strongly recommends corticosteroids for hospitalized adults with severe bacterial CAP (strong recommendation, moderate certainty)
- CAPE COD trial (NEJM 2023): Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV daily (50 mg q6h) in severe CAP requiring ICU/intermediate care → ↓ 28-day mortality (6.2% vs 11.9%, NNT ~18), ↓ intubation, ↓ vasopressor use
- Duration: 200 mg/day for 4–7 days based on clinical improvement, then tapered (total 8–14 days)
- Excluded patients already in septic shock
- No recommendation for or against steroids in less severe CAP
- Avoid in influenza pneumonia (without bacterial superinfection)
- Duration: Minimum 5 days; continue until clinically stable (temp ≤37.8°C, HR ≤100, RR ≤24, SBP ≥90, SpO2 ≥90% on RA, tolerating PO, baseline mental status) for ≥48 hours
- De-escalation: If empiric MRSA or Pseudomonas coverage was started, de-escalate to standard CAP therapy within 48 hours if cultures/MRSA nasal PCR are negative and patient is improving

sections.title: Community Acquired (Non-ICU)
lines: Coverage against community acquired organisms plus M. catarrhalis, Klebsiella, S. aureus
- β-lactam (e.g. ceftriaxone 1–2g daily OR ampicillin-sulbactam 1.5–3g q6h OR cefotaxime 1–2g q8h OR ceftaroline 600mg q12h) PLUS
- Macrolide (e.g. azithromycin 500 mg daily or clarithromycin 500 mg BID) OR
- Doxycycline 100mg IV/PO BID (if contraindications to both macrolides and fluoroquinolones) OR

sections.title: ICU, Low Risk of MRSA/Pseudomonas
lines: - Ceftriaxone 1-2g IV + (moxifloxacin 400mg IV or levofloxacin 750mg IV)
- (Moxifloxacin or levofloxacin) + (aztreonam 1-2g IV or clindamycin 600mg IV)

sections.title: ICU, Risk of Pseudomonas (without MRSA risk)
lines: 2019 guidelines recommend single antipseudomonal β-lactam (changed from double gram-negative coverage in 2007 guidelines)
- Antipseudomonal β-lactam: Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g q6h OR Cefepime 2g q8h OR meropenem 1g q8h OR Imipenem 500mg q6h
- PLUS azithromycin 500mg IV daily OR respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750mg IV daily or moxifloxacin 400mg IV daily)
- If Pseudomonas is not isolated and patient is improving, de-escalate to standard CAP regimen

sections.title: ICU, Risk of MRSA
lines: Add MRSA coverage to appropriate regimen above
- Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8-12h (target AUC/MIC 400-600) OR Linezolid 600 mg IV q12h
- MRSA nasal PCR has a high negative predictive value (~95%); if negative, MRSA coverage can be safely discontinued

sections.title: Hospital Acquired Pneumonia (HAP)
lines: Pneumonia developing ≥48 hours after hospital admission in non-intubated patients
- Antipseudomonal β-lactam from two different classes with activity against Pseudomonas:
- Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g q6h OR Cefepime 2g q8h OR ceftazidime 2g q8h OR meropenem 1g q8h OR Imipenem 500mg q6h
- PLUS antipseudomonal non-β-lactam: Levofloxacin 750mg IV q24h OR ciprofloxacin 400mg q8h OR aminoglycoside (e.g. tobramycin, gentamicin, amikacin)
- PLUS Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h OR Linezolid 600mg IV q12h
- Single antipseudomonal β-lactam (from list above) may be sufficient
- Of note, the combination of vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam carries higher risk of AKI compared to cefepime + vancomycin
- Consider tobramycin or other aminoglycoside in place of fluoroquinolones given FDA 2016 warnings

sections.title: Ventilator Associated Pneumonia (VAP)
lines: Pneumonia developing ≥48 hours after endotracheal intubation
- Include an antibiotic from each of these 3 categories:
- 1. MRSA coverage: Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h OR Linezolid 600 mg IV q12h PLUS
- 2. Antipseudomonal β-Lactam: Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g q6h OR Cefepime 2g q8h OR meropenem 1g q8h OR Imipenem 500mg q6h OR Aztreonam 2g q8h PLUS
- 3. Antipseudomonal non-β-Lactam: Ciprofloxacin 400mg IV q8h OR Levofloxacin 750mg IV q24h OR aminoglycoside
- Single antipseudomonal β-lactam monotherapy (from list above) is acceptable

sections.title: Adjunctive Corticosteroids
lines: Updated guidance based on CAPE COD trial (2023) and SCCM 2024 Focused Update:
- The SCCM 2024 Focused Update strongly recommends corticosteroids for adult patients hospitalized with severe bacterial CAP (strong recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence)
- No recommendation for or against steroids in less severe CAP
- The CAPE COD trial (NEJM 2023): IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day in severe CAP requiring ICU/intermediate care admission showed:
- Duration: hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for 4 or 7 days based on clinical improvement, then tapered (total 8 or 14 days)
- Excluded patients already in septic shock

- REMAP-CAP (2025): Fixed-dose hydrocortisone 200 mg/day x 7 days in severe CAP triggered a futility stopping rule for 90-day mortality; however, this trial enrolled a more severely ill population with higher rates of septic shock than CAPE COD
- If patient has severe CAP (meets IDSA/ATS severity criteria, hypoxic, or being admitted to the ICU), consider hydrocortisone 200 mg IV daily (50 mg q6h) or methylprednisolone 40 mg IV daily
- No clear benefit in non-severe CAP
- Avoid in active influenza pneumonia (without bacterial superinfection) per 2019 ATS/IDSA

sections.title: Aspiration Pneumonia
lines: See also: Aspiration pneumonia and pneumonitis

- 2019 ATS/IDSA guidelines recommend against routinely adding anaerobic coverage beyond standard CAP empiric antibiotics in suspected aspiration pneumonia (conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence)
- Exception: Add anaerobic coverage (e.g. ampicillin-sulbactam, clindamycin, or carbapenem) if lung abscess or empyema is suspected

- Rationale: More recent studies show anaerobes are uncommon causes of aspiration pneumonia; unnecessary anaerobic coverage increases risk of Clostridioides difficile infection without mortality benefit
- Aspiration pneumonitis (chemical/inflammatory reaction without infection): supportive care only; antibiotics are not indicated unless infection develops

sections.title: Influenza-Associated Pneumonia
lines: - Anti-influenza treatment (e.g. oseltamivir) should be prescribed to all adults with CAP who test positive for influenza, regardless of duration of illness or hospitalization status
- Standard antibacterial treatment should also be initially prescribed alongside antivirals in patients with clinical and radiographic evidence of CAP who test positive for influenza
- Avoid routine corticosteroids in influenza pneumonia

sections.title: Treatment Duration and De-escalation
lines: - Continue until the patient achieves clinical stability, defined as:
- De-escalation: If empiric MRSA or Pseudomonas coverage was started, de-escalate to standard CAP therapy within 48 hours if cultures and MRSA nasal PCR are negative and the patient is improving

sections.title: Treatment Failure
lines: Consider the following if patient is not improving at 48-72 hours:
- Resistant or unusual organism (obtain cultures if not already done)
- Complications: empyema, lung abscess, parapneumonic effusion
- Consider CT chest for complications not visible on CXR

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Use clinical judgment plus PORT Score (PSI) to guide disposition per IDSA 2019 guidelines
- No hypoxia, hemodynamic instability, or significant comorbidities
- Admit to ICU (PSI class V, or meeting major/minor criteria):
- Requiring vasopressors or mechanical ventilation (major criteria)
- 3 or more minor criteria: RR >30, PaO2/FiO2 <250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, BUN >20, WBC <4, platelets <100, hypothermia, hypotension requiring aggressive fluids

sections.title: Prognosis
lines: - Half of patients are still symptomatic at 30 days, with a significant minority experiencing chest pain, malaise or mild dyspnea even 2 to 3 months after treatment
- In adults with CAP whose symptoms have resolved within 5-7 days, it is not recommended to routinely obtain follow-up chest imaging
- Consider follow-up imaging in 7-12 weeks for patients at higher risk for malignancy (e.g. smokers >50 years) to ensure resolution and exclude underlying malignancy

- (Moxifloxacin or levofloxacin) + (aztreonam 1-2g IV or clindamycin 600mg IV)

sections.title: ICU, Risk of Pseudomonas (without MRSA risk)
lines: 2019 guidelines recommend single antipseudomonal β-lactam (changed from double gram-negative coverage in 2007 guidelines)
- Antipseudomonal β-lactam: Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g q6h OR Cefepime 2g q8h OR meropenem 1g q8h OR Imipenem 500mg q6h
- PLUS azithromycin 500mg IV daily OR respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750mg IV daily or moxifloxacin 400mg IV daily)
- If Pseudomonas is not isolated and patient is improving, de-escalate to standard CAP regimen

sections.title: ICU, Risk of MRSA
lines: Add MRSA coverage to appropriate regimen above
- Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8-12h (target AUC/MIC 400-600) OR Linezolid 600 mg IV q12h
- MRSA nasal PCR has a high negative predictive value (~95%); if negative, MRSA coverage can be safely discontinued

sections.title: Hospital Acquired Pneumonia (HAP)
lines: Pneumonia developing ≥48 hours after hospital admission in non-intubated patients
- Antipseudomonal β-lactam from two different classes with activity against Pseudomonas:
- Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g q6h OR Cefepime 2g q8h OR ceftazidime 2g q8h OR meropenem 1g q8h OR Imipenem 500mg q6h
- PLUS antipseudomonal non-β-lactam: Levofloxacin 750mg IV q24h OR ciprofloxacin 400mg q8h OR aminoglycoside (e.g. tobramycin, gentamicin, amikacin)
- PLUS Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h OR Linezolid 600mg IV q12h
- Single antipseudomonal β-lactam (from list above) may be sufficient
- Of note, the combination of vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam carries higher risk of AKI compared to cefepime + vancomycin
- Consider tobramycin or other aminoglycoside in place of fluoroquinolones given FDA 2016 warnings

sections.title: Ventilator Associated Pneumonia (VAP)
lines: Pneumonia developing ≥48 hours after endotracheal intubation
- Include an antibiotic from each of these 3 categories:
- 1. MRSA coverage: Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h OR Linezolid 600 mg IV q12h PLUS
- 2. Antipseudomonal β-Lactam: Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g q6h OR Cefepime 2g q8h OR meropenem 1g q8h OR Imipenem 500mg q6h OR Aztreonam 2g q8h PLUS
- 3. Antipseudomonal non-β-Lactam: Ciprofloxacin 400mg IV q8h OR Levofloxacin 750mg IV q24h OR aminoglycoside
- Single antipseudomonal β-lactam monotherapy (from list above) is acceptable

sections.title: Adjunctive Corticosteroids
lines: Updated guidance based on CAPE COD trial (2023) and SCCM 2024 Focused Update:
- The SCCM 2024 Focused Update strongly recommends corticosteroids for adult patients hospitalized with severe bacterial CAP (strong recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence)
- No recommendation for or against steroids in less severe CAP
- The CAPE COD trial (NEJM 2023): IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day in severe CAP requiring ICU/intermediate care admission showed:
- Duration: hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for 4 or 7 days based on clinical improvement, then tapered (total 8 or 14 days)
- Excluded patients already in septic shock

- REMAP-CAP (2025): Fixed-dose hydrocortisone 200 mg/day x 7 days in severe CAP triggered a futility stopping rule for 90-day mortality; however, this trial enrolled a more severely ill population with higher rates of septic shock than CAPE COD
- If patient has severe CAP (meets IDSA/ATS severity criteria, hypoxic, or being admitted to the ICU), consider hydrocortisone 200 mg IV daily (50 mg q6h) or methylprednisolone 40 mg IV daily
- No clear benefit in non-severe CAP
- Avoid in active influenza pneumonia (without bacterial superinfection) per 2019 ATS/IDSA

sections.title: Aspiration Pneumonia
lines: See also: Aspiration pneumonia and pneumonitis

- 2019 ATS/IDSA guidelines recommend against routinely adding anaerobic coverage beyond standard CAP empiric antibiotics in suspected aspiration pneumonia (conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence)
- Exception: Add anaerobic coverage (e.g. ampicillin-sulbactam, clindamycin, or carbapenem) if lung abscess or empyema is suspected

- Rationale: More recent studies show anaerobes are uncommon causes of aspiration pneumonia; unnecessary anaerobic coverage increases risk of Clostridioides difficile infection without mortality benefit
- Aspiration pneumonitis (chemical/inflammatory reaction without infection): supportive care only; antibiotics are not indicated unless infection develops

sections.title: Influenza-Associated Pneumonia
lines: - Anti-influenza treatment (e.g. oseltamivir) should be prescribed to all adults with CAP who test positive for influenza, regardless of duration of illness or hospitalization status
- Standard antibacterial treatment should also be initially prescribed alongside antivirals in patients with clinical and radiographic evidence of CAP who test positive for influenza
- Avoid routine corticosteroids in influenza pneumonia

sections.title: Treatment Duration and De-escalation
lines: - Continue until the patient achieves clinical stability, defined as:
- De-escalation: If empiric MRSA or Pseudomonas coverage was started, de-escalate to standard CAP therapy within 48 hours if cultures and MRSA nasal PCR are negative and the patient is improving

sections.title: Treatment Failure
lines: Consider the following if patient is not improving at 48-72 hours:
- Resistant or unusual organism (obtain cultures if not already done)
- Complications: empyema, lung abscess, parapneumonic effusion
- Consider CT chest for complications not visible on CXR

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Use clinical judgment plus PORT Score (PSI) to guide disposition per IDSA 2019 guidelines
- No hypoxia, hemodynamic instability, or significant comorbidities
- Admit to ICU (PSI class V, or meeting major/minor criteria):
- Requiring vasopressors or mechanical ventilation (major criteria)
- 3 or more minor criteria: RR >30, PaO2/FiO2 <250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, BUN >20, WBC <4, platelets <100, hypothermia, hypotension requiring aggressive fluids

sections.title: Prognosis
lines: - Half of patients are still symptomatic at 30 days, with a significant minority experiencing chest pain, malaise or mild dyspnea even 2 to 3 months after treatment
- In adults with CAP whose symptoms have resolved within 5-7 days, it is not recommended to routinely obtain follow-up chest imaging
- Consider follow-up imaging in 7-12 weeks for patients at higher risk for malignancy (e.g. smokers >50 years) to ensure resolution and exclude underlying malignancy

items: Other Associated with Normal/↑ Respiratory Effort

sections.title: Background
lines: - Active fluid secretion or leakage with high protein content
- Imbalance between hydrostatic (e.g. CHF) and oncotic (e.g. nephrotic syndrome)

sections.title: Common
lines: - Occurs in 40% of patients hospitalized with pneumonia
- Occurs in 30% of patients with PE

sections.title: Less Common
lines: - Both via hypoalbuminemia and transdiaphragmatic leakage of ascites

sections.title: Work-Up
lines: - Earliest sign is blunting of costophrenic angle
- Lateral decubitus with affected side down requires 50-75 cc of fluid for visualization
- PA view requires 200-250 cc of fluid
- Supine view may only show a generalized hazy appearance of affected hemithorax
- Fluid collects in isolation between lung base and diaphragm
- May not cause blunting of costophrnic angle or meniscus appearance
- Suspect if "hemidiaphragm" (actually fluid) is elevated and flattened
- Lateral decubitus with suspected side down will show free-flowing pleural fluid

sections.title: Exudative versus Transudative (Light's Criteria)
lines: - If one of the following is present the fluid is virtually always an exudate
- If none is present the fluid is virtually always a transudate
- Pleural fluid LDH > two thirds of upper limit for serum LDH

sections.title: Exudative Work-up
lines: - Gram stain and culture (place 10cc into blood culture bottle at the bedside)
- RBC >100K: trauma, malignancy, pneumonia, or pulmonary infarction
- Neutrophil predominance (>50%): parapneumonic, pulmonary embolism, pancreatitis
- Lymphocytic predominance (>50%): malignancy, TB, PE, viral pleuritis
- Low glucose (<60) seen in parapneumonic, empyema, malignant, TB, and RA
- May be left at room temperature for up to 1hr with out affecting results
- In parapneumonic effusions, <7.10 predicts development of empyema or persistence and indicates need for thoracostomy tube drainage
- Amylase: >100 in pleural effusions due to pancreatitis or esophageal rupture

sections.title: Management
lines: - Therapeutic thoracentesis with max drainage 1-1.5L to avoid reexpansion pulmonary edema
- Patient positioning (lateral decubitus) for unilateral pleural effusions
- Most of the time, "Good lung to Ground" to improve V/Q mismatch
- Exceptions in which "bad" lung should be "down":
- Failure to respond to antibiotic treatment
- Effusion involving >50% of thorax or air-fluid level on CXR
- Diuretic therapy resolves >75% of effusions within 2-3d

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - All new pleural effusions of non-trace size typically require admission

sections.title: _intro
lines: "Spontaneous" essentially refers to all pneumothoraces of "non-traumatic" etiologies

sections.title: Background
lines: - bullae/blebs, emphysema, cystic fibrosis, PJP pneumonia, lung abscess, tuberculosis, neoplasm, catamenial

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Sudden onset pleuritic chest pain evolving to dull constant ache over days
- Most often occurs at rest, not during exertion
- Tachypnea, hypoxemia, increased work of breathing

sections.title: Emergent
lines: - Other Associated with Normal/↑ Respiratory Effort

sections.title: Clinically Stable
lines: Defined as having all of the following:
- SaO2 >90% on room air and patient can speak in whole sentences

sections.title: Workup
lines: - Displaced visceral pleural line without lung markings between pleural line and chest wall
- Expiratory films DO NOT improve accuracy
- Lateral decubitus films with suspected side up do increase sensitivity. Good approach in pediatrics to avoid CT

sections.title: Lung ultrasound of pneumothorax
lines: - No lung sliding seen (not specific for pneumothorax)
- May also identify "lung point": distinct point where you no longer see lung sliding (pathognomonic)
- Absence of lung sliding WITHOUT lung point could represent apnea or right mainstem intubation
- Evaluate other intercostal spaces because pneumothorax may only be seen in least dependent area of thorax
- Bar Code appearance/"Stratosphere" sign on M-mode (absence of "seashore" waves)
- Ultrasound has greater sensitivity than chest x-ray for pneumothorax in trauma patients

sections.title: Estimating Pneumothorax Size
lines: - On a conventional, upright posterior-anterior chest radiograph:
- Very small: <1 cm interpleural distance (confined to upper 1/3 of chest) OR only seen on CT
- Small: ≤3cm lung apex to cupola (chest wall apex) on CXR
- Large: >3cm lung apex to cupola (chest wall apex) on CXR

sections.title: Management
lines: Supplemental oxygen (non-rebreather mask) initially for all

sections.title: Unstable
lines: - Needle decompression followed by chest tube insertion
- ATLS guidelines recommend 5cm angiocath at 2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line
- More recent evidence shows higher success rates with 4th/5th intercostal space at the anterior or mid-axillary line

sections.title: First Episode
lines: - Observe on supplemental oxygen (non-rebreather mask) for 6 hours; repeat CXR and discharge if no progression; return in 24 hours for a recheck
- If fail, admit with chest tube to suction for thoracoscopy (VATS)^

- 2020 study supports conservative therapy vs chest tube. however there are issues with study including “significant drop out rate, the relatively large number of protocol violations, the large inferiority margins and the short intervention time.”
- unilateral primary spontaneous pneumothorax of 32% or more on chest radiography according to the Collins method (sum of interpleural distances, >6 cm)

- Secondary pneumothorax, defined as pneumothorax occurring in the setting of acute trauma (including iatrogenic) or underlying lung disease including but not limited to COPD, pulmonary fibrosis, TB, cystic fibrosis, lung cancer and asthma that requires regular preventative medication or has been symptomatic within the last two years
- Previous spontaneous pneumothorax on the same side 3. Coexistent haemothorax (i.e. spontaneous haemopneumothorax)

- Clinical instability suggesting tension pneumothorax; respiratory distress persisting despite oxygen and parenteral narcotic analgesia (RR >30/min or SpO2 <90%), SBP <90 mmHg, HR greater than or equal to SBP.
- Social circumstances whereby the patient either does not have adequate support after discharge to re-attend hospital if required, or is unlikely to present for study follow up.
- Air travel within the next 12 weeks if this cannot be deferred should the pneumothorax be slow to resolve"
- Observed for a minimum of 4 hours then repeat chest X-ray.
- Discharge if no supplementary oxygen and walking comfortably,
- clinically significant symptoms persisted despite adequate analgesia
- chest pain or dyspnea prevented mobilization
- patient was unwilling to continue with conservative treatment

- the patient’s condition became physiologically unstable (systolic blood pressure of <90 mm Hg, heart rate in beats per minute greater than or equal to systolic blood pressure in millimeters of mercury, respiratory rate of >30 breaths per minute, or Spo2 of <90% while the patient was breathing ambient air)
- repeat chest radiograph showed an enlarging pneumothorax along with physiological instability.

sections.title: Recurrent OR Hemopneumothorax
lines: - Admit with chest tube for thoracoscopy (VATS)^
^If thoracoscopy (VATS) is not readily available, chemical pleurodesis through the chest tube

sections.title: Secondary Pneumothorax (Stable)
lines: - Asymptomatic AND very small (<1 cm interpleural distance)
- Observation with supplemental oxygen; repeat CXR in 12-24 hours
- Chest tube (some centers may choose needle aspiration under ultrasound guidance)
- Observation alone associated with some mortality

sections.title: Needle Aspiration of Pneumothorax
lines: - Use thoracentesis or "pig-tail" kit, if available
- Place in 2nd IC space in midclavicular line or 4th/5th IC space in anterior axillary line
- Withdraw air with syringe until no more can be aspirated
- Assume a persistent air leak (failure) if no resistance after 4 liters of air has been aspirated AND the lung has not expanded
- Once no further air can be aspirated:
- Place closed stopcock and secure catheter to the chest wall
- If adequate lung expansion has occurred, remove catheter
- Following another two hours of observation, obtain another CXR
- If the lung remains expanded, may discharge patient
- May discharge with follow-up within two days
- If 2.5 L of air has been aspirated, and a significant PTX remains, tube thoracostomy is indicated
- NEJM video on needle aspiration of pneumothorax.

sections.title: Adult Chest Tube Sizes
lines: - Traumatic hemothorax ("any acute hemothorax visible on chest radiograph")

sections.title: Secondary
lines: - All admitted (even if small and clinically stable)

sections.title: Special Instructions
lines: - Can consider flying 2 weeks after full resolution of traumatic pneumothroax

sections.title: Esophagitis Types
lines: - Infectious Mainly seen in patients w/ immunosuppression (HIV/AIDS, cancer, steroids)
- Esophageal candidiasis: often an AIDS defining lesion

sections.title: Work-Up
lines: - Consider HIV workup if unknown causation, risk factors

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: - Generally clinical diagnosis in ED (requires EGD for conclusive diagnosis)

sections.title: Management
lines: - Fluconazole: 200mg PO loading dose x1 followed by 100-200 mg PO for 7-14 days

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Admit if unable to tolerate PO or if underlying immunosuppression (e.g. HIV)

sections.title: Background
lines: - Bleeding originating proximal to ligament of Treitz
- In the acute setting, the hemoglobin/hematocrit may be normal until dilutional anemia appears after volume resuscitation
- Older patients -> peptic ulcer disease, esophagitis, gastritis; younger patients -> Mallory-Weiss tears, GI varices, gastropathy

sections.title: Risk Factors
lines: - RR of bleeding for COX-1 inhibitors is 4.5 (3.82-5.31)
- RR of bleeding for COX-2 inhibitors is 1.88 (0.96-3.71)

sections.title: Prehospital
lines: - Airway: suction to prevent aspiration, provide oxygen as needed
- Breathing: maintain patient in position of comfort
- Circulation: monitor for early signs of shock and provide fluid resuscitation if hypotensive. Blood products should be individualized based on local protocols
- Antiemetics can be given to decrease nausea and vomiting
- Assume the patient is hepatitis positive and wear appropriate personal protective gear

sections.title: History
lines: - Vomiting + retching followed by hematemesis is more likely Mallory-Weiss (esophageal)

sections.title: Physical Exam
lines: - Normal vital signs do not preclude the possibility of a severe bleed
- Altered mental status -> poor cerebral perfusion
- In the stable patient may indicate the anemia of a subacute/chronic bleed, in the unstable patient may indicate poor perfusion and massive blood loss
- Spider angiomata, palmar erythema, jaundice, gynecomastia, hepatomegaly, ascites
- Swallowed blood may result in coffee-ground emesis or melena
- Only 20% of patients with a positive fecal occult have an identified upper GI bleed.

sections.title: Workup
lines: - BUN/creatinine >30 suggests UGI if no history of renal failure (increased absorption/digestion of hb)
- More useful for diagnosing chronic occult bleeding (it could be positive for up to 2 weeks after an acute bleed)
- False-positive: vitamin C, red meat, methylene blue, bromide preparations, turnips, horseradish
- ECG (if >40 yo or if suspicious for silent MI, especially from demand ischemia)

sections.title: NG Lavage Controversy
lines: - Positive aspirate proves strong evidence for an upper GI source of bleeding
- Can assess presence of ongoing active bleeding
- Negative aspirate does not conclusively exclude upper GI source
- Provides useful information in only minority of patients without hematemesis
- Erythromycin 200mg IV can provide equal endoscopy conditions as lavage

sections.title: Diagnosis
lines: - Endoscopy frequently required for definitive diagnosis of underlying etiology

sections.title: Resuscitation
lines: - Place 2 large bore IVs (or sheath introducer/rapid infusion catheter) and monitor airway status
- Crystalloid IVF can be used for initial resuscitation but should be limited due to the dilutional anemia and coagulopathy that can result (i.e. IV fluid use in non-compressible hemorrhage)

sections.title: Proton pump inhibitor
lines: - Intermittent dosing of pantoprazole, esomeprazole, or omeprazole 40 mg IV BID not inferior to continuous infusion dosing
- Reduces the rate of re-bleeding and need for surgery if there is an ulcer, but does not reduce morbidity or mortality
- There is a mortality benefit in Asian patients

sections.title: Antibiotics
lines: For short-term prophylaxis against SBP and bacteremia
- OR ciprofloxacin IV or PO 500mg BID x7 days
- Patients with cirrhosis or history of ETOH abuse (regardless of whether bleeding is variceal or not)
- Prior to endoscopy or as soon as possible after endoscopy

sections.title: Other Medications
lines: - Consider octreotide (50 mcg IV bolus, then 50 mcg/hr continuous, maintained at 2-5 days in patients with concern for variceal bleeding)
- 0.4 unit bolus, then infuse at 0.4 - 1 unit/min
- Give with IV nitroglycerin at 10 - 50 mcg/min to bolster portal hypotension and reduce vasopressin systemic effects
- Associated with many vasoconstrictive complications to include peripheral necrosis, dysrhythmias, myocardial ischemia
- Terlipressin (analog of vasopressin, available outside U.S.)
- Alternative to vasopressin with mortality benefit
- Given as 2mg IV q4 hrs, then decrease to 1mg IV q4 hrs until bleeding stops
- tranexamic acid (TXA) initially thought to help, NNT = 30, no one harmed; but HALT-IT trial RCT found it did not reduce death from GI bleeding

sections.title: Packed red blood cell transfusion
lines: - In hemodynamically stable patients, the goal transfusion threshold should be 7 g/dl; NICE guidelines recommend avoidance of over-transfusion
- Failure to improve perfusion and vital signs after infusion of 2L NS

sections.title: Other Blood Products
lines: - FFP can be used to correct anticoagulated patients, but is not indicated in cirrhotics with variceal bleeding

sections.title: Balloon tamponade (e.g., Sengstaken-Blakemore or Minnesota Tubes)
lines: For life-threatening hemorrhage if endoscopy is not available
- Tracheal compression (consider intubation prior to balloon insertion)

sections.title: Endoscopy
lines: Should be performed at the discretion of the gastroenterologist; within 12 hrs for variceal bleeding
- Early endoscopy does not necessarily improve clinical outcomes
- Consider erythromycin 3mg/kg IV over 20-30min, 30-90min prior to endoscopy
- Achieves endoscopy conditions equal to lavage

sections.title: Intubation
lines: Protection of airway from massive aspiration, especially prior to endoscopy; does not protect against pneumonia or cardiopulmonary events
Have bed-side push-dose pressors on hand
- NGT (salem sump to remove stomach contents)
- Increases tone of lower esophageal sphincter
- Chest and HOB elevation to 45 degrees - consider intubating from 45 degrees to prevent gastric contents coming up
- RSI - consider halving sedation dosages for lost blood volume
- Succinylcholine and vecuronium increases LES tone
- Intubation with strong chance for first pass
- Slow and gentle BVM breaths at 10 breaths/min if first pass fails
- Trendelenberg if vomiting, keeping emesis out of lungs (have many suctions available before this happens)
- Meconium aspirator may be hooked up to ETT for large bore suction
- Antibiotics not needed in early phase of aspiration
- Chemical pneumonitis in first 24 hours, not bacterial pneumonia
- Early antibiotics may predispose patient to resistant bacterial superinfection
- SIRS-like response often occurs from aspiration, but otherwise not sepsis if there is no other concerning source or suspicion
- Consider withholding early antibiotics, but doing the rest of the sepsis treatments
- Erythromycin 3mg/kg IV over 20-30min, 30-90min prior to endoscopy; Achieves endoscopy conditions equal to lavage

sections.title: Admission
lines: - Anyone with a Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score above 0 (see discharge section below); consider the clinical Rockall risk score too

sections.title: Consider Discharge
lines: If Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score of 0 (<1% chance of requiring intervention):. Must meet ALL of the following:
- Patient did NOT present with melena
- Patient did NOT present with syncope

sections.title: Background
lines: - Loss of blood from the GI tract distal to the ligament of Treitz
- Diverticulosis cause majority; other conditions include colitis, angiodysplasia, polyps, colorectal cancer, hemorrhoids, anal fissures, inflammatory bowel disease
- Majority of cases originate distally to ileocecal valve, rather than small intestines
- Consider recent procedures such as abdominal surgeries or colonoscopies/polypectomies
- Must consider upper GI bleed (especially rapid transit) as a source, as a significant number of lower GI bleeds have a concurrent upper GI bleed, brisk or not
- 80% of lower GI bleeding will resolve spontaneously

sections.title: Medication Risk Factors
lines: - Obtain a thorough medication history to assess for new antiplatelets or anticoagulants

sections.title: Type of blood
lines: - Left colonic bleeding tends to be bright red, whereas right colonic is usually maroon and mixed with stool
- May represent upper GI source if bleeding is brisk; usually accompanied by hematemesis and hemodynamic instability
- Usually represents bleeding from upper GI source (see upper GI bleed)
- May represent slow bleeding or slow stool transit from lower GI source

sections.title: Undifferentiated lower gastrointestinal bleeding
lines: - Consider in patients with gastrointestinal bleeding and known abdominal aortic aneurysms or aortic grafts

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: - Digital rectal exam for guaiac or assessment of anorectal structural abnormalities
- Note that guaiac tests have low sensitivity, many false positive etiologies (red meat, red jello, certain fruits/veggies, iron), and may not change management clinically
- Consider chart review to search for prior colonoscopy/endoscopy results

sections.title: Workup
lines: - Consider q3-12hr serial Hgb, depending on suspected severity of bleed
- Initial Hgb may be normal if bleeding is acute
- BUN may be elevated if bleeding occurs from site high in GI tract, due to heme digestion to nitrogenous substances reflected in BUN
- CTA; Requires brisk bleeding rate (0.4-0.5 ml/min) for detection
- Tagged red blood cell scan. This is not typically an emergency study and is only recommended if CTA is unavailable or contraindicated
- ECG (if concern for silent ischemia in patients likely to have CAD)

sections.title: Definitive studies
lines: - Anoscopy if source of bleeding cannot be identified on external exam

sections.title: Management
lines: - NPO, if there is foreseeable endoscopy or surgery
- Consider transfusing pRBCs/platelets for unstable patients or with very low hemoglobin (<7). with cardiovascular disease use trigger of 8 and target of 10 hemoglobin.
- Base decision to transfuse on individual clinical factors. Active bleeding and tachycardia may call for transfusion despite a normal Hgb
Categorize as stable versus unstable using shock index: <1 stable; >1 unstable or suspect active bleeding
- CT angiography is preferred for hemodynamically unstable patients due to speed
- Positive CTA demonstrating extravasation/blush calls for IR consult for transcatheter arteriography and subsequent embolization.
- Consult GI for emergent colonoscopy, as it is the diagnostic/therapeutic procedure of choice (within 12-24 hours); upper endoscopy may be needed if CTA does not reveal source of GI bleeding
- Patients with a positive CTA are more likely to have a source found on subsequent colonoscopy
- Consult surgery if endoscopy and IR embolization fail or are not available

sections.title: Major Bleed and Existing Coagulopathy
lines: - PCC (preferred) or FFP for patients on warfarin
- Vitamin K 10mg IV (best bioavailability in critical patients)

- Consider targeted reversal agents for DOACs in life-threatening LGIB refractory to initial resuscitation treatments, if the DOAC was taken in the past 24 hours: See Anticoagulant reversal for life-threatening bleeds
- Platelets should be administered to thrombocytopenic patients to a goal of 30-50, depending if endoscopy is planned
- ACG recommends against Tranexamic acid as it has no evidence for benefit but may increase VTE

sections.title: Special situations
lines: - Marathon runners - 16% will have hematochezia within 24-48 hrs of race and 85% will be guaiac positive

sections.title: Discharge
lines: - Oakland score can help determine if outpatient management is feasible; a score of <8 can be considered for safe discharge
- Based on a recent meta-analysis, the Oakland score, compared to other LGIB risk scores, has good performance in predicting safe discharge, major bleeding, and need for transfusion
- Bleeding from hemorrhoids, anal fissures, or known IBD (hemodynamically stable)
- Minor, self-terminating bleed with no other indication for admission (shock index >1; low risk score calculated)

sections.title: Admission
lines: - Identified as high risk based on Oakland score

lines: - Balloon tamponade for massive GI bleeding

sections.title: Background
lines: - Patients with immunosuppression often have delayed or atypical presentations
- Fever is not a reliable marker for surgical disease
- Abdominal pain may be particularly misleading in elderly or diabetics
- Consider pain in any abdominal or pelvic region in a female of child-bearing age, including pre-teens, is an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - May be associated with nausea, vomiting or diarrhea
- Fever may be present in pain from infectious etiology

sections.title: Epigastric Pain
lines: - Peptic ulcer disease with or without perforation

sections.title: RUQ Pain
lines: - Peptic ulcer disease with or without perforation

sections.title: Left upper quadrant abdominal pain
lines: - Peptic ulcer disease with or without perforation

sections.title: LLQ Pain
lines: - Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's Disease, Ulcerative Colitis)

sections.title: Gynecologic/Obstetric
lines: - Normal variants may be noted on exam but generally do not cause pain or other symptoms
- Nabothian cysts: Epithelial cells within mucous glans that appear as yellow inclusions on the cervix
- Cervical Ectropion: Edothelial cells on the exterior of the cervix
- Parous cervix: The is no longer round but may have multiple shapes after birth

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: - Pregnancy test in all females of childbearing age — this is mandatory
- Vitals: Tachycardia and hypotension suggest serious pathology (hemorrhage, sepsis, perforation)
- Point-of-care ultrasound: FAST exam (free fluid), RUQ (gallbladder), aorta (AAA), renal (hydronephrosis)

sections.title: Management
lines: - Pain control: Do not withhold analgesia — multiple studies confirm it does not mask surgical findings
- Ketorolac 15-30 mg IV, acetaminophen 1g IV, or opioids for severe pain
- Antiemetics: Ondansetron 4 mg IV for nausea/vomiting
- IVF: Fluid resuscitation for dehydrated or hemodynamically unstable patients
- Antibiotics: Early if infection suspected (sepsis, perforated viscus, appendicitis)
- Surgical consultation: Emergent for peritonitis, perforation, ischemic bowel, ruptured AAA, ruptured ectopic

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Admit: Surgical abdomen, hemodynamic instability, intractable pain/vomiting, inability to tolerate PO, suspected serious pathology requiring observation or further workup
- Discharge: Benign exam with improvement after treatment, reliable follow-up, clear return precautions (worsening pain, fever, vomiting, inability to tolerate PO)

- The two most notoriously missed conditions are appendicitis and small bowel obstruction.. When discharging patients with abdominal pain, clear instructions should be given for return if there are red flags.

sections.title: Background
lines: Generally classified by GI and Non-GI causes:

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: Varies widely depending on clinical presentation

sections.title: Management
lines: - Address electrolyte derangements and dehydration as needed
- Inhaled isopropyl alcohol (sniffing an alcohol wipe) has been shown to reduce mild to moderate nausea and vomiting

sections.title: Disposition

sections.title: Background
lines: - Can involve any part of the GI tract from the mouth to the anus
- All layers of the bowel are involved
- Reason why fistulas and abscesses are common complications

sections.title: Extraintestinal Symptoms (50%)
lines: - Pain/stiffness of spine, hips, neck, rib cage
- Low back pain with morning stiffness
- Acute blurring of vision, photophobia, pain, perilimbic scleral injection
- Eye burning or itching with out visual changes or pain; scleral and conj hyperemia
- Painful, red, raised nodules on extensor surfaces of arms/legs
- Violaceous, ulcerative lesions with necrotic center found in pretibial region or trunk
- Increased risk for calcium oxalate stones due to hyperoxaluria

sections.title: Colitis
lines: - Ischemic bowel disease (e.g. mesenteric ischemia, strangulated hernia)

sections.title: Work-Up
lines: - Rule out alternate etiologies for symptoms
- Evaluate for complications (e.g. fistulae, abscess, obstruction)
- Type and screen (if concern for significant bleeding)
- Fecal calprotectin (sensitive indicator of intestinal inflammation, unreliable in select Crohn's patients)
- CT A/P if concern for small bowel obstruction, perforation, or toxic megacolon
- Most useful diagnostic test in patients with acute symptoms who have known or suspected Crohn
- Findings: bowel wall thickening, mesenteric edema, local abscess, fistulas

sections.title: Acute Flare Management
lines: - Methylprednisolone (e.g., 30mg IV bid) or prednisone (e.g., 60 mg day 1, then 40 mg daily x 4 days), OR
- Budesonide for mild to moderate disease due to fewer systemic side effects

sections.title: Chronic Treatment
lines: Alterations should be discussed with GI
- Aminosalicylates (5-ASA) - Mild-to-moderate Crohn's disease. Give with probiotics.
- Caution: Can cause folate deficiency so give with folic acid, and can cause hemolytic anemia in G6PD patients
- Active moiety of sulfasalazine, and formed from prodrug balsalazide
- Balsalazide or Olsalazine - Bypasses small intestine to deliver drug into large intestine (better for UC)
- Anti-diarrheal - Use caution in patients with active inflammation as can precipitate toxic megacolon
- Cholestyramine 4g once to six times daily
- Prednisone - 40-60mg/day with taper once remission induced
- Do not start if any suspicion of infection (ie C. diff colitis)
- Double edge sword: Reduction of bone density in addition to underlying disease process(decreased Ca absorption)
- Immunomodulators - Steroid-sparing agents used in fistulas and patients with surgical contraindication. Slower onset.
- Anti-TNF - Medically resistant moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease
- Adalimumab (Humira), Natalizumab or certolizumab pegol can also be used

sections.title: Medication Dosing
lines: Methylprednisolone 20mg IV q6hr IV Prednisone 40-60mg daily with taper once remission induced PO

sections.title: Inpatient Admission
lines: - Significant metabolic derangements (i.e. electrolyte imbalance or severe dehydration)

sections.title: Surgical Intervention
lines: Consult EARLY if any of the following suspicions

sections.title: Complications
lines: - Due to stricture or bowel wall edema
- Can be intraperitoneal, retroperitoneal, interloop, or intramesenteric
- More severe abdominal pain than usual
- Hip or back pain and difficulty walking (retroperitoneal abscess)
- Occurs due to extension of intestinal fissure into adjacent structures
- Suspect if changes in patient's symptoms (e.g. BM frequency, amt of pain, wt loss)
- Erosion into a bowel wall vesel
- Can be associated with massive GI bleeding
