sections.title: Workup
lines: Workup to confirm diagnosis, assess severity, and search for precipitating cause (e.g., infection, ACS)
- BMP (glucose, BUN/Cr, Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻, anion gap)
- Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) — preferred ketone marker for diagnosis, severity assessment, and monitoring resolution; ideally point-of-care
- VBG (arterial blood gas is rarely needed)
- CBC (leukocytosis is common in DKA even without infection — >25,000 or left shift more suggestive of infection)
- ECG — evaluate for hyperkalemia/hypokalemia, ischemia, arrhythmia
- Urinalysis — ketonuria may be a useful screen but serum BHB is preferred (see below)
- Blood cultures — if concern for sepsis or bacteremia
- Lactate — if concern for sepsis or tissue hypoperfusion
- Troponin — if chest pain or concern for ACS (interpret with caution in CKD)
- Pregnancy test — in all women of childbearing age
- HbA1c — helpful in assessing chronic glycemic control and distinguishing new-onset T1D from poorly controlled known diabetes

sections.title: Diagnosis
lines: Diagnosis is made based on the presence of acidosis AND ketonemia in the setting of diabetes

sections.title: Key Laboratory Pearls
lines: - Blood Gas: VBG is sufficient — pH difference from ABG is ±0.02 units

- Urinary ketones: May give a false negative later in DKA — the urine dipstick detects acetoacetate, not beta-hydroxybutyrate. As DKA worsens, the ratio shifts toward BHB, so urine ketones may paradoxically appear negative in severe DKA
- Bicarb may be normal despite DKA due to compensatory/contraction alkalosis — the elevated anion gap or BHB may be the only clues

- Corrected sodium: Na⁺ decreases by ~1.6 mEq/L for every 100 mg/dL increase in glucose above 100 (some use 2.4 mEq/L per 100 mg/dL for glucose >400). The corrected sodium should rise as glucose falls during treatment — if it is falling, suspect excessive free water administration (risk of cerebral edema)
- ETCO₂: An ETCO₂ ≥35 mmHg is 100% sensitive to rule out DKA; an ETCO₂ ≤21 mmHg is 100% specific for DKA in patients with glucose >550
- Leukocytosis is common in DKA even without infection (stress response); WBC >25,000 or bandemia is more suggestive of true infection

sections.title: Management
lines: - If the patient has an insulin pump, shut it off and remove the subcutaneous catheter

sections.title: Volume Repletion
lines: - Administer 15-20 mL/kg/h isotonic crystalloid during the first hour (typically 1-1.5L)
- Most important step in treatment since osmotic diuresis is the major driving force
- Most adult patients are 3-6L depleted; aim to correct ~50% of fluid deficit in first 8-12 hours
- Lactated Ringers is preferred over NS — may resolve DKA faster and causes less hyperchloremic acidosis
- When blood glucose (BG) <250-300 mg/dL → add a D10 infusion at an equal rate to LR to prevent hypoglycemia while continuing insulin to clear ketones
- Patients can eat and drink if mental status is intact
- Use caution in patients with CHF, chronic kidney disease, or ESRD — smaller boluses with frequent reassessment

sections.title: Potassium (Most Important!)
lines: - Check K⁺ BEFORE starting insulin. Do not give insulin until K⁺ supplementation is underway if K⁺ <3.5

sections.title: Other Electrolytes
lines: - Sodium: Calculate corrected Na⁺ (see above). If truly hyponatremic, use NS. If hypernatremic, consider LR or half-NS.
- Hypophosphatemia: Replete if <1.0 mg/dL (IV K₂PO₄ — has the added benefit of providing K⁺). Severe hypophosphatemia can cause cardiac/respiratory dysfunction and hemolytic anemia.
- Hypomagnesemia: Replete if Mg <2.0 mg/dL (2g MgSO₄ IV over 1 hour)

sections.title: Insulin Overview
lines: - A bolus dose is NOT recommended — no benefit and may increase hypoglycemic episodes
- Expect BG to fall by 50-100 mg/dL per hour with adequate insulin and fluids
- Refractory hyperglycemia → consider unrecognized infection, inadequate fluid resuscitation, or insulin delivery failure

sections.title: Intravenous Insulin (Standard for Moderate-Severe DKA)
lines: - Fixed rate: 0.1 units/kg/hr (or 0.14 units/kg/hr without bolus; or 0.05 units/kg/hr per some protocols)
- Fixed rate infusion has improved outcomes over variable rate
- Do NOT stop insulin infusion until DKA has resolved — resolution requires clearance of ketones, not merely correction of glucose
- If BHB is not available, normalization of anion gap is an acceptable surrogate
- When BG <250-300 mg/dL → add D10 infusion; do NOT decrease insulin below 0.05 units/kg/hr until ketones clear
- Maintain BG between 150-250 mg/dL until resolution of acidosis

sections.title: Subcutaneous Insulin (Appropriate for Mild DKA Only)
lines: SC regimen requires rapid-acting insulin (e.g., aspart, lispro). Appropriate only for mild DKA (pH 7.25-7.3, alert, tolerating PO, able to void). Poor perfusion may impair absorption.
- Initial: 0.3 units/kg SC, then 0.1 units/kg SC every hour
- When BG <250: add D5 0.45% NS; reduce to 0.05 units/kg/hr SC
- Target BG ~150 mg/dL until DKA resolution
- Initial: 0.3 units/kg SC, then 0.2 units/kg SC at 1 hour, then 0.2 units/kg SC q2hr
- When BG <250: add D5 0.45% NS; reduce to 0.1 units/kg q2hr SC
- Target BG ~150 mg/dL until DKA resolution

sections.title: Transition to Basal-Bolus Insulin
lines: - Start basal insulin (glargine) 1-2 hours BEFORE discontinuing IV insulin infusion
- Early basal: Glargine 0.3 U/kg SC ×1 early in DKA course (protects against rebound hyperglycemia, eliminates the 1-2h overlap waiting period)
- Traditional: Close the anion gap / clear BHB → start basal insulin 1-2h before stopping infusion → verify patient is eating before fully transitioning

sections.title: Bicarbonate
lines: - No evidence supports the use of sodium bicarb in DKA, with a pH >6.9
- However, no studies have been performed for patients with pH <6.9 and the most recent ADA guidelines recommend it for patients with pH <7.1
- Generally NOT recommended — multiple studies show no benefit in DKA resolution or time to discharge
- Consider only if pH <6.9 (or <7.0 per some protocols) with hemodynamic instability
- Shifts oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve leftward → decreased O₂ delivery

sections.title: Additional Management Considerations
lines: - VTE prophylaxis: DKA is a hypercoagulable state — consider prophylactic-dose heparin or enoxaparin (adjust for renal function) in immobilized or critically ill patients
- Infection: Treat empirically if suspected; do not wait for culture results to initiate antibiotics
- Continuous telemetry: Hyperkalemia and hypokalemia are both arrhythmogenic; monitor throughout treatment
- Administration of IV Thiamine may help shift body back towards aerobic metabolism and accelerate clearance of lactate and resolution of acidemia

sections.title: Intubation
lines: - Avoid intubation in DKA whenever possible — this is a critical ED pearl
- During sedation/paralysis, loss of compensatory hyperventilation → precipitous pH drop that can cause cardiac arrest
- Severe gastroparesis in DKA → high aspiration risk
- Awake DKA patients can generally achieve greater minute ventilation than a mechanical ventilator
- Set the ventilator to match the patient's pre-intubation respiratory rate and tidal volume (high RR, high Vt)
- Avoid paralyzing the patient if possible
- See Intubation in severe metabolic acidosis for more detail

sections.title: Subsequent Monitoring
lines: - BMP Q2hr initially (then Q4hr as improving); include anion gap calculation
- BHB Q2-4hr if available (preferred over anion gap for monitoring resolution)
- Check VBG pH PRN based on clinical status
- Assess insulin dose adequacy Q1hr (BG should fall 50-100 mg/dL per hour)
- Monitor corrected sodium trend — should be rising as glucose falls
- K⁺ with every BMP — and whenever insulin rate is changed
- Sliding scale insulin to be started once DKA has fully resolved and patient is eating a full diet

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Admit to ICU or step-down: Moderate-severe DKA (pH <7.24), AMS, hemodynamic instability, significant comorbidity, need for IV insulin infusion
- Admit to monitored bed: Mild DKA on SC protocol, but requiring observation for resolution and precipitant evaluation

- Consider ED treatment and discharge (rare): Only for mild DKA in a known, reliable patient with clear precipitant (e.g., insulin pump failure), DKA fully resolved before discharge (BHB <0.6 or anion gap closed, pH >7.3, bicarb ≥18, BG <200, tolerating PO, K⁺ normal), and close follow-up within 24-48 hours

- Discharge education: Sick day rules (never stop basal insulin, check BG and ketones when ill, maintain hydration), when to seek care (persistent vomiting, BG >300, positive ketones), insulin access resources if cost is a barrier
- Schedule outpatient follow-up within 1-2 weeks if medications were changed (or within 1 month)

sections.title: Complications
lines: - Cerebral Edema in DKA: More common in pediatric DKA; risk factors include excessive free water, rapid glucose correction, failure of corrected sodium to rise, and bicarbonate use
- Hypokalemia: Most dangerous iatrogenic complication — from insulin-driven intracellular K⁺ shift without adequate repletion
- Hypoglycemia: From excessive insulin without adequate dextrose supplementation
- ARDS/pulmonary edema: From aggressive fluid resuscitation, especially in patients with cardiac or renal comorbidities
- Venous thromboembolism: DKA is a prothrombotic state

Insulin 0.1 units/kg/hr IV infusion (no bolus); reduce to 0.02-0.05 units/kg/hr when BG <250 IV drip — Do NOT stop until DKA resolved; no bolus recommended Insulin 0.3 units/kg SC initial, then 0.1-0.2 units/kg SC q1-2h SC — Mild DKA only (pH 7.25-7.3, alert, tolerating PO); poor perfusion impairs absorption Sodium bicarbonate 100 mEq in 400 mL sterile water IV over 2 hours IV drip — Generally NOT recommended; consider only if pH <6.9 with hemodynamic instability

sections.title: Background
lines: - Extreme, decompensated hypothyroidism with end-organ dysfunction
- True endocrine emergency with mortality 30-60% even with treatment
- Misnomer: patients are not always comatose and myxedema is not always present
- Most common in elderly women with undiagnosed or undertreated hypothyroidism
- Medications: amiodarone, lithium, sedatives, opioids, anesthetics

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Classic triad: altered mental status + hypothermia + precipitating event
- Altered mental status: confusion, lethargy, obtundation → coma
- Hypothermia (may be severe, <32C; absence of fever despite infection is classic)
- Bradycardia and hypotension (refractory to vasopressors until thyroid hormone replaced)
- Hypoventilation with hypercapnia and hypoxia (respiratory failure)
- Hyponatremia (due to decreased free water excretion — SIADH-like)
- Hypoglycemia (concurrent adrenal insufficiency or hepatic dysfunction)

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: - TSH: markedly elevated in primary hypothyroidism (most common)
- May be low/normal in central (pituitary/hypothalamic) hypothyroidism
- Free T4: very low or undetectable
- Cortisol level (before starting steroids) — rule out concurrent adrenal insufficiency
- ECG: bradycardia, low voltage, prolonged QT, possible J (Osborn) waves
- Infectious workup: blood/urine cultures, CXR (infection is most common precipitant)

sections.title: Immediate
lines: - Airway management: intubation for respiratory failure or severe AMS
- Passive rewarming (avoid active external rewarming which can cause vasodilation and cardiovascular collapse)
- Treat precipitant (antibiotics for suspected infection, dextrose for hypoglycemia)

sections.title: Thyroid Hormone Replacement
lines: - Loading dose: 200-400 mcg IV (or 4 mcg/kg lean body weight)
- IV liothyronine (T3) may be added for severe cases:
- 5-20 mcg IV loading dose, then 2.5-10 mcg IV q8h
- T3 has faster onset of action (~4 hours vs 24 hours for T4)
- Use with caution in elderly / cardiac patients (arrhythmia risk)
- Route must be IV — GI absorption unreliable due to ileus and mucosal edema

sections.title: Stress-Dose Steroids
lines: - Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h — give BEFORE or concurrent with thyroid hormone
- Rationale: thyroid hormone replacement increases cortisol metabolism; if concurrent adrenal insufficiency exists, this can precipitate adrenal crisis
- Discontinue steroids once adrenal insufficiency ruled out

sections.title: Supportive Care
lines: - Vasopressors may be needed but often refractory until thyroid hormone takes effect
- Avoid sedatives and opioids (impair respiratory drive)

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Serial monitoring: TSH, free T4, electrolytes, glucose, cortisol
- Improvement in vital signs expected within 24-48 hours
- Mental status may take days to weeks to normalize
- Long-term oral levothyroxine replacement once stabilized

sections.title: Background
lines: - Difference between severe thyrotoxicosis and thyroid storm is clinical diagnosis
- Must empirically treat before laboratory confirmation
- Death caused by multi-organ dysfunction, congestive heart failure, respiratory failure, dysrhythmias, DIC, hypoxic brain injury, or sepsis

sections.title: Spectrum of Thyroid Disease
lines: - Myxedema coma << hypothyroidism < euthyroid > hyperthyroidism >> thyroid storm

sections.title: Classic Triad
lines: - Often out of proportion to fever
- Altered mental status (agitation, confusion, delirium stupor, coma, seizure)
- Diarrhea, nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain

sections.title: Apathetic Hyperthyroidism
lines: - Strikingly different rare form, dominated by depressed mental status, cardiac complications
- Treatment with antithyroid therapy is still mainstay

sections.title: Workup
lines: - Mild elevation in AST, ALT, LDH, bilirubin, ALP may be seen

sections.title: Management
lines: Identify precipitant (i.e. med noncompliance, DKA, infection). When in doubt of diagnosis, the EP should treat given the high mortality rate, as a few doses of anti-thyroid medication are unlikely to harm euthyroid patient

sections.title: Supportive care
lines: - Do not aggressively cool as this can lead to vasoconstriction
- Careful cooling measures (ice packs & cooling blankets)
- Acetaminophen (avoid aspirin or NSAIDS because they displace thyroid hormone from TBG)
- D5NS (most patients have depleted glycogen stores)
- Crackles in lungs are likely high output heart failure, NOT fluid overload
- Rate control, inotropes, diuretics as needed (short acting always better)

sections.title: Treat Increased Adrenergic Tone
lines: - Propranolol PO 60-80 mg q4hr (if can tolerate PO, no PR form)
- Propranolol IV 1-2mg over 10 min; if tolerates then 1-2mg boluses q15 minutes until HR <100
- Followed by drip at dose required for heart rate control (3-5mg/hr)
- Relative contraindications are same as for other medical conditions (e.g. CHF, Reactive Airway Disease, see alternative therapies)
- In addition to decreasing peripheral conversion, propranolol will improve tremor, hyperpyrexia, and agitation
- Unlike other beta-blockers, propranolol also partially blocks conversion of T4 to T3
- B1 selective so can be used with active CHF, asthma, etc
- Does not have T4 to T3 blocking properties of propranolol
- Option for patients in whom beta-blockers are contraindicated

sections.title: Block New Hormone Synthesis
lines: Thionamides are the main class of medications which prevent new hormone synthesis by inhibiting the iodination of tyrosine residues by thyroid peroxidase (TPO) enzymes. Propylthiouracil (PTU) is prefered over methimazole because it will also bock T4→T3 conversion
- PTU 500-1000mg PO or NG followed by 250mg q4hr
- May provide PR, but PO or NG are preferred routes (IV formulations not available in US)
- PTU recommended in the first trimester of pregnancy with transition to methimazole afterwards
- Note black box warning of hepatotoxicity so check LFTs prior
- Avoid in patients with significant liver disease; use methimazole instead
- Theoretically first line and offers advantage over methimazole
- PTU has earlier onset of action and capacity to inhibit peripheral conversion of T4 to T3
- However, no significant difference in mortality between PTU and methimazole
- Methimazole 20-25mg q4hr (80 - 100 mg daily in divided doses)
- IV formulations may be available in Europe
- Should be avoided in first trimester of pregnancy (freely crosses placenta, birth defects)
- Available in IV formulations outside America, but use supported by case reports only
- Give 1hr after PTU or methimazole to prevent increased hormone production (Jod-Basedow effect)
- Block hormone release: (Wolff-Chaikoff effect) only after hormone synthesis is inhibited. Iodine concentration leads to transient decrease of T3/T4
- 5 drops (0.25 mL or 250mg) orally every 6 hours
- Avoid potassium iodide if patient is on amiodarone
- Can substitute radiocontrast dyes (Iopanoic acid, ipodate and iopanoate), PO Lugol solution, OR IV sodium iodide
- Lithium inhibits thyroid hormone release from the gland and reduces iodination of tyrosine residues, but its use is complicated by the toxicity that can ensue
- Treatment of choice for iodine-induced hyperthyroidism as the result of contrast load or amiodarone
- Lugol’s Solution 8 drops PO q 6 (alternative iodine source)
- Sodium Iodide 0.5mg IV Q 12 hours (alternative iodine source)
- Inhibits enterohepatic circulation of thyroid hormone by binding to conjugated products and promote excretion

sections.title: Adrenal Insufficiency Treatment
lines: Often there may be associated adrenal insufficiency (also blocks T4>T3)
- Hydrocortisone 300mg IV bolus, followed by 100mg TID for several days OR
- Note that corticosteroids also inhibit conversion of T4 to T3 and block release of hormone from thyroid gland

sections.title: Plasmapheresis
lines: - For recalcitrant thyroid storm, with remaining cardiac and neurologic symptoms
- Especially in the case of fulminant liver failure, in which anti-thyroid drugs are contraindicated
- Removes cytokines, auto-antibodies, thyroid hormones, thyroid hormone bound proteins

sections.title: Antibiotics
lines: - Second most common etiology of thyroid storm (after medication noncompliance) is infection
- Low threshold to start broad spectrum antibiotics

sections.title: Additional Interventions
lines: - Consider L-Carnitine (1 g PO q 12h) - blocks T3 & T4 entry into cell nuclei peripherally
- Consider Cholestyramine (4g PO q 6h) - decreases GI hormone recycling

sections.title: Disposition
lines: Propranolol 60-80 mg PO q4h; or 1-2 mg IV over 10 min, then 1-2 mg IV q15min until HR <100, then 3-5 mg/hr drip PO/IV — Also decreases T4→T3 conversion; improves tremor, hyperpyrexia, agitation Esmolol 250-500 mcg/kg IV loading, then 50-100 mcg/kg/min drip IV drip — B1 selective; safe with active CHF, asthma; does not block T4→T3 conversion PTU 500-1000 mg PO/NG load, then 250 mg PO q4h PO/NG — Black box warning for hepatotoxicity; preferred in 1st trimester pregnancy Methimazole 20-25 mg PO q6h (can give PR at same dose) PO/PR — Often more effective in severe or refractory cases; consider if hepatic concerns with PTU SSKI (Potassium iodide) 5 drops (250 mg) PO q6h (give 1 hour after PTU/methimazole) PO — Must give AFTER thionamide to prevent Jod-Basedow effect; avoid if on amiodarone Lithium 300 mg PO q8h PO — Consider if iodine allergy; inhibits hormone release Hydrocortisone 300 mg IV bolus, then 100 mg IV TID IV Dexamethasone 4 mg IV q6h IV — Also inhibits T4→T3 conversion and thyroid hormone release

sections.title: Background
lines: - Life-threatening emergency resulting from acute cortisol deficiency
- Mortality up to 25% if untreated; rapidly fatal without intervention
- Most common cause: stress event in patient with chronic adrenal insufficiency on glucocorticoid replacement who does NOT increase dose ("stress dosing")
- Can also occur as first presentation of undiagnosed adrenal insufficiency

sections.title: Causes of Adrenal Insufficiency
lines: - Autoimmune adrenalitis (Addison disease — most common in developed countries)
- Infections: TB (most common worldwide), CMV, HIV, fungal
- Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome — meningococcemia, anticoagulation, DIC)
- Pituitary tumors, surgery, radiation, Sheehan syndrome
- Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid use → HPA axis suppression
- Even short courses >2 weeks can suppress HPA axis

sections.title: Precipitants of Crisis
lines: - Non-compliance or abrupt withdrawal of chronic steroids
- GI illness with vomiting (unable to take oral steroids)

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Refractory hypotension/shock — does NOT respond to IV fluids or vasopressors until cortisol replaced
- Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain (may mimic acute abdomen)
- Hypoglycemia (especially in children; cortisol is counterregulatory)
- Dehydration (cortisol deficiency + aldosterone deficiency in primary AI)
- In chronic primary AI: hyperpigmentation (increased ACTH → MSH), vitiligo, salt craving

sections.title: Classic Lab Pattern
lines: - Hyperkalemia (primary AI only — aldosterone deficiency; absent in secondary/tertiary)

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis
lines: - Sepsis / septic shock (most common misdiagnosis — and most common precipitant)

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: - Random cortisol level (draw BEFORE giving steroids if possible, but do NOT delay treatment):
- Cortisol <3 mcg/dL: diagnostic of adrenal insufficiency
- Cortisol 3-18 mcg/dL in acutely stressed patient: suspicious (should be elevated in stress)
- Cortisol >18 mcg/dL in acute illness: effectively rules out AI
- High ACTH = primary AI; Low/normal ACTH = secondary/tertiary
- BMP: hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis
- TSH (concurrent hypothyroidism in autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome)
- Infectious workup: blood cultures, UA, CXR, lactate (identify precipitant)
- ACTH stimulation test (cosyntropin test): NOT needed acutely — do NOT delay treatment for this test

sections.title: Immediate
lines: - Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus — give immediately if suspected (even before lab confirmation)
- Then hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6-8h (or continuous infusion 200 mg/24h)
- If hydrocortisone unavailable: dexamethasone 4 mg IV (does not interfere with subsequent cortisol testing)
- IV fluids: aggressive NS resuscitation (patients are often 2-3L volume depleted)
- D5NS if hypoglycemic — correct hypoglycemia with D50W 25-50 mL IV
- Vasopressors if refractory hypotension (norepinephrine) — shock typically improves rapidly with steroids
- Treat precipitant: antibiotics for infection, etc.

sections.title: Key Principles
lines: - Do NOT delay steroids for diagnostic testing
- Hydrocortisone at stress doses provides both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid activity (no need for separate fludrocortisone in acute phase)
- Hypotension refractory to fluids and vasopressors in a critically ill patient → think adrenal crisis
- Correct electrolytes (but hyperkalemia usually resolves with hydrocortisone and fluids)

sections.title: Taper
lines: - Once stable: taper to maintenance over 2-4 days
- Primary AI also needs fludrocortisone 0.05-0.1 mg PO daily (mineralocorticoid replacement)

sections.title: Prevention
lines: - Medical alert bracelet for all patients with adrenal insufficiency
- Sick day rules: double or triple oral glucocorticoid dose during illness
- Injectable hydrocortisone at home for emergencies (patient education)
- Stress dosing prior to surgery: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV before induction

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - ICU admission for hemodynamic instability or altered mental status
- Monitored bed for less severe presentations
- Patient and family education on stress dosing before discharge

items: Sepsis / septic shock (most common misdiagnosis — and most common precipitant)

sections.title: Background
lines: - If albumin goes up more acidotic (since albumin is an acid)
- If difference shrinks (i.e. more Cl) more acidotic
- Principle of electrical neutrality requires more H+ to offset the additional Cl
- If difference increases (i.e. more Na) more alkalotic
- Principle of electrical neutrality requires more bicarb to offset the additional Na

sections.title: Strong ion gap (SIG)
lines: - Strong ions include Na, Cl, lactate, ketoacid, toxic alcohols

sections.title: Base Deficit (BD)
lines: - Eliminates the respiratory component of acidosis so only left with the metabolic component
- Is equivalent to the amount of base (or acid) you would have to add to get to pH 7.4
- Base excess of -6 = base deficit of 6
- If base deficit is normal but patient is acidotic must all be from CO2
- If base deficit is abnormal must explain by SID, weak acids, or unmeasured strong ions
- If no BD is available 24.2 – serum bicarb can be used as okay substitute

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: Diagnosis is based on clinical history as well as labs:

sections.title: Stuart Step Wise Approach
lines: - Based on a stepwise approach taught about by Dr. Weingart based on the Stewart's Strong Ion Difference

sections.title: Determine pH
lines: - If pH >7.45 then patient's primary problem is alkalosis
- If pH <7.35 the patient's primary problem is acidosis
- The body never over-corrects any acid-base disorder!

sections.title: Calculate Strong Ion Difference (SID)
lines: - Low SID is <38 and indicates a strong ion acidosis = hyperchloremic acidosis = non-gap acidosis and causes include
- Any fluid that has SID of <24 can cause acidosis (e.g. NS, 1/2NS, D5W)
- Calculate Urine Anion Gap: (Urine Na + K – Cl); if negative, not RTA
- Type IV: Hyperkalemic; from aldosterone deficiency, diabetes
- High SID is >38 and indicates a metabolic alkalosis and causes include:

sections.title: Evaluate the Lactate
lines: - If >2 then the patient has hyperlactatemia
- If >4 and the patient has an infection they should be considered Severe Sepsis
- Always consider the differential for a Lactic Acidosis (Lactate)
- Calculate the strong ion gap (SIG) to explain the base deficit
- If SIG >2 this is a SIG metabolic acidosis = anion gap acidosis and the causes include:
- Lactic Acidosis (from short gut/blind loop - will not show on lactate assay)
- If SIG is negative (very rare) the differential includes:

sections.title: Calculate the osmolar gap
lines: - Indicated if have elevated SIG without explanation
- Osm Gap = Measured Osmal – (2 Na + Gluc/18 + BUN/2.8 + ETOH/3.7)
- Positive if osm gap >10 and differential includes:

sections.title: Determine pH
lines: - If pH within normal range, then acid base disorder not likely present.
- pH may be normal in the presence of a mixed acid base disorder, particularly if other parameters of the ABG are abnormal.

sections.title: Calculate the delta gap
lines: - This is to determine a coexistent metabolic alkalosis or non-gap acidosis
- DKA more likely to have a ratio closer to 1 due to urine ketone loss (esp if patient not dehydrated)
Suggests a pre-existing elevated HCO3 level so consider:

sections.title: Calculate the starting bicarbonate
lines: - The purpose of this calculation is to assess the body’s ability to change HCO3 in response to a metabolic acid. In cases with a pure anion gap metabolic acidosis, the rise in anion gap from 12 should equal the fall in HCO3 from from 24

sections.title: Calculate compensations
lines: - Will allow for identification of a secondary process

sections.title: Determinants of compensation
lines: - PaCO2 = last two digits of pH
Respiratory acidosis and alkalosis (acute acid-base changes based on PCO2 and HCO3):
- For every ↑ or ↓ of PCO2 by 1 the pH changes by 0.008
- For every ↑ or ↓ of HCO3 by 1 the pH changes by 0.015
Estimate of baseline PCO2 in patients with Acute Respiratory Acidosis:
- HCO3 increases by 4 for every 10 mmHg ↑ in pCO2 above 40
- In chronic respiratory acidosis, kidneys retain HCO3, which takes a few days
- HCO3 decreases by 5 for every 10 mmHg decrease in pCO2 below 40

sections.title: IV Fluids
lines: - Fluid that has SID of 38 would be basic b/c it would dilute out the albumin (weak acid)
- Fluid that has SID identical to patient's serum bicarb is pH neutral
- If SID of fluid is greater than patient's bicarb level then it is alkalotic
- If SID of fluid is less than patient's bicarb level then it is acidotic

sections.title: Examples
lines: - (SID = 0) so is acidotic so causes hyperchloremic acidosis
^Consider balanced solution (LR) in patients with low pH (e.g. DKA)

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Mixed acid-base disorders suggesting serious underlying pathology
- Mild single acid-base disorder with identified correctable cause

sections.title: Background
lines: - Patients often not symptomatic until <120meq/L, although this level varies by patients and may be higher if the change occurred abruptly
- Too fast of sodium correction (>10 mmol/L/day), especially if chronic, can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis)

sections.title: Symptoms from Rapid Correction of Sodium
Differential Diagnosis of Hypotonic Hyponatremia (by Volume Status)
Euvolemic
lines: - urine sodium is greater than 20-40 mEq/L

sections.title: Pseudohyponatremia
lines: - Na+ decreases by 2.4mEq/L for each 100mg/dL increase in glucose over 100mg/dL

sections.title: Diagnosis
lines: - Calculated osm (in true hyponatremia the osm is reduced)

sections.title: Hypertonic Hyponatremia
lines: Defined as osmolarity > 295mmol/L with the following causes:
- Sodium decreases by 2.4mEq/L for each 100mg/dL increase in glucose over 100mg/dL

sections.title: Isotonic (pseudo) hyponatremia
lines: Defined as osmolarity > 275-295mmol/L. Often referred to as pseudo hyponatremia because the elevated lipids or proteins interfere with the laboratory sodium reading. The following are common causes:

sections.title: Hypotonic Hyponatremia
lines: Defined as an osmolarity < 275 mmol/L and categorized as hypovolemic, hypervolemic or euvolemic

sections.title: General Management
lines: Must have sufficient confidence that the symptoms are caused by hyponatraemia; see Clinical Features for definition of categories.

sections.title: NOT Severe/Moderately-Severe (Including Asymptomatic)
lines: - Start prompt diagnostic assessment and provide cause-specific treatment
- Check serum sodium concentration after 4 hours
- Aim for a 5 mmol/l per 24-h increase in serum sodium concentration
- Limit increase to 10 mmol/l in the first 24 h (8 mmol/l during every 24 h thereafter), until a serum sodium concentration of 130 mmol/l is reached
- Manage the patient as in moderately-severe symptomatic hyponatraemia if the serum sodium concentration decreases 10 mmol/l

sections.title: Moderately Severe Symptoms
lines: - 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL bolus over 20 min
- Start prompt diagnostic assessment and provide cause-specific treatment
- Check serum sodium concentration after 1, 6 and 12 hours
- Aim for a 5 mmol/l per 24-h increase in serum sodium concentration
- Limit increase to 10 mmol/l in the first 24 h (8 mmol/l during every 24 h thereafter), until a serum sodium concentration of 130 mmol/l is reached
- Desmopressin 2 mcg IV q8h IV to prevent overcorrection
- Manage the patient as in severely symptomatic hyponatraemia if the serum sodium concentration further decreases despite treating the underlying diagnosis (2D).

sections.title: Severe Symptoms
lines: - 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL bolus over 20 min
- Check serum sodium concentration after 20 min
- Repeat infusion of 150 ml 3% hypertonic saline for the next 20 min
- Repeat twice or until a target of 5 mmol/l increase in serum sodium concentration is achieved
- Each 100 mL will raise sodium by ~2 mmol/l
- In general, 200-400 mL of 3% hypertonic saline is reasonable dose in most adult patients with severe symptomatic hyponatremia, which may be given IV over 1-2 hr until resolution of seizures.

- If you do not have 3% hypertonic saline you can give two ampules (100ml) of crash cart hypertonic bicarbonate (1 mEq/ml sodium bicarbonate equivalent to giving ~200 ml of 3% saline, which will raise the serum sodium by ~3 mM).
- Sodium bicarbonate should be given slowly (each ampule over 5-10 minutes). Bicarbonate is contraindicated in patients with metabolic alkalosis.
- 2 mL/kg of 3% over 10-60 minutes can be infused with a repeat of up to 3 times.

sections.title: Hypertonic hyponatremia
lines: - Correct underlying disorder which is often hyperglycemia
- Often volume depleted due to osmotic diuresis and normal saline provides adequate volume repletion

sections.title: Hypotonic hyponatremia
lines: - Give normal saline, but be cautious of raising the serum sodium more than 10 mmol/L/day and causing osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis)

sections.title: Calculating Sodium Replacement Therapy
lines: Max correction 10mEq/L in first 24hr (8 mmol/l during every 24 h thereafter), until a serum sodium concentration of 130 mmol/l is reached (lowers risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome)

sections.title: Step 1
lines: - TBW(kg) = Wt(kg) x 0.6 = [Wt(lb) x 0.45] x 0.6 = Wt(lb) x 0.27

sections.title: Step 3
lines: Calculate NS rate to be given over 24hr
- NS rate (cc/hr) = TBW x mEq deficit x 0.27
- If using 3% sodium chloride (to avoid volume overload) divide above rate by 3.33

sections.title: DDAVP Combined with Hypertonic Saline
lines: - Limited evidence suggests usage of DDAVP in combination with HTS can safely increase sodium, while lowering risk for over-correction
- DDAVP prevents free water excretion renally
- Give 3% hypertonic saline based on calculations above
- Patients must be PO water restricted
- Goal sodium is 6 mEq/L over first 24 hours

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Admit if symptomatic or if Na <125mEq/L
- Manage severely symptomatic patients in "an environment where close biochemical and clinical monitoring can be provided" (e.g. ICU)

sections.title: Corrected Sodium
lines: - Katz MA. Hyperglycemia-induced hyponatremia — calculation of expected serum sodium depression. N Engl J Med. 1973;289(16):843-844. PMID 4763428.
- Hillier TA, Abbott RD, Barrett EJ. Hyponatremia: evaluating the correction factor for hyperglycemia. Am J Med. 1999;106(4):399-403. PMID 10225241.
- Classic formula (Katz): Corrected Na = Measured Na + 1.6 × (Glucose − 100) / 100
- Revised formula (Hillier): Corrected Na = Measured Na + 2.4 × (Glucose − 100) / 100 (preferred when glucose >400)

sections.title: Sodium Deficit
lines: - Adrogué HJ, Madias NE. Hyponatremia. N Engl J Med. 2000;342(21):1581-1589. PMID 10824078.
- Adrogué HJ, Madias NE. Hypernatremia. N Engl J Med. 2000;342(20):1493-1499. PMID 10816188.
- Correction rate: Do not exceed 8-10 mEq/L per 24 hours for hyponatremia to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome.

sections.title: Calculated Serum Osmolality
lines: - Osmolal gap = Measured Osm – Calculated Osm. Gap >10 suggests unmeasured osmoles (toxic alcohols, mannitol, etc.).
- Purssell RA, et al. Derivation and validation of a formula to calculate the contribution of ethanol to the osmolal gap. Ann Emerg Med. 2001;38(6):653-659. PMID 11719745.

sections.title: Causes of Hypernatremia
lines: Usually secondary to decreased Total Body Water

sections.title: Hypernatremia
lines: - Renal Na retention (secondary to poor perfusion)

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: - Fractional excretion of sodium can help determine etiology

sections.title: Management
lines: - Normal saline until perfusion deficits corrected
- Then switch to 1/2NS until UOP = >0.5 mL/kg/hr
Avoid lowering Na more than 10-15 mEq/L/day (~0.5-1.0 mEq/L/hr initially)

sections.title: Water Deficit
lines: - Free water deficit = (0.6 x wt in kg) x [(serum Na/140) – 1]
- Each liter H2O Deficit increases Na by 3-5 meq/L

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Tailor to underlying cause and severity

sections.title: Complications
lines: - Brain edema if corrected too quickly
- Brain shrinkage leading to cerebral vessel traction:
- Venous congestion, thrombosis of venous sinuses

sections.title: Free Water Deficit
lines: - TBW = Weight × correction factor (Male 0.6, Female 0.5; reduce by 0.1 for elderly)
- Correction rate: Do not decrease Na by >10–12 mEq/L per 24 hours to avoid cerebral edema.
- Adrogué HJ, Madias NE. Hypernatremia. N Engl J Med. 2000;342(20):1493-1499. PMID 10816188.

sections.title: Background
lines: - Most common electrolyte abnormality encountered in clinical practice
- Severe: <2.5 mEq/L (risk of arrhythmia, respiratory failure)
- Every 1 mEq/L decrease in serum K represents ~200-400 mEq total body deficit

sections.title: Causes
lines: - Diuretics (loops, thiazides — most common medication cause)

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - PACs, PVCs → atrial or ventricular tachycardia → torsades de pointes → VF

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis
lines: - Diabetic ketoacidosis (total body K depleted despite possible normal level)

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: - ECG (look for U waves, flattened T waves, prolonged QT)
- BMP: K level, bicarbonate (alkalosis?), glucose, creatinine
- Magnesium level (hypokalemia refractory to replacement if Mg not corrected)
- Consider: urine K (spot urine K/Cr ratio or 24h K), urine chloride, TSH, cortisol/aldosterone if unexplained
- Digoxin level if on digoxin (hypokalemia increases digoxin sensitivity)

sections.title: Guiding Principles
lines: - Always check and replace magnesium first — hypokalemia is refractory to correction with concurrent hypomagnesemia
- Oral replacement preferred when possible (better tolerated, less risky)
- IV replacement for severe hypokalemia, ECG changes, or NPO patients

sections.title: Mild Hypokalemia (3.0-3.5 mEq/L)
lines: - Oral KCl 20-40 mEq PO q2-4h (typical total dose 40-100 mEq/day)

sections.title: Moderate Hypokalemia (2.5-3.0 mEq/L)
lines: - KCl 10-20 mEq/hr IV via peripheral line (max 40 mEq/L concentration peripherally)
- Max infusion rate: 10-20 mEq/hr (peripheral); up to 40 mEq/hr via central line with cardiac monitoring

sections.title: Severe Hypokalemia (<2.5 mEq/L or ECG Changes)
lines: - KCl 20-40 mEq/hr IV via central line
- Magnesium sulfate 2g IV (if Mg not checked yet, give empirically)

sections.title: Special Situations
lines: - DKA: K may be normal or elevated on presentation but total body stores are depleted
- Replace K before or concurrent with insulin when K <5.3
- Do NOT start insulin if K <3.3 — replace K to >3.3 first
- Refractory hypokalemia: check and replace magnesium; consider amiloride or spironolactone

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Admit if K <2.5, symptomatic, ECG changes, arrhythmia, or ongoing losses
- Continuous telemetry for K <3.0 or ECG changes
- Discharge if mild (3.0-3.5), asymptomatic, clear correctable cause, tolerated PO replacement, normal ECG
- Close follow-up with recheck in 24-48 hours

items: Diabetic ketoacidosis (total body K depleted despite possible normal level)

sections.title: Background
lines: - Life-threatening when >6.5 mEq/L or with ECG changes
- Most common electrolyte disorder causing cardiac arrest
- Renal excretion is primary mechanism of potassium regulation

sections.title: Causes
lines: - Acute kidney injury / chronic kidney disease
- Medications: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, K-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride), NSAIDs, trimethoprim, heparin
- Transcellular shift (K moves out of cells):
- Tissue destruction: rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, hemolysis, burns
- Increased intake: excessive supplementation, salt substitutes (KCl)
- Pseudohyperkalemia: hemolyzed sample, prolonged tourniquet, thrombocytosis, leukocytosis

sections.title: ECG Changes (Progressive)
lines: - Peaked T waves (earliest change, typically >5.5 mEq/L)
- ECG changes do NOT reliably correlate with K level — some patients arrest without warning

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis
lines: - Acute kidney injury / chronic kidney disease

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: - Stat ECG (most urgent — look for peaked T's, widened QRS)
- BMP: potassium level, creatinine (renal function), glucose, bicarbonate
- Repeat K level if unexpected (rule out pseudohyperkalemia)
- Digoxin level if on digoxin (hyperkalemia potentiates digitalis toxicity)
- Consider: CK, uric acid, phosphorus (tumor lysis), cortisol (adrenal insufficiency)

sections.title: Step 1: Cardiac Membrane Stabilization
lines: - Calcium (does NOT lower K; protects myocardium from arrhythmia):
- Calcium gluconate 10%: 10-20 mL IV over 2-3 minutes (preferred; less tissue necrosis if extravasates)
- Calcium chloride 10%: 5-10 mL IV (via central line preferred; 3x more elemental calcium)
- Onset: 1-3 minutes; duration 30-60 minutes; may repeat in 5-10 min if ECG unchanged
- Give immediately if ECG changes present or K >6.5
- Caution in digoxin toxicity: calcium may worsen toxicity → use cautiously or consider digibind first

sections.title: Step 2: Shift Potassium Intracellularly
lines: - Regular insulin 10 units IV + D50W 25g (50 mL) IV
- Onset: 15-30 min; duration 4-6 hours; lowers K by 0.5-1.2 mEq/L
- Monitor glucose q30min x 4h (hypoglycemia occurs in up to 20%)
- Give D50 before or simultaneously with insulin
- Onset: 15-30 min; lowers K by 0.5-1.5 mEq/L
- Additive with insulin; 40% of patients are non-responders
- Minimal effect as monotherapy; useful in setting of severe metabolic acidosis
- Do NOT rely on bicarb alone to lower potassium

sections.title: Step 3: Remove Potassium from Body
lines: - Loop diuretics (furosemide 40-80 mg IV): if adequate renal function
- Delayed onset (hours); controversial efficacy; risk of bowel necrosis
- Newer potassium binders; better tolerated than Kayexalate
- Lokelma 10g PO may lower K within 1 hour
- Hemodialysis (most effective method of K removal):
- Indicated for: refractory hyperkalemia, severe renal failure, K >7 despite medical therapy

sections.title: Cardiac Arrest from Hyperkalemia
lines: - Standard ACLS + calcium 10-20 mL IV push

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Admit if K >6.0, ECG changes, renal failure, or ongoing cause
- ICU if severe (>7.0), ECG changes, or refractory to treatment
- Continuous telemetry for all admitted patients
- Consider discharge if mild hyperkalemia (5.0-5.5), known chronic cause, normal ECG, correctable precipitant

sections.title: Background
lines: - 80% of cases associated with malignancy (most common among inpatients) or hyperparathyroidism (most common among outpatients)
- Symptoms most correlated with rate of rise of Ca, not absolute level

sections.title: Symptoms of hypercalcemia
lines: Mnemonic: Stones, Bones, Groans, Moans, Thrones, Psychic Overtones

sections.title: Asymptomatic or Ca <12 mg/dL
lines: - Advise to avoid factors that can aggravate hypercalcemia (thiazide diuretics, Li, volume depletion, prolonged inactivity, high Ca diet)

sections.title: Mildly symptomatic Ca 12-14 mg/dL
lines: - May not require immediate therapy; however, an acute rise may cause symptoms necessitating treatment as described for severe hypercalcemia (see below)

sections.title: Symptomatic or Severe hypercalcemia (Ca >14 mg/dL)
lines: - Patients are likely dehydrated and require saline hydration as initial therapy

sections.title: Hydration
lines: - Isotonic saline at 200-300 mL/hour; adjust to maintain urine output at 100-150 mL/hour

sections.title: Calcitonin
lines: - Consider adding calcitonin 4 units/kg SC or IV q12hr in patients w/ Ca >14 mg/dL (3.5 mmol/L) who are also symptomatic (lowers Ca w/in 2-4hr)
- Tachyphylaxis limits use long term, but is a great choice for emergent cases

sections.title: Bisphosphonates
lines: Give for severe hypercalcemia due to excessive bone resorption (lowers Ca within 12-48hr)[≥12 mg/dL][≥3 mmol/L]
- Caution in renal failure, though bisphosphonates have been safely used in pts with pre-existing renal failure

sections.title: Diuresis
lines: - Only consider in patients with renal insufficiency or heart failure and volume overload

sections.title: Dialysis
lines: - Severe hypervolemia not amenable to diuresis
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (unable to provide fluids)

sections.title: Corticosteroids
lines: Decrease Ca mobilization from bone and are helpful with steroid-sensitive tumors (e.g. lymphoma, MM)

sections.title: Background
lines: - Phosphate required in function of all hematologic cells (RBCs, WBCs, platelets)

sections.title: Causes of Hypophosphatemia
lines: - Primary renal phosphate wasting (rare genetic disorders)
- Osmotic diuresis (most often due to glucosuria)
- Proximally acting diuretics (e.g. acetazolamide and some thiazide diuretics)

sections.title: Harbor UCLA Adult Treatment Guidelines
lines: - Minimize or eliminate all dextrose-containing IV solutions
- 1 tab K-phos neutral 250mg Q hour x 5 doses
- Each tab contains phosphorus 8 mmol, Na 13 mEq, K1.1 mEq
- Recheck serum phosphate after last dose, and repeat dosing if continues to be <2mg/dl
- Minimize or eliminate all dextrose-containing IV solutions
- Give 15 mmol of IV potassium phosphate over 2.5 hours (contains 22 mEq K)
- Peripheral administration may cause burning at injection site
- Consider central venous administration, if available
- Repeat dosing regimen if serum phosphate remains <2mg/dl
- Minimize or eliminate all dextrose-containing IV solutions
- Exceptions: vasopressors, sedatives, analgesics, antibiotics, blood products, NS
- Give 45 mmol of IV potassium phosphate over 7 hours (contains 66 mEq of K)
- Peripheral administration may cause burning at injection site
- Consider central venous administration, if available
- If patient can tolerate PO, ALSO follow steps 1 above

sections.title: Background
lines: - Majority of cases of community-acquired ARF is secondary to volume depletion although consideration of pre-renal, post renal, and renal causes are important.

sections.title: Chronic Kidney Disease Stages
lines: - Useful if patient's baseline creatinine is unknown
- Stage 1: Kidney damage (e.g. proteinuria) and normal GFR; GFR >90
- Stage 2: Kidney damage (e.g. proteinuria) and mild decrease in GFR; GFR 60-89
- Stage 3: Moderate decrease in GFR; GFR >30-59
- Stage 4: Severe decrease in GFR; GFR 15-29
- Stage 5: Kidney failure (dialysis or kidney transplant needed); GFR <15

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Acute renal failure itself has few symptoms until severe uremia develops:
- Nausea/vomiting, drowsiness, fatigue, confusion, coma, pericarditis
- Patients more likely to present with symptoms related to underlying cause:
- Thirst, orthostatic lightheadedness, decreasing urine output
- Darkening urine and edema (esp with preceding pharyngitis or cutaneous infection)
- Alternating oliguria and polyuria is pathognomonic of obstruction

sections.title: Prerenal
lines: - GI: decreased intake, vomiting and diarrhea
- Decreased cardiac output: decompensated heart failure, tamponade, massive pulmonary embolus
- Thrombosis: atherosclerosis, vasculitis, sickle cell disease
- Observed shortly after initiation of therapy

sections.title: Intrinsic
lines: - Caused by more advanced disease due to the prerenal causes
- Aminoglycosides, radiocontrast, amphotericin B, heme pigments (rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis)
- Uric acid, calcium oxalate from Ethylene Glycol Toxicity, Multiple myeloma (immunoglobin light chains), amyloidosis
- Acute interstitial nephritis: typically a drug reaction (NSAIDs, Penicillins and antibiotics, Diuretics, phenytoin)
- Goodpasture syndrome, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's) HSP, SLE, membranoproliferative GN
- Preeclampsia, HUS, DIC, TTP, vasculitis (PAN, SCD, atheroembolism)

sections.title: Postrenal
lines: - Diabetes mellitus, spinal cord disease, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease
- Cancer of prostate, bladder, cervix, or colon
- Tumor: Ureter, uterus, prostate, bladder, colon, rectum; retroperitoneal lymphoma
- Retroperitoneal fibrosis: idiopathic, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, propranolol

sections.title: Work-up
lines: - Urinalysis, urine sodium, urine creatinine, urine urea
- Iron studies with low Fe, low TIBC, low iron saturation, normal ferritin
- Secondary rise in PTH, high phos, low calcium

sections.title: Imaging
lines: - Test of choice in setting of acute renal failure
- Useful to determine cause of post renal failure (identification of abdominal masses etc.)
- Should generally not be used with IV contrast due to potential risk for CIN
- Indicated if hydronephrosis found on ultrasound in order to define the location of obstruction

sections.title: Diagnosis
lines: - Acute tubular necrosis: protein, tubular epithelial cells

sections.title: Management
lines: - Note: Postobstructive diuresis can result in significant volume loss and death
- Typically occurs when obstruction has been prolonged / has resulted in renal failure
- Admit patients with persistent diuresis of >250 mL/h for >2hr

sections.title: Dialysis
lines: - I: Ingestions (lithium, ASA, methanol, ethylene glycol, theophylline)

sections.title: Phlebotomy to Treat Pulmonary Edema
lines: - Possible last ditch effort to tide patient over to formal dialysis if hours away
- If traditional pulmonary edema treatments are not working for SCAPE patient, one may attempt to remove 200-300 cc of blood as a bridge to dialysis
- If Hb too low, may consider temporary venous tourniquets on each leg proximally q30 min to reduce preload volume to the heart, alternating legs

sections.title: Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FENa)
lines: - FENa is unreliable on diuretics — use FEUrea instead
- Low FENa (<1%) can be seen in contrast nephropathy, rhabdomyolysis, early obstruction
- Espinel CH. The FENa test: use in the differential diagnosis of acute renal failure. JAMA. 1976;236:579-581. PMID 947239.
- Steiner RW. Interpreting the fractional excretion of sodium. Am J Med. 1984;77:699-702. PMID 6486145.

sections.title: Creatinine Clearance (Cockcroft-Gault)
lines: - Cockcroft DW, Gault MH. Prediction of creatinine clearance from serum creatinine. Nephron. 1976;16(1):31-41. PMID 1244564.
- Formula: CrCl = [(140 − age) × weight (kg)] / [72 × serum Cr (mg/dL)] × 0.85 if female.
- Note: Use IBW or adjusted BW in obese patients. Not validated in AKI or rapidly changing creatinine.

sections.title: Schwartz Equation (Pediatric GFR)
lines: - Schwartz GJ, Muñoz A, Schneider MF, et al. New equations to estimate GFR in children with CKD. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2009;20(3):629-637. PMID 19158356.
- Bedside Schwartz (2009): eGFR = 0.413 × height (cm) / serum creatinine (mg/dL). Valid for ages 1-16 years.

sections.title: Background
lines: - Breakdown of skeletal muscle releasing intracellular contents into the circulation
- Key toxins: myoglobin (nephrotoxic), creatine kinase (CK), potassium, phosphate, uric acid
- Acute kidney injury (AKI) occurs in 15-40% of cases
- Overall mortality ~5%; higher with AKI, DIC, or compartment syndrome

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Classic triad: myalgias, weakness, dark urine (tea/cola-colored)
- Full triad present in <10% of cases
- May be asymptomatic with only lab abnormalities

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: - CK >5x upper limit of normal (typically >1,000 U/L) diagnostic
- CK >5,000 U/L: significant risk of AKI
- Peak CK at 24-72 hours; monitor serial levels
- Urinalysis: urine dipstick positive for "blood" but no RBCs on microscopy (myoglobinuria)
- BMP: potassium (may be severely elevated), creatinine, BUN, calcium, phosphate, bicarbonate
- CBC, LDH, uric acid, coagulation studies
- ECG — evaluate for hyperkalemia changes (peaked T waves, wide QRS)
- Consider compartment pressures if clinical concern

sections.title: Aggressive IV Fluid Resuscitation
lines: - Normal saline at 200-300 mL/hr (or 1-2 L/hr initially if severely hypovolemic)
- Target urine output 200-300 mL/hr until CK trending down and urine clears
- Monitor for fluid overload, especially in elderly and those with cardiac/renal disease
- Bicarbonate drip (150 mEq NaHCO3 in 1 L D5W) may be considered to alkalinize urine (target urine pH >6.5) — evidence is limited

sections.title: Treat Hyperkalemia
lines: - Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV for cardiac membrane stabilization if ECG changes
- Insulin 10 units regular IV + D50W 50 mL IV
- Sodium bicarbonate, Albuterol nebulizer, Kayexalate or patiromer

sections.title: Other
lines: - Treat underlying cause (cool if hyperthermic, correct electrolytes)
- Compartment syndrome: emergent fasciotomy if pressures >30 mmHg or clinical diagnosis
- Monitor for and treat DIC if present

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Discharge may be considered for mild rhabdomyolysis (CK <5,000, normal renal function, normal K) with close follow-up and oral hydration

- ↑ Scharman EJ, et al. Prevention of kidney injury following rhabdomyolysis: a systematic review. Ann Pharmacother. 2013;47(1):90-105. PMID 23324509.

sections.title: _intro
lines: This page is for adult patients; for pediatric patients see hematuria (peds)

sections.title: Background
lines: - Hematuria can be macroscopic/gross or microscopic
- Microscopic hematuria generally defined as >3 RBCs per high-power field of an uncontaminated sample
- Hematuria can also be divided into glomerular and nonglomerular causes
- Make sure hematuria is not myoglobin (due to rhabdo), hemoglobinuria (due to hemolysis), or bleeding from non-urinary source (ex. menstruation)
- Hematuria + pain suggests UTI or nephrolithiasis
- Hematuria + no pain suggests malignancy, hyperplasia, or vascular cause

sections.title: Types of hematuria
lines: - Blood at beginning of micturition with subsequent clearing
- Blood between voiding only (voided urine is clear)
- Suggests lesions at distal urethra or meatus
- Suggests disease of kidneys, ureters, or bladder
- Blood seen at end of micturition after initial voiding of clear urine
- Suggests disease at bladder neck or prostatic urethra
- Tends to occur with kidney disease
- Brown urine with RBC casts and proteinuria

sections.title: Blunt Trauma
lines: - Microscopic Hematuria with Shock (SBP<90 mm Hg)
- The degree of hematuria does not correlate with significance of renal injury

sections.title: Hematuria
lines: - Erosion or mechanical obstruction by tumor
- Papillary necrosis: sickle cell disease, diabetes, NSAID use
- Vascular: arteriovenous malformations, emboli, aortocaval fistula
- Myoglobinuria - positive blood, no RBCs: rhabdomyolysis
- Stings/bites by insects/reptiles having venom with anticoagulant properties

sections.title: Labs
lines: - Urine microscopy can show abnormal RBC morphologies suggesting glomerular source of hematuria
- Microscopic hematuria associated with proteinuria suggests glomerular disease and requires further investigation (as an outpatient)
- Urine dipstick may be performed quickly in some centers but has high false-positive rate

sections.title: Imaging
lines: - Utilize multiphasic CT urography ("hematuria protocol") to assess for pathology in the kidney and urinary collecting system
- A noncontrast phase is useful for visualizing stones or hydronephrosis
- A nephrographic phase has contrast enhancing renal parenchyma, useful for pyelonephritis and renal tumors
- A delayed excretory phase visualizes urothelial and bladder tumors
- Ultrasound useful to assess for hydronephrosis or a Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
- Ultimately, cystoscopy and/or kidney biopsies may be necessary as follow-up procedures after the final disposition

sections.title: Diagnosis
lines: - Isolated hematuria with dysmorphic red cells or red cells with a decreased mean corpuscular volume (MCV), should prompt an evaluation for glomerulopathy (e.g., IgA nephropathy & Alport's syndrome)
- Isolated hematuria may be elusive. In some series, more than half of the patients have microhematuria with no definable cause.

sections.title: Management
lines: - Often associated with intravesicular clot formation and bladder outlet obstruction
- Use triple-lumen urinary drainage catheter with intermittent or continuous bladder irrigation
- Adequate urinary drainage must be ensured; otherwise consult urology

sections.title: Outpaient
lines: - Hemodynamically stable without life-threatening cause of hematuria
- Able to tolerate oral fluids, antibiotics, and analgesics as indicated
- No significant anemia or acute renal insufficiency

sections.title: Referral Considerations
lines: - Patients <40 yr: refer to primary care provider for repeat UA within 2wk
- Patients >40 yr with risk factor for urologic cancer: refer to urologist within 2wk
- Occupational exposure to chemicals or dyes
- Consider nephrology referral for signs of glomerular hematuria such as concommittant AKI, proteinuria, dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts

sections.title: Admission
lines: - Intolerance of oral fluids and medications
- High risk of developing complications (pulmonary edema, volume overload, hypertensive emergency)
- Pregnant women (hematuria can accompany preeclampsia, pyelonephritis or obstructing nephrolithiasis)

sections.title: Background
lines: - Urologic emergency characterized by sudden inability to pass urine
- Most common cause is benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Frequency, urgency, hesitancy, dribbling, decrease in voiding stream

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: - CBC (if suspect infection or massive hematuria)
- Incomplete retention is PVR > 50ml and > 100ml in patients > 65 years of age
- Post-void residual of 150-200 cc is particularly concerning

sections.title: Bladder Decompression
lines: - Pass 14-18F Foley catheter (larger if blood clots)
- Rate of decompression: rapid complete drainage

- At one time, rapid complete bladder decompression was thought to increase the rate of potential complications, however partial drainage and clamping does not reduce these complications and may increase risk for UTI
- If unable to pass Foley, consider:

sections.title: Other Considerations
lines: - Use 20-24F triple-lumen catheter to irrigate bladder until clear
- Consider α-blocker as outpatient if concern for BPH (e.g. tamsulosin 0.4mg QHS)
- Results in significant increase in voiding success
- Consider for precipitated retention (e.g. stricture, prostatitis, cancer) or need for suprapubic catheterization

sections.title: Admission
lines: - Post-obstructive diuresis >200mL/hr for 2 hours or 3L over 24 hours (will need fluids and electrolyte monitoring/repletion)

sections.title: Discharge
lines: - Otherwise consider discharge with catheter placed to leg bag and urology follow up within 1 week

sections.title: Background
lines: - The most common cause is infection of residual bladder urine with urea-splitting organisms (Proteus, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Staphylococcus,Mycoplasma, Providentia stuartii, Serratia, and Morganella morganii)
- Urine pH abnormalities, either high or low

sections.title: Renal damage
lines: - Irreversible renal damage can occur within 3 weeks in patients with a complete obstruction
- Most have no rise in creatinine because unobstructed kidney functions at up to 185% of its baseline capacity

sections.title: Epidemiology
lines: - More common in hot dry climates

sections.title: Infection
lines: - 8-15% of kidney stones have urinary co-infection
- Fever, pyuria >10 WBC/hpf, and peripheral WBC >11.3 (any one) best predictors of concomitant UTI

sections.title: Types
lines: - Calcium (~80%): Mostly calcium oxylate >> calcium phosphate
- Hyperparathyroidism, hypercalcemia of malignancy, sarcoidosis, increased absorption, loop diuretics, IBD
- Associated with infection with urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus, klebsiella, pseudomonas, staph,Providentia stuartii, Serratia, and Morganella morganii
- 25% of patients with gout develop kidney stones

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Acute onset, crampy, intermittent, unable to find position of comfort
- Location of pain depends on location of stone:
- Mid ureter: lower anterior quadrant of abdomen
- UVJ: Can mimic a UTI (frequency, urgency, dysuria)

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis
lines: Nephrolithiasis is most common misdiagnosis given to patients with rupturing AAA

sections.title: Flank Pain
lines: - May or may not be due to nephrolithiasis
- Appendicitis (appendix may be pushed to RUQ in pregnancy)

sections.title: Lower Back Pain
lines: - Thoracic and lumbar fractures and dislocations

sections.title: Labs
lines: - Hematuria cannot be used to rule-out or rule-in stone (sensitivity 71-95%; specificity 18-49%)
- The absence of pyuria cannot exclude a complicating UTI (sensitivity 86%; specificity 79%)
- Consider for all patients OR those at higher risk (female, pyuria, or cystitis symptoms)
- CBC: If concern for infection (>15k concerning)

sections.title: Imaging
lines: - Consider tailoring your choice of imaging based upon the patient's age, clinical likelihood of stones, risk factors, and prior history of stones
- In young patients, even with no prior history of kidney stones, reasonable approaches may be bedside ultrasound or no imaging
- In middle aged patients with prior history of stones, it may be reasonable to perform a bedside ultrasound although no imaging can be appropriate as well
- In middle aged patients with no prior history of stones, CT imaging is reasonable
- In elderly patients, even with prior history of stones, CT is recommended in order to avoid missing alternative etiologies such as dissection, AAA, or diverticulitis.
- Consider non-contrast CT abdomen and pelvis (KUB protocol) for:
- Older patients with other possible diagnosis
- Avoid CT in young (<50 years old), health patients with known history of nephrolithiasis with presentation consistent with renal colic
- In comparison of diagnosis by CT vs. U/S (by EP) vs. U/S (by radiologist):
- No difference in rate of missed high-risk diagnoses that resulted in complications (pyelo/sepsis/diverticular abscess)
- No difference in rate of serious adverse events, pain scores, return emergency department visits, or hospitalizations

sections.title: Imaging Findings
lines: - Note: Hydronephrosis, hydroureter, hydrocalyx alone indicate obstructive uropathy, stone must be seen or collected (if passed) in order to diagnose nephrolithiasis as the etiology.
- Renal: Does not cause pain, and usually considered an incidental finding

sections.title: Pain
lines: - Ketorolac 15mg IV or Ibuprofen 600mg PO Q6hrs PRN if the patient can tolerate oral medications
- Avoid high dose NSAIDS in patients with renal failure or insufficiency.
- Ketorolac 15 mg has similar effects to the traditional 30 mg dosage.
- Severe pain not controlled with NSAIDS

sections.title: Expulsion Therapy
lines: - Consider Tamsulosin 0.4mg PO QHS (discontinued after successful expulsion; average 1-2 weeks)

- The American Urological Association (AUA) advocates the use of medical expulsive therapy in the form of alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) for uncomplicated distal ureteric stones ≤10 mm (Strong recommendation). The EAU suggests that alpha-blockers be used only in distal ureteric stones >5 mm because a large randomized controlled trial demonstrated no benefit in using alpha-blockers for distal ureteric stones of <5 mm.
- See EBQ:Alpha-blockers for ureteral stone expulsion discussion of evidence
- 76% vs 48% passage rates in tamsulosin vs no treatment, respectively
- Only patients with stones ≥ 5 mm benefited
- Review of 55 RTCs, with NNT of 4
- Tamsulosin number needed to harm (orthostatic hypotension)= 19 (give at night, to reduce side effect rate)
- Use of IV fluids to "flush out" stone has NOT been shown to improve clinical outcomes

sections.title: Infected Urolithiasis
lines: Inpatient observation is often the safest disposition for patients with infected stones due to the risk of progressing to sepsis. All antibiotics should take into account patient's previous sensitivities and local antibiograms. Treatment is targeted at E. coli, Enterococcus, Klebsiella, Proteus mirabilis, S. saprophyticus.

sections.title: Outpatient
lines: Consider one dose of Ceftriaxone 1g IV or Gentamicin 7mg/kg IV if the regional susceptibility of TMP/SMX or Fluoroquinolones is <80%
- Ciprofloxacin 500mg PO BID x7 days OR
- Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole DS 160/800mg PO BID x14 days OR
- Cephalexin 500mg QID PO x 10-14 days (OR consider 1000mg BID) OR
- Cefdinir 300mg BID PO x 10-14 days OR
- Cefpodoxime 200mg PO BID x 10 days OR
- Cefixime 400mg PO daily x 10 days OR

sections.title: Adult Inpatient Options
lines: - Ceftriaxone 1gm IV QD (Preferred in pregnancy) OR
- Gentamicin 3mg/kg/day divided q8hr +/- ampicillin 1–2 gm q4hr OR

sections.title: Pediatric Outpatient Options
lines: - Cephalexin 25-50mg/kg/day PO divided q6-8h x 10-14 days (max 500mg/dose) OR
- Cefixime 8mg/kg PO daily x 10-14 days (max 400mg) OR
- Cefdinir 14mg/kg/day PO divided BID x 10 days (max 600mg/day) OR
- Cefpodoxime 10mg/kg/day PO divided BID x 10 days (max 200mg/dose) OR
- TMP/SMX 6-12mg/kg/day (TMP) PO divided BID x 10-14 days

sections.title: Pediatric Inpatient Options
lines: - Ampicillin/Sulbactam 3g IM/IV q6 hours x 14 days

sections.title: Medication Dosing
lines: Ketorolac 15mg IV — 15mg has similar efficacy to 30mg; avoid in renal failure Ibuprofen 600mg Q6hrs PRN PO — Avoid in renal failure or insufficiency Tamsulosin 0.4mg QHS PO

sections.title: Admission
lines: Recommended for any of the following:
- Proximal urinary tract infection, as evidence by:
- Single or transplanted kidney with obstruction
Also consider admission for patients with:
- Solitary kidney or transplanted kidney without obstruction

sections.title: Discharge
lines: - Small stone in patient with adequate analgesia and able to arrange urology follow up within 7d

sections.title: _intro
lines: This page is for adult patients; see urinary tract infection (peds) for pediatric patients.

sections.title: Genitourinary infection
lines: "UTI" frequently refers specifically to acute cystitis, but may also be used as a general term for all urinary infections; use location-specific diagnosis.

sections.title: Definitions
lines: - Recurrence of symptoms within month despite treatment
- Caused by same organism and represents treatment failure
- Usually due to a different organism
- If patient has >3 recurrences in 1 yr consider tumor, calculi, diabetes
- For menopausal or postmenopausal women with recurrent infection consider empiric treatment for genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM)

sections.title: Risk Factors
lines: - Anatomic abnormality of urinary tract or external drainage system
- Nephrolithiasis, neurogenic bladder, polycystic renal disease, recent instrumentation
- Advanced age in men (BPH, recent instrumentation, recent prostatic biopsy)
- Advanced neurologic disease (CVA with disability, Spinal Cord Injuries)

sections.title: Microbiology
lines: - Most common pathogen is E. coli
- Anaerobic organisms are rarely pathogenic (do not grow well in urine)
- Complicated acute cystitis is more likely to be caused by pseudomonas or enterococcus

sections.title: Complicated
lines: Suspect pyelonephritis, infected kidney stone, or other disease process in patients who have inadequate or atypical response to treatment

sections.title: Gynecologic/Obstetric
lines: - Normal variants may be noted on exam but generally do not cause pain or other symptoms
- Nabothian cysts: Epithelial cells within mucous glans that appear as yellow inclusions on the cervix
- Cervical Ectropion: Edothelial cells on the exterior of the cervix
- Parous cervix: The is no longer round but may have multiple shapes after birth

sections.title: Dysuria
lines: - Trauma to vagina, urethra, or bladder

sections.title: WBC count
lines: - WBC >5 in patient with appropriate symptoms is diagnostic
- Lower degrees of pyuria may still be clinically significant in presence of symptoms
- False negative may be due to: dilute urine, systemic leukopenia, obstruction, recent antibiotic use with incomplete treatment
- WBC 1-2 with bacteriuria can be significant in men
- More likely represents urethritis or prostatitis from STI
- High WBCs w/o bacteria, consider TB, Chlamydia, Appendicitis

sections.title: Nitrite
lines: - Very high specificity (>90%) in confirming diagnosis
- Low sensitivity (enterococcus, pseudomonas, acinetobacter are not detected)

sections.title: Blood Culture
lines: - Organisms in blood cultures matched those in urine cultures 97% of time

sections.title: Management
lines: - Consider local resistance patterns (if >10-20% use a different agent)
- Avoid use of fluoroquinolones for uncomplicated cystitis if possible
- 100-200mg TID after meals x 2 days for pain control (bladder analgesic)
- Warn of discoloration of urine and tears. Don’t wear contact lens due to risk of staining.
- Women who use spermicides or diaphragm
- TMP/SMX DS (160/800mg) 1 tab BID x 3d (Females) x7days (Males), OR
- Avoid using fluoroquinolone for the first-line treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infections (UTIs) in women.
- Lower clinical and microbiologic success compared to nitrofurantoin TID for 5 days
- Ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1 AND azithromycin 1gm PO x1 AND nitrofurantoin ER 100mg BID x5d, OR
- Levofloxacin 500mg QD x 14d (covers urinary pathogens, GC, and chlamydia)
- GC resistance to fluoroquinolones is increasing
- Gentamicin 3mg/kg/day divided q8hr +/- ampicillin 1–2 gm q4hr, OR

sections.title: Pediatric
lines: - TMP/SMX 6-12mg/kg/day (TMP) PO divided BID x 7-10 days
- Cephalexin 25-50mg/kg/day PO divided q6-8h x 7-10 days (max 500mg/dose)
- Nitrofurantoin 5-7mg/kg/day PO divided q6h x 7-10 days; avoid in infants <1 month

sections.title: Pediatric Inpatient
lines: - Gentamicin 2.5mg/kg IV q8hrs +/- Ampicillin 50mg/kg IV q6hrs

sections.title: Uncomplicated
lines: - Admit for inability to tolerate PO

sections.title: Complicated
lines: - Consider admission for period of observation and/or culture results

sections.title: AIDS
lines: - TMP-SMX resistance is increased due to its use in PCP pneumonia prophylaxis
- Fluoroquinolones should be initial antibiotic of choice
- Most acute cystitis is caused by typical pathogens or common STI organisms

sections.title: Pregnant Women
lines: - New ACOG guidelines: If asymptomatic, get a culture and only treat if >100k CFUs

sections.title: Supportive Measures
lines: - If severe obstruction suspected, may pass a Foley gently

- Consider α-blocker for outflow obstruction and urinary reflux
- Terazosin 5mg/d PO for 4 weeks or long-term

lines: - Must consider as a ddx in all acute scrotal pain
- May lead to testicular ischemia and subsequent infertility
- A clear precipitating factor is not necessary identified; half occur during sleep
- First peak in first year of life

sections.title: Clinical Features
lines: - Abrupt onset testicular pain associated with nausea or vomiting
- May have previous similar intermittent, self-resolving episodes
- May present after scrotal trauma with persistent pain
- May present as lower abd pain; thus, inquire specifically about scrotal pain in males with abd pain
- Absent cremasteric reflex on affected side (99% sensitivity)

sections.title: Work-Up
lines: - Do not delay urologic consultation for work-up
- Consult urology immediately if strongly suspicious for torsion
- Bedside U/S has a SN 0.95 and SP 0.94 compared to a gold standard of radiology U/S

sections.title: TWIST Score
lines: - Proposed score for assessing testicular torsion in children
- PPV 100% when >5 points (Suggesting stat urological consult)
- Scores from 2-5 patients require U/S for further assessment

sections.title: Management
lines: - Typically done if surgical management is not immediately available
- Urological consultation for detorsion and orchipexy
- Surgical exploration is the gold standard; without surgery, difficult to determine if manual detorsion has worked

sections.title: Manual Detorsion
lines: - Not definitive treatment. Temporizing measure if urologist not immediately available
- May require conscious sedation or parenteral analgesia if severe pain is anticipated
- Grasp spermatic cord as it enters scrotum, track up to external ring, create skin wheal, and inject 10 mL lidocaine directly into the anterior, lateral, medial portions of cord
- "Open the book" by twisting testicle outward and laterally
- Grasping testicle with thumb and forefinger, rotate 180 degrees in medial to lateral direction
- Repeat rotation 2 - 3 times until testicle is detorsed and pain decreases
- If pain is worse after rotation or if rotation is not successful, attempt to rotate testicle in opposite direction
- In a small percentage of cases, testis is actually laterally rotated and thus, medial rotation is needed

sections.title: Background
lines: - Sustained (> 4h) erection not associated with sexual stimulation
- May lead to erectile dysfunction and penile necrosis

sections.title: Non-Ischemic (High-Flow)
lines: - Usually self-resolves and does not require intervention
- Usually does not cause ischemia or sexual dysfunction

sections.title: Acute Ischemic Priapism (Low-Flow)
lines: - Veno-occlusion causing pooling of deoxygenated blood in cavernous tissue
- May progress to ischemia and necrosis without intervention

sections.title: Causes
lines: - Arterio-cavernosal shunt due to groin or straddle injury

sections.title: Evaluation
lines: Tests should should be performed simultaneously with and not delay definitive treatment.

sections.title: Workup
lines: - Consider penile duplex Doppler ultrasound (if acute ischemic versus non-ischemic unclear).
- Consideration of leukemia or undiagnosed sickle cell disease
- May require exchange transfusion in sickle cell disease
- Consider urinalysis/toxicologic screen if unclear etiology

sections.title: Diagnosis
lines: - Helps differentiate between high- from low-flow
- Low flow causes hypoxic, hypercarbic, and acidotic cavernosal blood gases
- Penile duplex Doppler ultrasound when the diagnosis of acute ischemic versus non-ischemic priapism is unclear.

sections.title: High-Flow Priapism
lines: - Consult urology for consideration of surgical correction or embolization by interventional radiology

sections.title: Low-Flow Priapism
lines: Conservative therapies (e.g., observation, oral medications, cold compresses, exercise) are unlikely to be successful and should not delay definitive therapies.
- Pain control (e.g., morphine) and/or penile nerve block
- Aspirate 25mL of blood from cavernosum, up to two times
- Irrigate cavernosum with 25mL of cold (10°C) saline

sections.title: Aspiration of corpus cavernosum
lines: - Risk of impotence is high even with treatment
- Prep the area with chlorhexidine and drape appropriately
- Penile nerve block or local anesthesic at puncture site
- Insert 18 gauge needle into penile shaft at 2 and 10 o'clock positions (or 3 and 9 o'clock positions)
- Aspirate blood (usually 20 - 30 cc on each side)
- May follow with intracavernosal injections (most common is phenylephrine)

sections.title: α/β-2 Agonist
lines: - Dose: 0.25-0.5mg SQ in deltoids OR 5-10mg PO, may repeat in q20min
- Dilute phenylephrine 1ml of 1mg/ml in 9mL NS for final concentration of 100mcg/mL
- For 500 mcg/ml, take 0.5 ml of 10mg/ml phenylephrine, and dilute in 9.5 cc NS
- Inject base of penis with 19-Ga needle (after blood aspiration to confirm position)
- 100-200 mcg every 3-5min (max 1000 mcg) until resolution or 1 hour
- Ensure patient fully monitored, with BP, HR, pulse oximetry
- Reflex bradycardia is expected, so consider dosages relative to toleration of drop from baseline HR
- Only one side needs to be injected since there exists a vascular channel between the 2 corpora cavernosa
- Compress injection area to prevent hematoma formation
- Use with caution in cardiovascular disease
- In pediatric population, intracavernosal injection of epinephrine instead of phenylephrine has been shown more successful in achieving detumescence
Wrap penis in elastic bandage after detumescence is achieved

sections.title: Refractory
lines: - Emergent urology consult for possible shunt procedure (can often be done in ED)

- Urology should perform a distal corporoglanular shunt, with or without tunneling, in patients with persistent acute ischemic priapism after intracavernosal phenylephrine and corporal aspiration, with or without irrigation.
- Urology should consider corporal tunneling in patients with persistent acute ischemic priapism after a distal corporoglanular shunt.

- Urology should counsel patients that there is inadequate evidence to quantify the benefit of performing a proximal shunt (of any kind) in a patient with persistent acute ischemic priapism after distal shunting.

sections.title: Sickle Cell Disease
lines: - Transfusion for goal HCT>30% with consultation for partial exchange transfusion (HGB-S<30%)
- Exchange transfusion is associated with ASPEN syndrome (Association of Sickle cell Priapism, Exchange transfusion & Neurological events)

sections.title: Disposition
lines: - Admit if refractory to treatment or need or IR or surgical intervention
- May discharge home if treatment is successful with close follow-up by urology

sections.title: Prognosis
lines: - Counsel all patients with persistent acute ischemic priapism that there is the chance of erectile dysfunction.
- Counsel patients with an acute ischemic priapism event >36 hours that the likelihood of erectile function recovery is low.
